exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 - a promise you build by hand

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB01_TaskMachinery/Ex1.cs`. Nothing in this file is an
`async` method: you are building tasks directly, the way the compiler's builder
does.

- `Promise.Deferred<T>()` returns a `(Task<T> Task, Action<T> Complete)` pair.
  The task is pending until `Complete(value)` is called, then carries `value`.
- `Promise.Immediate(int value)` returns an already-completed `Task<int>` —
  `task.IsCompletedSuccessfully` must be `true` the instant it is returned.
- `Promise.Failed(string message)` returns a `Task<int>` that is already
  faulted with an `InvalidOperationException` carrying `message`. It must be
  **returned faulted**, not thrown at the caller: `Promise.Failed("x")` on its
  own must not throw.
- `Promise.Cancelled(CancellationToken token)` returns a `Task<int>` in the
  `Canceled` state for that token.

Example:

```csharp
var (task, complete) = Promise.Deferred<string>();
task.IsCompleted   // false
complete("ok");
await task         // "ok"
```

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb01_task_machinery ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

A `Task` is not a unit of work. It is a notification that something finished,
plus a slot for the result. Nothing in this exercise runs anything — you are
just building notifications and, in one case, handing back the button that
fires it.

Start with the question "who calls `SetResult`?" and the shape of `Deferred`
falls out.

## Hint 2

```csharp
var source = new TaskCompletionSource<int>();
Task<int> task = source.Task;      // pending
source.SetResult(7);               // now completed
```

`TaskCompletionSource<T>` is exactly the promise/future split: `Task` is the
consumer half, `SetResult`/`SetException`/`SetCanceled` are the producer half.
For the other three methods the framework already has the finished forms —
look for the static factories on `Task` that build a completed, a faulted and a
cancelled task without any machinery at all.

## Hint 3

`Task.FromResult`, `Task.FromException<T>` and `Task.FromCanceled<T>` are the
three factories, and the last one needs a token that is *already* cancelled —
it throws if you hand it a live one.

The interesting decision is `Failed`. Compare these two:

```csharp
static Task<int> A(string m) => Task.FromException<int>(new InvalidOperationException(m));
static Task<int> B(string m) => throw new InvalidOperationException(m);
```

`B` throws at the call site, before the caller ever holds a task. `A` hands
back a task that will throw when awaited. The gate calls the method without
awaiting it first, so it can tell which one you wrote. Decide for yourself
which behaviour a caller writing `var t = Failed("x"); await Other(); await t;`
is expecting.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it from the caller's side. Write the four lines of consuming code you
wish existed, then implement whatever makes them compile:

```csharp
var (task, complete) = Promise.Deferred<string>();
Assert(!task.IsCompleted);
complete("ok");
Assert(await task == "ok");
```

The tuple return is a hint in itself — you must produce something that carries
the completion button separately from the task.

## Hint 2

Think about the *states* a task can be in, because the gate checks them
directly: `IsCompletedSuccessfully`, `IsFaulted`, `IsCanceled`, and the
`Status` property that names them (`RanToCompletion`, `Faulted`, `Canceled`).

Each of your four methods produces a task in a different one of those states,
and one of them starts in `WaitingForActivation` and moves. Write down which
method targets which status before you write any code; the API names you need
follow the status names closely.

## Hint 3

For the cancelled case, note that a task is `Canceled` rather than `Faulted`
only when it is completed with an `OperationCanceledException` whose
`CancellationToken` matches. That is why `Task.FromCanceled<int>(token)`
demands an already-cancelled token, and why

```csharp
Task.FromException<int>(new OperationCanceledException(token))
```

is not the same thing — it produces `Faulted`, and the gate will see the
difference. The distinction is not pedantry: `WhenAll`, ASP.NET Core logging
and every retry policy you will ever write branch on exactly that status.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 - the synchronous prefix and the cached fast path

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB01_TaskMachinery/Ex2.cs`.

An `async` method runs on the caller's thread until its first real suspension.
Prove it, then exploit it.

- `Prefix.CountAsync(Task<string> body, List<string> log)` adds `"entered"` to
  `log`, awaits `body`, adds `"resumed"`, and returns `body.Result.Length`.
  The gate calls it with a pending task and asserts that `log` already contains
  `"entered"` **before** anything is awaited — and that `"resumed"` is not
  there yet.
- `Prefix.LookupAsync(int key)` returns `Task<int>`. For `key` `0`, `1` or `2`
  it must return a **cached, already-completed** task — the same `Task<int>`
  instance every call, so `ReferenceEquals(LookupAsync(1), LookupAsync(1))` is
  `true`. For any other key it returns a task completing with `key * 10`,
  and it may allocate.
- `Prefix.WasSynchronous(Func<Task> call)` returns `true` when `call()`
  returns an already-completed task and `false` otherwise.

Example: `await Prefix.LookupAsync(2)` is `20`, and the two calls that produced
it are the identical object.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb01_task_machinery ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`CountAsync` is the easy half and the trap is in reading the requirement, not
writing the code: `"entered"` must be logged before the first `await`. Put the
statement above the `await` and the compiler does the rest — the code before
the first suspension point is in the same straight line as the call.

For `LookupAsync`, ask what "the same instance every call" rules out.
`Task.FromResult(10)` builds a new task each time it runs.

## Hint 2

```csharp
private static readonly Task<int> Zero = Task.FromResult(0);
```

A `static readonly` field is built once, at type initialisation, and handed out
for free forever after. Three of those, selected by a `switch` expression, and
your hot path allocates nothing.

For `WasSynchronous`, remember what "already completed" means on a task you
have just been handed: `IsCompleted` is `true` immediately, without awaiting.

## Hint 3

`LookupAsync` is a good place to notice that it does not need to be `async` at
all. A method returning `Task<int>` may simply `return` a task — no state
machine is generated, no builder, no boxing. Marking it `async` and writing
`return await ...` would add all three for nothing.

For the slow path you have a choice: `Task.FromResult(key * 10)` (synchronous,
still allocates a task) or an actual `async` continuation. Either satisfies the
gate. Deciding which one an API *should* do is the real content: returning a
completed task from a method whose contract says "this may do I/O" is fine;
returning one from a method that genuinely does I/O and pretending is not.

`IsCompleted` covers faulted and cancelled too. If you want "finished with a
result", `IsCompletedSuccessfully` is the narrower property — pick the one that
matches what you are actually claiming.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Approach this by asking what the gate can even see. It cannot look inside your
method; it can only observe the `log` list at moments it chooses, and the
identity of the tasks you return. So each requirement is really a statement
about *when* an observable effect happens relative to the call returning.

Draw the timeline for `CountAsync` first: call → ??? → caller gets a task →
gate completes `body` → ??? → task completes.

## Hint 2

Reference identity is a stronger requirement than equal values, and it is the
whole point of the second method. Two different `Task<int>` objects holding
`10` are not `ReferenceEquals`. So somewhere in your type there must be exactly
three long-lived objects.

Where do long-lived per-type objects live in C#? Static fields, initialised
once. A `static readonly Task<int>[]` indexed by key, or three named fields, or
a `Dictionary<int, Task<int>>` built in a static constructor — all fine; pick
the one you would want to read in six months.

## Hint 3

The interesting corner is what happens for a key outside the cache, and whether
your method should be `async`.

```csharp
public static Task<int> LookupAsync(int key) => key switch
{
    0 or 1 or 2 => Cache[key],
    _ => Task.FromResult(key * 10),
};
```

That version has no state machine anywhere. An `async` version would compile
and pass, but every call would build a builder and a task even for cache hits —
which is the exact cost this exercise exists to make visible. The BCL applies
the same trick internally for small integers and booleans, which is why
`Task.FromResult(true)` is cheaper than you would guess.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 - implement the awaiter pattern

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB01_TaskMachinery/Ex3.cs`. `await` is not defined in terms
of `Task`; it is defined in terms of a shape. Build a type that fits it.

- `Later<T>` is a class holding a value and a "ready" flag, with:
  - `LaterAwaiter<T> GetAwaiter()`
  - `void Publish(T value)` — sets the value, marks it ready, and runs any
    continuation that is waiting.
- `LaterAwaiter<T>` is a `struct` implementing `INotifyCompletion` with exactly
  the three members the compiler requires: `bool IsCompleted`,
  `void OnCompleted(Action continuation)`, `T GetResult()`.
- `Later<T>.Fail(Exception error)` marks it ready with a failure; `GetResult()`
  must then throw that exception — the original instance, not a wrapper.

Once you are done, this must compile and run in `Consume`:

```csharp
public static async Task<int> Consume(Later<int> later) => await later + 1;
```

Publishing `4` makes `Consume` return `5`. If `Publish` happens before the
`await`, no continuation is ever registered.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb01_task_machinery ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The compiler does not look for an interface on the awaited expression. It looks
for a method called `GetAwaiter` that returns something with three members. If
your type has them with the right names and signatures, `await` works; if one
name is wrong, you get a compile error that talks about "awaitable".

So the design question is only: where do you keep the value, the ready flag,
and the pending continuation?

## Hint 2

```csharp
public readonly struct LaterAwaiter<T> : INotifyCompletion
{
    private readonly Later<T> source;
    public LaterAwaiter(Later<T> source) => this.source = source;
    public bool IsCompleted => source.IsReady;
    public void OnCompleted(Action continuation) => source.Register(continuation);
    public T GetResult() => source.Read();
}
```

The awaiter is a thin, allocation-free view over the state. All the state lives
in the class, because a struct copied into the state machine cannot be the
thing that later gets mutated.

## Hint 3

Two orderings must both work, and they are the whole exercise.

If `Publish` already happened, `IsCompleted` is `true`, the compiler skips
`OnCompleted` entirely, and `GetResult` runs on the caller's thread — no
continuation, no suspension. If it has not, `OnCompleted` hands you the
continuation to store, and `Publish` must invoke it.

For the failure case, `GetResult` should rethrow the stored exception. The
plain `throw error;` resets the stack trace; the framework's own awaiters use
`ExceptionDispatchInfo.Capture(error).Throw()` to preserve it. Either passes
the gate — decide which one you would ship, and why the BCL bothered.

Left to you: whether `Publish` calls the continuation inline or queues it with
`ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem`. Inline is what the default
`TaskCompletionSource` does, and ex5 is about the trouble that causes.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Read the requirement as a state machine of its own: `Later<T>` has three
states — waiting with nobody listening, waiting with a continuation
registered, and ready. Publishing moves you to ready and, from the middle
state, must fire the stored callback.

Enumerate the transitions on paper first. The bugs in hand-written awaiters are
almost always a missing transition, not a syntax problem.

## Hint 2

Notice which member the compiler calls in which order, because it explains why
`IsCompleted` exists at all:

```
awaiter = expr.GetAwaiter();
if (awaiter.IsCompleted) goto resume;   // no allocation, no suspension
awaiter.OnCompleted(continuation);
return;
resume:
value = awaiter.GetResult();
```

`IsCompleted` is a pure optimisation hook. If you hard-coded it to `false`,
your type would still work correctly — it would just always suspend, which is
precisely what `Task.Yield()` does deliberately.

## Hint 3

The member you may be tempted to skip is `ICriticalNotifyCompletion`. The BCL's
awaiters implement both it and `INotifyCompletion`: `OnCompleted` captures
`ExecutionContext` and `UnsafeOnCompleted` does not, because the caller has
already captured it and capturing twice is waste. Implementing only
`INotifyCompletion` is correct — the compiler falls back to it — so leave that
decision to yourself once the basic version passes.

One thing not to leave to taste: a struct awaiter must not hold the mutable
state. The state machine copies your awaiter into a field; if the ready flag
lived in the struct, the copy would never see `Publish`. Keep the struct as a
pointer to the class and the problem disappears.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 - forcing a suspension with Task.Yield

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB01_TaskMachinery/Ex4.cs`.

- `Yielding.AlwaysAsync(List<string> log)` adds `"before"`, yields, adds
  `"after"`, and returns `log.Count`. The gate calls it **without awaiting**
  and asserts that the returned task is not yet completed and that `log`
  contains only `"before"`.
- `Yielding.SometimesAsync(Task<int> work, List<string> log)` adds `"before"`,
  awaits `work`, adds `"after"`. Called with an already-completed task it must
  return an already-completed task, with both entries logged — no suspension at
  all.
- `Yielding.NeverCompletesSynchronously(Func<Task> call)` returns `true` if
  `call()` returns a task that has *not* completed by the time it returns.

Expected: `NeverCompletesSynchronously(() => AlwaysAsync(log))` is `true`;
`NeverCompletesSynchronously(() => SometimesAsync(Task.FromResult(1), log))` is
`false`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb01_task_machinery ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two methods, deliberately opposite. One must never finish before it returns;
one must finish before it returns when its input is already done.

The second one needs nothing special — an `await` on a completed task simply
does not suspend. Write it plainly and it behaves. The first needs an awaitable
that is never complete.

## Hint 2

```csharp
await Task.Yield();
```

`Task.Yield()` returns a `YieldAwaitable`, whose awaiter reports
`IsCompleted => false` unconditionally. The compiler therefore always takes the
suspend branch, and the continuation is posted to the current
`SynchronizationContext` if there is one, or to the thread pool if there is not.

Note it is not a `Task` — you cannot store it in a `Task` variable or pass it
to `WhenAll`. It exists only to be awaited.

## Hint 3

Be careful with what the gate observes for `AlwaysAsync`: it holds the task and
checks the log *immediately*, so the ordering has to be guaranteed, not likely.
`await Task.Yield()` gives that guarantee because the return from `MoveNext` is
part of the same synchronous call the gate made.

`Task.Delay(0)` and `Task.CompletedTask` do **not** — the first returns an
already-completed task in current .NET, and the second obviously does. That is
the trap: a delay of zero is not a yield.

Left to you: whether `AlwaysAsync` should also work under a
`SynchronizationContext` that posts continuations back to a single thread. It
will — but the continuation would then be queued behind whatever else that
context is running, which is exactly why `Task.Yield()` in a UI event handler
lets the UI repaint.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the observable contract rather than the API. "The task is not
completed when the method returns" is a statement about the state machine: it
must have hit a suspend branch before the stub returned `builder.Task`.

Which awaitables guarantee a suspend branch? Exactly those whose awaiter says
`IsCompleted` is false. Go looking for one that says so unconditionally.

## Hint 2

There is a second way to get the same effect, worth knowing because you will
see it in older code:

```csharp
await Task.Factory.StartNew(() => { }, CancellationToken.None,
    TaskCreationOptions.None, TaskScheduler.Default);
```

That also always suspends, but it allocates a task and queues a delegate to do
nothing. `Task.Yield()` expresses the intent directly and costs a queue
operation without the task. Use the second one when a code reviewer needs to
see the reason.

## Hint 3

The subtle part is `SometimesAsync`, and specifically resisting the urge to
make it deterministic too. It is deliberately the method whose behaviour
depends on its input — completed input, synchronous completion; pending input,
suspension.

That is the state of most real async methods, and it is why the guidance
"callers must not depend on synchronous completion" exists. A caller that works
today because a cache is warm will change behaviour the day the cache misses,
and if their correctness depended on ordering, that is a production incident
with no code change attached to it. `Task.Yield()` is one blunt way to remove
the dependence during testing; a better one is to write callers that do not
have it.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 - continuation hijacking

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB01_TaskMachinery/Ex5.cs`.

By default, `TaskCompletionSource<T>.SetResult` runs every waiting continuation
**inline, on the thread that called it**, before `SetResult` returns. This
exercise makes that visible and then removes it.

- `Hijack.Inline()` returns a `TaskCompletionSource<int>` created with the
  default constructor.
- `Hijack.Detached()` returns one created with
  `TaskCreationOptions.RunContinuationsAsynchronously`.
- `Hijack.CompleteAndReport(TaskCompletionSource<int> source, List<string> log)`
  adds `"completing"` to `log`, calls `source.SetResult(1)`, adds `"completed"`,
  and returns the log's count.

The gate awaits `source.Task` in a continuation that appends `"continuation"`,
then calls `CompleteAndReport`. With `Inline()` the log ends up
`completing, continuation, completed`. With `Detached()` it is
`completing, completed` at that moment, and `"continuation"` arrives later.

- `Hijack.SafeSignalAsync(List<string> log)` must be written so that the caller
  of its completion button never runs the awaiting code. Signature:
  `(Task Task, Action Signal) SafeSignalAsync(List<string> log)`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb01_task_machinery ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The two factory methods are one argument apart. The value of this exercise is
not writing them — it is being able to state, without looking it up, what the
default does.

Say it out loud: `SetResult` does not just store a value. It walks the
continuation list and *calls* it. Your thread is now executing somebody else's
method body.

## Hint 2

```csharp
var source = new TaskCompletionSource<int>(
    TaskCreationOptions.RunContinuationsAsynchronously);
```

The non-generic `TaskCompletionSource` (added in .NET 5) takes the same option.
Note the option lives on `TaskCreationOptions` even though nothing is being
"created" in the usual sense — an artefact of reusing the enum.

For `SafeSignalAsync`, the same option is the entire answer; the shape is the
`Deferred` pair from ex1 with `Task` instead of `Task<T>`.

## Hint 3

Why this matters more than it looks. Picture a connection reader loop:

```csharp
while (true)
{
    var frame = await socket.ReadFrameAsync();
    pending[frame.Id].SetResult(frame.Payload);   // inline continuations
}
```

With the default source, `SetResult` runs the request handler's remaining code
— parsing, business logic, maybe another await that suspends — on the reader
thread, and the loop does not read the next frame until it is done. One slow
handler stalls every connection on that reader.

Worse, if `SetResult` is called while holding a lock, the continuation runs
under that lock. Take a second lock in the handler and you have inverted your
lock ordering without writing a single `lock` statement in the handler.

Left to you: whether to ever use the default. There is a real case — a hot,
short continuation where the thread hop costs more than the work — but it has
to be a decision, not the shape you got because you typed `new`.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Approach it as an ordering puzzle, ignoring the API. Three events: "completing"
logged, the awaiter's code runs, "completed" logged. Two of the six possible
orderings are achievable, and the gate names both.

If the awaiter's code can appear *between* the other two, the completion call
must be synchronously invoking it. That is your model of the default. Now find
the switch.

## Hint 2

There is a way to reason about which behaviour you have without a log at all:

```csharp
int before = Environment.CurrentManagedThreadId;
source.SetResult(1);
```

If the continuation observes the same managed thread id as the completer, it
ran inline. If it observes a pool thread's id, it was queued. Recording thread
ids is how you diagnose this in a real system where you cannot inject a log
list.

The gate uses a log because thread ids are not deterministic; your production
debugging will use the ids.

## Hint 3

There is a third option people reach for, and it is worth knowing why it is
inferior:

```csharp
Task.Run(() => source.SetResult(1));    // "get off my thread"
```

This does queue the completion, so continuations do not run on your thread. But
you have paid for a whole extra work item and a closure, and you have moved the
completion itself later in time, which changes when `IsCompleted` becomes true
for anyone polling. `RunContinuationsAsynchronously` completes the task
immediately and queues only the continuations — strictly better.

The remaining decision is scope: set the option on every `TaskCompletionSource`
you create in library code by default, or reason about each one? The BCL's own
guidance and Stephen Toub's blog both say default it on. Have your own answer
ready, because it is a common follow-up question.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 - what flows across an await

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB01_TaskMachinery/Ex6.cs`. The class holds one field:

```csharp
private static readonly AsyncLocal<string?> Correlation = new();
```

- `Ambient.SetCorrelation(string value)` assigns it.
- `Ambient.ReadAsync(Task gate)` returns the current correlation, awaits
  `gate`, and returns `$"{before}|{after}"` — the value read before the await
  and the value read after it. Both must be the value the caller set.
- `Ambient.ReadFromPoolAsync()` returns the correlation value observed inside
  `Task.Run`. It must see the caller's value.
- `Ambient.MutateInsideAsync(string value)` sets the correlation to `value`
  inside a `Task.Run` and returns what the **caller** sees afterwards — which
  is the caller's original value, not `value`.
- `Ambient.SuppressedAsync()` starts pool work with `ExecutionContext` flow
  suppressed and returns what that work observes: `null`.

Example: with correlation `"req-7"`, `ReadAsync` gives `"req-7|req-7"`,
`MutateInsideAsync("req-9")` gives `"req-7"`, `SuppressedAsync()` gives `null`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb01_task_machinery ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`AsyncLocal<T>` is not thread-local. It is *context*-local, and the context is
captured at every suspension and every work-item queue, then restored when the
continuation runs.

So the first three methods are the "it just works" cases, and your job is
mostly to write them plainly and be unsurprised. The fourth is the one with an
answer people get wrong.

## Hint 2

The rule in one line: `ExecutionContext` flows **downward**, and the copy is
made at the moment work is started or a continuation is registered.

```csharp
Correlation.Value = "a";
await Task.Run(() => { Correlation.Value = "b"; });   // writes into a copy
Console.WriteLine(Correlation.Value);                  // still "a"
```

`AsyncLocal` writes replace the current context with a modified copy for the
current logical thread of control. The caller's context is untouched, so
nothing comes back up.

## Hint 3

For the last method, the API is `ExecutionContext.SuppressFlow()`, which
returns an `AsyncFlowControl` that you must dispose to restore flow — a
`using` statement is the natural shape. Work started while flow is suppressed
gets no context at all, so `AsyncLocal` reads come back as `default`.

```csharp
using (ExecutionContext.SuppressFlow())
{
    return await Task.Run(() => Correlation.Value);
}
```

That is a real technique with a narrow use: starting long-lived background
work from inside a request, where inheriting the request's context would keep
request-scoped objects alive far longer than the request. It is also the
mechanism behind "why does my correlation id vanish in this one background
service".

Worth deciding for yourself: whether `AsyncLocal` is ever an acceptable way to
pass data *into* a call chain. It is how logging scopes and `HttpContext`
work — but it is invisible at the call site, so a method that depends on one
has a parameter it does not declare.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Try predicting all four answers before writing anything. Write them down. Then
implement, run, and see which prediction was wrong — that is the one worth
understanding, and for most people it is either the `Task.Run` read or the
mutation.

The mental model that gets all four right: think "copy-on-write dictionary
attached to the current logical call, snapshotted whenever work is scheduled".

## Hint 2

Distinguish the two contexts, because the names are close and only one is
involved here:

- `ExecutionContext` — ambient *state*: `AsyncLocal`, security context,
  culture in some hosts. Flows automatically to continuations,
  `Task.Run`, timers, and `ThreadPool.QueueUserWorkItem` (unless you use the
  `Unsafe` variants).
- `SynchronizationContext` — a *scheduler*: "post this continuation here".
  Captured by `await` unless you write `ConfigureAwait(false)`.

`ConfigureAwait(false)` does not stop `AsyncLocal` from flowing. That is a
common and confident wrong answer in interviews.

## Hint 3

The corner worth exploring after the gate passes: nested writes.

```csharp
Correlation.Value = "outer";
await Inner();          // Inner sets it to "inner" and awaits something
// back here: "outer"
```

Each async method's writes are visible to itself and everything it starts
afterwards, and invisible to its caller. That gives you a genuinely useful
property — a scope you cannot leak out of — and the surprising one that a
`finally` block cannot "restore" a value the caller never lost.

`AsyncLocal<T>` also has a `valueChangedHandler` constructor overload that
fires whenever the value changes because of a context switch. It is a debugging
tool, and reading its callback fire order is the fastest way to build an
accurate mental model of when contexts are restored.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 - Task.Run is not async

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB01_TaskMachinery/Ex7.cs`.

- `Offload.ComputeAsync(int[] values)` runs a CPU-bound sum (`values.Sum()`
  is fine) on the thread pool and returns `Task<int>`. This is the legitimate
  use of `Task.Run`.
- `Offload.Wrapped(Func<Task<int>> work)` returns `Task<Task<int>>` — the shape
  you accidentally get from `Task.Run(() => SomethingAsync())` when overload
  resolution picks the `Func<Task<int>>` as a plain result. Return it without
  unwrapping.
- `Offload.Unwrapped(Func<Task<int>> work)` returns `Task<int>` from the same
  starting point, using `.Unwrap()`.
- `Offload.Direct(Func<Task<int>> work)` returns `Task<int>` by simply calling
  `work()` — no `Task.Run` at all — because wrapping already-async work in
  `Task.Run` buys nothing on a server.
- `Offload.SameThread(Func<Task<int>> work)` returns `true` when `Direct` did
  not introduce a thread hop: it invokes `work` and reports whether the
  observed managed thread id equals the caller's.

`await Offload.Wrapped(() => Task.FromResult(3))` gives you a `Task<int>`, not
`3`. `await Offload.Unwrapped(...)` gives you `3`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb01_task_machinery ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`Task.Run` has two families of overloads: one taking `Func<TResult>` (giving
`Task<TResult>`) and one taking `Func<Task<TResult>>` (giving `Task<TResult>`,
already unwrapped). Which one you hit depends on the delegate's declared type,
and `Func<Task<int>>` matches the *first* family with `TResult = Task<int>`.

That is where `Task<Task<int>>` comes from. It is not a compiler quirk; it is
exactly what you asked for.

## Hint 2

```csharp
Task<Task<int>> nested = Task.Run<Task<int>>(() => work());
Task<int> flat = nested.Unwrap();
```

`Unwrap` is an extension on `Task<Task<T>>` (and `Task<Task>`) that returns a
proxy task completing when the inner one does, propagating its result,
exception and cancellation. `await await nested` does the same thing and reads
worse.

For `SameThread`, capture `Environment.CurrentManagedThreadId` before the call
and compare it with whatever `work` observed.

## Hint 3

The point of `Direct` is the one to take away. On ASP.NET Core, wrapping an
async call in `Task.Run` gives you: one more thread-pool queue operation, one
more delegate, a lost synchronous fast path, and — under heavy load — a
*worse* outcome, because you have doubled the number of pool work items per
request while the actual I/O still uses no thread at all.

The legitimate `Task.Run` cases are narrow: CPU-bound work invoked from a UI
thread, and CPU-bound work you deliberately want parallelised. On a server, if
something is CPU-bound, running it on the request's own pool thread is usually
right — the pool is already the pool.

Left to you: whether `ComputeAsync` should be async at all. A method whose only
asynchrony is `Task.Run` is announcing "I am CPU work someone decided to move";
some teams treat that as a code smell and make the caller do the offloading,
because the caller knows whether it has a thread to spare.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at this from the type checker. Write the four signatures first, with
`throw new NotImplementedException();` bodies, and get them to compile. The
`Task<Task<int>>` one will resist being written by accident, which is
instructive — you have to *ask* for the nesting explicitly here, whereas in
real code you get it by not looking.

Then fill the bodies in, in order.

## Hint 2

A quick way to see which overload you are getting, without reading the docs:
hover the call, or write `var x = Task.Run(() => work());` and let the IDE tell
you `x`'s type. If it says `Task<int>`, the async-aware overload won; if it
says `Task<Task<int>>`, the plain one did.

The rule: a lambda that the compiler infers as `async` (`async () => await
work()`) binds to the `Func<Task<TResult>>` overload and comes back flat. A
lambda returning an existing task binds by its declared delegate type.

## Hint 3

Two related traps worth checking after the gate passes.

`Task.Factory.StartNew(() => SomethingAsync())` has the same nesting problem
and no async-aware overload at all — it *always* gives you `Task<Task<T>>`, and
it defaults to `TaskScheduler.Current` rather than `Default`, which under a
custom scheduler is a genuinely surprising bug. `Task.Run` exists precisely
because `StartNew` had too many footguns; treat `StartNew` as legacy unless you
need `TaskCreationOptions.LongRunning`.

And `async void` lambdas: `Task.Run(async () => { await work(); })` binds to the
`Action` overload if the lambda is inferred as `async void`, giving you a task
that completes when the lambda *starts* suspending — a fire-and-forget you did
not ask for. Making the lambda return `Task` avoids it.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 - splitting the wrapper from the state machine

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB01_TaskMachinery/Ex8.cs`.

An `async` method captures *every* exception onto its returned task, including
argument validation that should have blown up at the call site. Fix it by
splitting.

- `Split.Bad(string? name, Task<int> work)` is the wrong version: an `async`
  method that throws `ArgumentException` for a null-or-empty `name` and then
  awaits `work`. Calling `Split.Bad(null, pending)` must **not** throw; the
  returned task must be faulted.
- `Split.Good(string? name, Task<int> work)` is a **non-async** method that
  validates eagerly — `Split.Good(null, pending)` throws
  `ArgumentException` at the call site — and otherwise returns
  `GoodCoreAsync(name, work)`.
- `Split.GoodCoreAsync(string name, Task<int> work)` is the private async core
  returning `name.Length + await work`.
- `Split.NoStateMachine(int value)` returns `Task<int>` for a method that never
  awaits anything: return a completed task directly rather than marking the
  method `async`.

The gate calls each method without awaiting and records whether the call threw
or the task faulted.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb01_task_machinery ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The difference between the two versions is one keyword and one extra method.
`async` means "capture everything into the task"; no `async` means "this is an
ordinary method that happens to return a task, and it throws like any other
method".

Write `Good` with no `async` on it and let the compiler tell you what it needs.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public static Task<int> Good(string? name, Task<int> work)
{
    ArgumentException.ThrowIfNullOrEmpty(name);     // throws here, at the call site
    return GoodCoreAsync(name, work);               // the async part
}

private static async Task<int> GoodCoreAsync(string name, Task<int> work) =>
    name.Length + await work;
```

`ArgumentException.ThrowIfNullOrEmpty` is the .NET 8 helper and it also
performs the null-state analysis, so `name` is non-nullable after it — which is
why the core can take a plain `string`.

`NoStateMachine` is the same trick with nothing to validate: drop `async`,
`return Task.FromResult(value);`.

## Hint 3

When the split is worth it: any public API where a caller could reasonably pass
a bad argument, and any API where the failure should be attributable to the
call rather than the await. When it is not worth it: private helpers whose
arguments are already validated, where the extra method is noise.

There is a second, sharper reason to know the difference, and it is where async
elision goes wrong:

```csharp
public static Task<int> Elided(Stream stream)
{
    using var reader = new StreamReader(stream);
    return ReadCoreAsync(reader);        // BUG: reader is disposed on return
}
```

Dropping `async`/`await` removes your frame from the stack trace and — with a
`using` or `try`/`finally` in scope — changes *when* the block exits. Elide
only when there is no enclosing `using`, `try` or `lock`. The validation
wrapper is safe precisely because it has none of those.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about what the caller's code looks like at the moment of failure:

```csharp
var t = Split.Bad(null, pending);   // no exception here
await SomethingElse();               // ...time passes...
await t;                             // ArgumentException surfaces here
```

Everything between the call and the await is time during which the caller
believes their arguments were fine. Sometimes that gap is milliseconds;
sometimes the task is stored in a list and awaited at the end of a batch, and
the stack trace points at the wrong place entirely.

The exercise is about closing that gap.

## Hint 2

A useful way to test which behaviour you have, in your own code, with no gate:

```csharp
Task<int> t;
try { t = Method(bad); }
catch (ArgumentException) { /* eager */ }
```

If the `catch` runs, validation is eager. If instead you reach the assignment
and only `await t` throws, it is deferred onto the task. The gate does exactly
this.

## Hint 3

Two variations worth thinking through once it passes.

**Iterators have the same problem.** A method with `yield return` validates
nothing until the first `MoveNext`, for the same reason — it is a state machine
too. The same wrapper split is the standard fix, and LINQ's own operators are
written that way throughout.

**`ValueTask` changes the calculus slightly.** For a method returning
`ValueTask<T>`, the wrapper split still works, but the next sector will show
you that the fast path matters more there, and a wrapper that returns
`new ValueTask<T>(cachedResult)` for the common case avoids the state machine
entirely — which is the same idea as `NoStateMachine` here, one level of
optimisation further along.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge - build an AsyncManualResetEvent

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB01_TaskMachinery/Challenge.cs`. Build the async
equivalent of `ManualResetEventSlim` out of the pieces from this sector: a gate
that many callers can await, that can be set, and that can be reset and used
again.

```csharp
public sealed class AsyncManualResetEvent
{
    public AsyncManualResetEvent(bool initiallySet);
    public bool IsSet { get; }
    public Task WaitAsync(CancellationToken token = default);
    public void Set();
    public void Reset();
}
```

Required behaviour:

- `WaitAsync` on a set event returns an already-completed task — no
  suspension, no allocation of a new source.
- `WaitAsync` on an unset event returns a pending task; `Set()` completes
  **every** waiter.
- `Set()` must not run any waiter's continuation on the calling thread.
- `Reset()` after `Set()` makes subsequent `WaitAsync` calls pend again;
  waiters who already completed are unaffected.
- A cancelled token cancels **that waiter only** — the returned task ends
  `Canceled`, other waiters keep waiting, and the registration is disposed so
  a long-lived token does not accumulate callbacks.
- `Set()` called twice is not an error; `Set()` with no waiters is not an error.

Example: two waiters pending, `Set()` completes both; `Reset()`; a third
`WaitAsync` pends again.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb01_task_machinery challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

There is one piece of state that does all the work: a
`TaskCompletionSource` representing "the current generation of waiters".
`WaitAsync` hands out its `Task`. `Set()` completes it. `Reset()` replaces it
with a fresh one.

Everything else — the set state, the already-completed fast path — can be
derived from that single field if you choose the representation carefully.

## Hint 2

```csharp
private volatile TaskCompletionSource source =
    new(TaskCreationOptions.RunContinuationsAsynchronously);

public bool IsSet => source.Task.IsCompleted;

public Task WaitAsync(CancellationToken token = default)
{
    Task current = source.Task;
    if (current.IsCompleted || !token.CanBeCanceled) return current;
    return current.WaitAsync(token);
}

public void Set() => source.TrySetResult();
```

`Reset` is the interesting one: replacing the field is easy, but two threads
resetting at once must not leave two different generations visible. An
`Interlocked.CompareExchange` that only swaps when the current source is
completed gives you that.

`TrySetResult` rather than `SetResult` because a double `Set()` must not throw.

## Hint 3

The cancellation requirement has a cheap correct answer and an instructive
hand-rolled one.

`Task.WaitAsync(CancellationToken)` (.NET 6+) gives you a task that completes
when either the original completes or the token fires, and it registers and
disposes the registration internally. That satisfies the requirement, and it is
what you should ship.

The hand-rolled version is worth writing once to see the shape:

```csharp
var waiter = new TaskCompletionSource(TaskCreationOptions.RunContinuationsAsynchronously);
CancellationTokenRegistration registration = token.Register(
    static state => ((TaskCompletionSource)state!).TrySetCanceled(), waiter);
_ = current.ContinueWith(...);   // complete the waiter when the gate opens
// and dispose the registration in both paths
```

Every line there is a leak or a race if you get it wrong: forgetting to dispose
the registration keeps the waiter alive as long as the token lives; using
`SetCanceled` instead of `TrySetCanceled` throws when both happen at once.

Left to you: whether `WaitAsync` should return `Task.CompletedTask` for the
already-set case instead of the source's task. Both are correct; one of them
tells the caller slightly less about your internals.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Enumerate the states and the transitions before you write a field. There are
two states (set, unset) and three operations, so six cells in the table — and
two of them (Set on set, Reset on unset) must be no-ops rather than errors,
which is exactly what "manual reset event" means.

Fill the table in, then ask what single piece of data distinguishes the two
states. If your answer needs both a `bool` and a task, you probably have a race
between them.

## Hint 2

The single-field trick is the one to reach for: a completed task *is* the set
state. That removes the possibility of the flag and the task disagreeing, which
is the classic bug in hand-rolled events — a waiter that arrives between "flag
set to true" and "task completed" and pends forever.

If you do keep two fields, the ordering rules are: set the flag *after*
completing the task, and check the task *before* the flag on the read side, and
now you are writing memory-ordering code by hand, which is the seventh
sector's problem, not this one's. Prefer the one field.

## Hint 3

The requirement most people miss is "waiters who already completed are
unaffected by `Reset`". That is automatic with the generation model: a
completed `Task` is immutable, so a waiter holding one is holding a finished
object no matter what you do to the field afterwards.

It is *not* automatic if you try to reuse one `TaskCompletionSource` across
resets — there is no un-complete operation, which is precisely why the
generation swap exists. `ManualResetValueTaskSourceCore<T>` in the next sector
does support reuse, via a version token that invalidates old waiters; note the
difference in guarantees. Reuse is an optimisation you buy with a stricter
contract on the consumer, every single time.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 - reading the trace

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB01_TaskMachinery/Review1.cs`. No new API here: the
question is whether you can predict, and then produce, an exact execution
order.

Implement `Trace.RunAsync(TaskCompletionSource<int> gate, List<string> log)`
so that calling it (without awaiting) and then completing `gate` produces
exactly this log:

```
start
sync-work
suspended        <- appended by the CALLER, after RunAsync returns
resumed
done
```

That is: `"start"` and `"sync-work"` must be written during the call itself;
nothing else may be. After the caller appends `"suspended"` and completes the
gate, the method resumes and appends `"resumed"` then `"done"`.

Also implement:

- `Trace.OrderOf(Func<List<string>, Task> body)` — runs `body` with a fresh
  log, waits for it, and returns the log joined with `","`.
- `Trace.ContinuationRanInline(TaskCompletionSource<int> gate)` — attaches a
  continuation that records its thread id, completes `gate`, and returns
  `true` if the continuation ran on the completing thread.
- `Trace.NeverSuspends(Task<int> completed, List<string> log)` — an async
  method awaiting an already-completed task, whose whole body therefore runs
  synchronously; `OrderOf` over it shows every entry present the instant it
  returns.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb01_task_machinery review1
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Take the trace and mark each line with who wrote it and on which side of the
suspension. Two of the five are the caller's; three are yours; the boundary is
exactly one `await`.

If you can draw that boundary correctly you have the method. If you cannot, the
thing to re-read is not this exercise but the fact that a method's *return* and
its *completion* are two different events separated by however long the awaited
thing takes.

## Hint 2

Test your understanding with a prediction before you run anything: what would
the log be if you moved `"sync-work"` to after the `await`? What if you awaited
`Task.CompletedTask` first, and *then* the gate? What if you replaced the
`await` with `gate.Task.GetAwaiter().GetResult()`?

The third is the interesting one: it produces a deadlock or a blocked thread,
because the caller is now inside your method waiting for something the caller
was going to complete after you returned.

## Hint 3

`NeverSuspends` closes the loop with ex2 and ex4. An async method awaiting an
already-completed task runs end-to-end inside the call, because every
`IsCompleted` check comes back true and no branch ever returns early.

That is a *behavioural* difference visible to callers, which is why "do not
depend on synchronous completion" is guidance rather than pedantry — the same
method is synchronous or not depending on its inputs, and a caller whose
correctness rests on the ordering breaks when a cache goes cold.

If you want to see the two shapes side by side, run `OrderOf` over
`NeverSuspends` and over `RunAsync` with an already-completed gate. Identical
source shape, identical result, different timing — and only one of them ever
returned control to the caller mid-method.

lessons.title: V3·CB1 — The Task machinery: what async really compiles to
lessons.summary: You have written async methods that work. This sector takes the lid off: the state machine the compiler emits, the awaiter pattern that makes await extensible, where continuations actually run, and why a TaskCompletionSource can hijack the thread that completed it.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·CB1 — The Task machinery: what async really compiles to

The earlier async sector gave you the working model: `await` suspends, the
thread goes back to the pool, the method resumes when the result arrives. That
model is enough to write correct request handlers, and most engineers never
need more. It is not enough to debug a hang, to explain why a stack trace has
`MoveNext` in it, to reason about `AsyncLocal`, or to answer the question every
senior interview eventually asks: what does the compiler actually emit?

So take the lid off. There is no magic in `async`. There is a source-to-source
transformation, one interface, one builder type, and a duck-typed pattern that
the language looks for by name. Everything else — `Task`, `ValueTask`,
`Task.Yield`, the awaitables in third-party libraries — is built on top of
those pieces by ordinary code you could have written yourself.

**The transformation.** An `async` method is not a method any more once the
compiler is done with it. Its body moves into a generated struct implementing
`IAsyncStateMachine`, with a single `MoveNext()` containing your code chopped
into segments at each `await`, dispatched by an integer state field. Every
local that lives across an `await` becomes a field on that struct, because
locals on a stack frame cannot survive a return and an async method *returns*
at its first real suspension. What is left of your original method is a stub:
create the state machine, hand it an `AsyncTaskMethodBuilder<T>`, call
`MoveNext()` once, return `builder.Task`.

Two consequences fall straight out, and both are testable behaviour rather than
trivia. First, **the code before the first await runs synchronously on the
calling thread**. A caller that does `var t = LoadAsync(); DoSomethingElse();`
has already executed your argument validation, your cache lookup and your log
line before it gets its task back. Second, **an async method that never
actually suspends never allocates a state machine on the heap and never
involves another thread at all**. The struct stays on the stack, the builder
hands back a cached completed task, and the whole call is as cheap as a normal
method plus a branch. That is the "fast path", and library authors bend over
backwards to preserve it.

**The awaiter pattern.** `await x` is not defined in terms of `Task`. The
compiler looks for a method `GetAwaiter()` on `x` — instance or extension —
returning a type that implements `INotifyCompletion` and exposes
`bool IsCompleted`, `void OnCompleted(Action)` and `T GetResult()`. That is
all. `Task<T>` satisfies it, `ValueTask<T>` satisfies it, `Task.Yield()`
returns a `YieldAwaitable` that satisfies it, and so can a type you write this
afternoon. The generated code reads roughly:

```csharp
var awaiter = x.GetAwaiter();
if (!awaiter.IsCompleted)                 // the fast path skips everything
{
    state = 0;
    builder.AwaitUnsafeOnCompleted(ref awaiter, ref this);   // may box the struct
    return;                               // control goes back to the caller
}
result = awaiter.GetResult();             // rethrows the original exception
```

`IsCompleted` being true is the whole optimisation: a completed task means no
boxing, no continuation delegate, no scheduling, just a straight-line read.
`GetResult()` is also where the exception unwrapping lives — it is the reason
`await` gives you an `InvalidOperationException` where `.Result` gives you an
`AggregateException` wrapping one. Different method, different contract.

**Where continuations run.** When the awaiter is not complete, the builder
registers a continuation. Where that continuation eventually executes depends
on the awaited thing, the captured `SynchronizationContext` or `TaskScheduler`,
and — most surprisingly — on who completes it. The default `TaskCompletionSource`
runs its continuations **synchronously, inline, on the thread that called
`SetResult`**. That is a performance decision (it avoids a thread hop) that
turns into a correctness disaster the moment your `SetResult` happens under a
lock, or on a socket-reading thread, or inside a loop that expected to keep
going. The fix is one flag —
`TaskCreationOptions.RunContinuationsAsynchronously` — and knowing it is a real
dividing line between engineers who have debugged an async production system
and engineers who have not.

**What flows across the gap.** The state machine does not carry your thread
with it, so anything thread-local is gone after an `await`. What survives is
`ExecutionContext`, which .NET captures at the suspension point and restores at
the resumption point. `AsyncLocal<T>` rides on that context, which is why an
`AsyncLocal` value set before an await is visible after it, and visible inside
work you start, but a value set *inside* that started work is not visible to
the caller afterwards. The context is copy-on-write and flows downward only.
Correlation ids work; using `AsyncLocal` as a mutable out-parameter does not.

**And what `Task.Run` is not.** `Task.Run` queues a delegate to the thread
pool. That is orthogonal to `async`: it is how you get CPU-bound work off the
current thread, and it does nothing useful for work that is already
asynchronous. `Task.Run(async () => await client.GetAsync(url))` burns a pool
thread to start something that would not have needed one, and the innocent-
looking `Task.Run(() => LoadAsync())` gives you a `Task<Task<string>>` unless
you unwrap it. The compiler's overload resolution saves you from the second one
most of the time; it will not save you from the first.

One more thing worth setting straight before you start, because it decides how
you read everything below: a `Task` is not a unit of work. It is a notification
that something has finished, with a slot for the result and a list of people to
tell. Some tasks happen to have work attached — the ones `Task.Run` creates —
but most tasks in a real service have no work and no thread anywhere: they are
promises that a network card will eventually interrupt. Once that lands, the
whole API stops looking arbitrary, and questions like "which thread is my task
running on" resolve into "none, that is the point".

Every exercise here is deterministic. Nothing sleeps, nothing races: the gates
drive completion with `TaskCompletionSource` and observe ordering with counters
and recorded thread ids, because a test that depends on timing teaches you the
wrong lesson about a mechanism that has no timing in it.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - csharp/v3cb01_task_machinery

## Notes

**`IAsyncStateMachine` is one interface with two methods.** `MoveNext()` and
`SetStateMachine(IAsyncStateMachine)`. The generated type is a `struct` in
release builds and a `class` in debug builds — that difference exists purely so
the debugger can watch it. The struct is boxed onto the heap exactly once, the
first time the method actually suspends, by
`AwaitUnsafeOnCompleted`. A method that never suspends is never boxed. When
people say "async allocates", this is the allocation they mean, and it is
conditional.

**Hoisted locals explain confusing stack traces and captures.** Because locals
that cross an `await` become fields, they are kept alive for the entire
suspension — including large buffers you thought were scoped to a block. If a
`byte[64 * 1024]` is in scope across a long await, it is rooted for that whole
time. Narrowing the scope of a local so it dies before the `await` is a real,
measurable memory optimisation in high-fan-out services.

**The builder is a policy object.** `AsyncTaskMethodBuilder<T>` creates the
task, plumbs `SetResult`/`SetException`, and decides how continuations attach.
You can substitute a different one with `[AsyncMethodBuilder(typeof(...))]`,
which is how `IAsyncEnumerable` methods, `ValueTask` pooling and library types
like `UniTask` work. The language provides the transformation; the builder
provides the semantics.

**`IsCompleted` is the whole fast path.** A method whose awaits are usually
already complete costs almost nothing. This is why `Stream.ReadAsync` on a
buffered stream, or a cache-hit lookup, can be async and still allocate zero.
It is also why you should not "optimise" by returning `Task.FromResult` from a
method that genuinely does I/O — you have moved the cost, not removed it.

**`Task.Yield` is the one awaitable that is never complete.** `IsCompleted`
returns `false` unconditionally, so the awaiting method always suspends and its
continuation is posted to the current context or the pool. Use it to break up a
long synchronous stretch inside an async method, or to force a method that
sometimes completes synchronously to always behave the same way — the latter is
mostly a testing tool.

**`TaskCompletionSource` completes on your thread unless you say otherwise.**
`SetResult` walks the continuation list and invokes it inline. So the caller of
`SetResult` executes arbitrary foreign code: the awaiting method's remainder,
and that method's caller's remainder, and so on until something genuinely
suspends. Inside a lock, that is a deadlock waiting for a lock ordering
mistake. On a dedicated I/O thread it is a stall of the entire receive loop.
`RunContinuationsAsynchronously` costs one thread-pool queue operation and
removes the whole category.

**`ExecutionContext` flows, `SynchronizationContext` is captured.** Two
different things with confusingly similar names. `ExecutionContext` carries
ambient state — `AsyncLocal`, impersonation, and so on — and flows to
continuations and to `Task.Run` delegates automatically. `SynchronizationContext`
answers "where should this continuation run", and `await` captures it only if
one is current. Suppressing the first is `ExecutionContext.SuppressFlow()`;
opting out of the second is `ConfigureAwait(false)`.

## ex1

Building a `Task<T>` by hand is the exercise that makes "a task is just a
promise" concrete. `TaskCompletionSource<T>` is a task plus the two buttons
that finish it. No thread, no scheduler, no work — a task is not a unit of
work, it is a notification that something has happened.

The already-completed and already-faulted forms matter for a practical reason:
`Task.FromResult` and `Task.FromException<T>` let a non-async method satisfy an
async signature with no state machine at all. And `Task.FromException` *returns*
a failure rather than throwing one, which is the behaviour a caller holding a
`Task` expects. Throwing eagerly from a `Task`-returning method is legal and
occasionally correct, but it surprises anyone who wrote
`var t = Foo(); await Bar(); await t;`.

## ex2

The synchronous prefix is where a whole class of bugs lives. Argument
validation, cache lookups and `ObjectDisposedException` checks placed after the
first `await` fire at a time the caller cannot predict, and the exception lands
on the task rather than at the call site. Placing them before the first await
does not fix that — the method is still async, so everything is captured onto
the task. Only splitting into a non-async wrapper does.

The cached-completed-task trick is worth internalising. `Task.FromResult(0)`
allocates; `Task.CompletedTask` and a `static readonly Task<int> Zero` do not.
For the common values in a hot API — zero, empty string, `true`/`false` — a
static cached task is free. The BCL does this internally for small `int`s and
for booleans.

## ex3

Writing an awaiter by hand takes `await` from "keyword" to "pattern". Three
members, one interface, and the compiler is satisfied. Notice what your awaiter
controls: whether to suspend at all (`IsCompleted`), where the continuation
runs (`OnCompleted` — you choose whether to post it somewhere or invoke it
inline), and what the result of the expression is (`GetResult`, including
throwing).

`ICriticalNotifyCompletion.UnsafeOnCompleted` is the second half of the
contract: it is `OnCompleted` without `ExecutionContext` capture, used by
infrastructure that captures the context itself. Implementing only
`INotifyCompletion` is correct and safe; implementing both is what the BCL
awaiters do to avoid capturing twice.

## ex4

Forcing asynchrony is a niche need with two real uses. One: you are holding a
lock or running on a thread you must release, and you want the rest of the
method elsewhere. Two: you are writing a test or a library API whose callers
must not be able to depend on synchronous completion, because that dependence
is a latent bug — a method that completes synchronously today and asynchronously
after a config change will break a caller who relied on ordering.

`await Task.Yield()` inside a loop is also the crude way to keep a long CPU
loop from monopolising a thread, though `Parallel` or a dedicated thread is
almost always the better answer. Yielding does not lower your priority; it just
gives other queued work a turn.

## Further reading

- [Async in depth](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/async-in-depth) — what happens during an I/O wait, and why no thread is involved.
- [How async/await really works in C#](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/how-async-await-really-works/) — Stephen Toub walks the generated state machine line by line.
- [`TaskCompletionSource`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.tasks.taskcompletionsource-1) — the promise half of the task API.
- [`INotifyCompletion`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.runtime.compilerservices.inotifycompletion) — the awaiter contract in one page.
- [`AsyncLocal<T>` and ExecutionContext](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/pfxteam/executioncontext-vs-synchronizationcontext/) — the two contexts, told apart properly.

# V3·CB1 — The Task machinery: what async really compiles to

`async` is a compile-time rewrite, not a runtime feature. Understanding the
rewrite converts a set of memorised rules ("don't block", "don't use async
void") into consequences you can derive. This sector walks the machinery and
then makes you build pieces of it.

## Concept 1 — the state machine

The compiler moves your method body into a generated type implementing
`IAsyncStateMachine`, and leaves behind a stub:

```csharp
// what you wrote
public static async Task<int> CountAsync(Task<string> body)
{
    string text = await body;
    return text.Length;
}

// roughly what the compiler emits
public static Task<int> CountAsync(Task<string> body)
{
    var sm = new <CountAsync>d__0
    {
        body = body,
        builder = AsyncTaskMethodBuilder<int>.Create(),
        state = -1,
    };
    sm.builder.Start(ref sm);      // calls MoveNext() once, synchronously
    return sm.builder.Task;
}
```

`MoveNext()` is a `switch` on `state`. Segment 0 runs up to the first `await`,
grabs an awaiter, and either falls straight through (awaiter already complete)
or stores the state, registers a continuation and returns.

**Consequences to keep:** code before the first await runs on the caller's
thread; locals crossing an await become fields and stay alive; a method that
never suspends never boxes the state machine.

## Concept 2 — the awaiter pattern

```csharp
public readonly struct Ready<T> { public T Value { get; init; }
    public Awaiter<T> GetAwaiter() => new(Value); }

public readonly struct Awaiter<T> : INotifyCompletion
{
    private readonly T value;
    public Awaiter(T value) => this.value = value;
    public bool IsCompleted => true;              // never suspend
    public void OnCompleted(Action continuation) => continuation();
    public T GetResult() => value;
}
```

`await new Ready<int> { Value = 7 }` now compiles. `await` is structural, not
nominal — which is why `ValueTask`, `YieldAwaitable`, `ConfiguredTaskAwaitable`
and library types all work without any special-casing in the language.

## Concept 3 — continuation scheduling

```csharp
var tcs = new TaskCompletionSource<int>();        // dangerous default
var tcs2 = new TaskCompletionSource<int>(
    TaskCreationOptions.RunContinuationsAsynchronously);   // what you want
```

With the first, `tcs.SetResult(1)` executes the awaiting method's remainder
*before returning*. Whoever called `SetResult` is now running foreign code, on
their thread, possibly under their lock. With the second, the continuation is
queued and `SetResult` returns immediately.

Use the default only when you have deliberately decided that inline completion
is what you want, and you control both sides.

## Concept 4 — ExecutionContext and AsyncLocal

```csharp
static readonly AsyncLocal<string> Correlation = new();

Correlation.Value = "req-42";
await SomethingAsync();          // still "req-42" here
await Task.Run(() => Correlation.Value);   // "req-42" — context was captured
// but a write inside that Task.Run is NOT visible out here
```

The context is captured at suspension and restored at resumption, copy-on-write.
Flow is downward. This is exactly the right shape for correlation ids and
exactly the wrong shape for returning data.

## Concept 5 — Task.Run is a different tool

`Task.Run` means "put this delegate on the thread pool". Use it for CPU-bound
work called from a UI thread. Do not use it to "make" an async method async, do
not wrap library calls in it on a server (you have added a queue hop and stolen
a pool thread), and remember `Task.Run(() => SomethingAsync())` returns
`Task<Task<T>>` when overload resolution does not pick the `Func<Task<T>>`
overload — `.Unwrap()` or an `async` lambda fixes it.

## Worked example — reading the generated shape

Take a method with a loop, because loops are where the state machine stops
being obvious:

```csharp
public static async Task<int> SumAsync(IReadOnlyList<Task<int>> work)
{
    int total = 0;
    foreach (Task<int> item in work)
        total += await item;
    return total;
}
```

`total` crosses an await, so it becomes a field. The enumerator crosses an
await, so it becomes a field too — which is why an async iteration over a
struct enumerator boxes it, and why `foreach` over a `List<T>` inside an async
method costs slightly more than outside one. There is one state, not one per
iteration: `MoveNext` re-enters at the same label and the loop variable lives
in the machine.

Now the failure mode this shape invites. That method awaits each task in turn,
which is correct here — the tasks were already running — but the identical
shape over a *factory* serialises everything:

```csharp
foreach (int id in ids)
    total += await LoadAsync(id);          // one round trip at a time
```

The state machine is not the problem; the placement of the call is. Start
everything, then await:

```csharp
Task<int>[] started = ids.Select(LoadAsync).ToArray();   // ToArray: enumerate once
total = (await Task.WhenAll(started)).Sum();
```

The `ToArray` matters: `Select` is lazy, and enumerating the query twice starts
every request twice.

## Worked example — a completed task costs nothing

```csharp
// suspends: boxes the state machine, allocates a delegate, queues a continuation
await Task.Delay(1);

// does not suspend: one branch, no allocation beyond the (cached) task
await Task.CompletedTask;
```

Both lines compile to the same `GetAwaiter`/`IsCompleted`/`GetResult` sequence.
The second one never reaches `AwaitUnsafeOnCompleted`, so none of the async
machinery's cost is paid. That single branch is what makes it reasonable for
the BCL to make everything async: the abstraction is free when it is not
needed.

## Common mistakes

1. **Validating arguments inside the async method.** The exception lands on the
   task, not at the call site. Split: non-async wrapper validates, async core
   does the work.
2. **Assuming await means another thread.** It does not. For I/O, no thread is
   involved during the wait at all.
3. **Default `TaskCompletionSource` in library code.** Inline continuations on
   the completing thread; a stall or a deadlock waiting to be discovered.
4. **`Task.Run(async () => await X())` on a server.** Pure overhead.
5. **Holding big buffers across awaits.** Hoisted locals are rooted for the
   whole suspension.
6. **Expecting `AsyncLocal` writes to flow back up.** They do not.
7. **`.Result` anywhere.** Blocks a thread and wraps exceptions; under a
   synchronization context it deadlocks outright.

## Interview angle

> "What does the compiler do with `async`?"

Rewrites the method into a state machine type implementing
`IAsyncStateMachine`; locals that live across awaits become fields; each await
becomes "get awaiter, check `IsCompleted`, either continue or store state,
register a continuation and return". The visible method becomes a stub that
starts the machine and returns `builder.Task`. Two things follow immediately:
the prefix before the first await is synchronous on the caller's thread, and a
method that never suspends allocates nothing extra.

Follow-ups worth having an answer to: how `await` is duck-typed (`GetAwaiter`,
`IsCompleted`, `OnCompleted`, `GetResult`); why `await` throws the original
exception where `.Result` throws `AggregateException` (different methods:
`GetResult` uses `ExceptionDispatchInfo`); and what
`RunContinuationsAsynchronously` prevents.

## Check yourself

1. Where does the code before the first `await` run?
2. When is the state machine boxed onto the heap?
3. Name the four members the compiler looks for to await a type.
4. What does `Task.Yield()`'s awaiter return from `IsCompleted`, and why?
5. Why does `await` throw a different exception type than `.Result`?
6. What thread runs a continuation after `tcs.SetResult(x)` by default?
7. Which context carries `AsyncLocal` values — and which one decides where a
   continuation runs?
8. Why does a write to an `AsyncLocal` inside `Task.Run` not affect the caller?
9. What is the type of `Task.Run(() => FooAsync())` if `FooAsync` returns
   `Task<int>` and overload resolution picks `Func<Task<int>>`? What if it does
   not?
10. Why can a large local array across an await increase peak memory?
11. Give a case where `Task.FromResult` is the right implementation and a case
    where it is a lie.
12. How would you force a sometimes-synchronous method to always yield?

# Reading - csharp/v3cb01_task_machinery

## How the rewrite came to be

C# 5 did not invent asynchronous programming; it invented a way to write it
that reads like the synchronous version. Before it, .NET had the Asynchronous
Programming Model (`BeginRead`/`EndRead`, `IAsyncResult`), then the
Event-based Asynchronous Pattern (`DownloadStringCompleted`), and both had the
same fatal property: control flow was inverted, so loops, `try`/`finally` and
`using` could not be expressed without either a hand-written state machine or a
tangle of nested callbacks. The Task-based Asynchronous Pattern plus `await`
kept ordinary control flow and moved the state machine into the compiler.

The mechanism was not new either. C# 2 already generated state machines for
iterators — `yield return` does the same trick with `IEnumerator.MoveNext`.
`async` reuses the idea with a different driver: instead of the consumer
calling `MoveNext`, a completed awaiter's continuation calls it. That kinship
is worth holding on to, because it is exactly the pair that `IAsyncEnumerable`
later fused: an async iterator's state machine is driven by *both*.

## The pieces, precisely

The generated type implements `IAsyncStateMachine`, holds the builder, the
state integer, the hoisted locals and a slot per pending awaiter. The builder —
`AsyncVoidMethodBuilder`, `AsyncTaskMethodBuilder`, `AsyncTaskMethodBuilder<T>`,
`AsyncValueTaskMethodBuilder<T>`, or one you supply with `[AsyncMethodBuilder]`
— owns the promise and the completion semantics. The awaiter is whatever
`GetAwaiter()` returned.

The first `MoveNext()` runs on the caller's thread, synchronously, inside
`builder.Start`. If the method reaches its end without suspending, the builder
calls `SetResult` before `Start` even returns, and the task the stub returns is
already completed. The struct never left the stack; the only allocation is the
task itself, and builders cache tasks for `void`-like and common cases. If the
method does suspend, `AwaitUnsafeOnCompleted` boxes the struct, stores the box
in the builder, and hooks a continuation that calls `MoveNext` on the box.

`GetResult()` is where the ergonomics live. For `Task`, it uses
`ExceptionDispatchInfo` to rethrow the stored exception with its original stack
trace, appending the current one rather than replacing it. `.Result` and
`.Wait()` go through a different path that wraps in `AggregateException`,
because a task can hold several exceptions and those APIs predate `await`.

## Where continuations run, in full

Three questions, answered in order, decide the resumption thread.

1. **Did the await capture a context?** `await task` captures
   `SynchronizationContext.Current` if non-null, otherwise
   `TaskScheduler.Current` if not the default. `ConfigureAwait(false)` skips
   the capture. ASP.NET Core installs no `SynchronizationContext`; WPF,
   WinForms and old ASP.NET do.
2. **Was the awaited thing already complete when awaited?** Then there is no
   continuation at all — execution simply continues on the current thread.
3. **Who completed it, and how?** For a `TaskCompletionSource` without
   `RunContinuationsAsynchronously`, the completer's thread runs the
   continuation inline. For a socket completion, an I/O completion port thread
   does. For `Task.Delay`, a timer thread queues it.

The failure mode of inline continuations is not subtle once you have seen it: a
message-loop thread calls `SetResult` for a reply, the awaiting request handler
resumes *on that loop thread*, does a database call, and the entire connection
stops reading. Libraries default to `RunContinuationsAsynchronously` for that
reason, and so should you unless the inline hop is measured and wanted.

## Why the transformation is a struct, and why that matters

The generated state machine is a `struct` in release builds. That is not an
implementation detail you can ignore, because it explains the whole cost model.
A struct lives on the stack of whoever called `MoveNext`, so a method that runs
to completion without suspending never puts anything on the heap. Only
`AwaitUnsafeOnCompleted` — reached exactly once, at the first genuine
suspension — copies it to the heap and hands the builder a reference. From then
on, every resumption operates on the boxed copy.

This is why "async allocates one object per call" is a half-truth. It allocates
one object per call *that suspends*, plus the task itself, plus one delegate.
Methods whose awaits are usually complete pay for none of that. It is also why
debug builds behave differently in a profiler: the compiler emits a class there
so the debugger can inspect the machine across the suspension, and your
allocation counts go up accordingly. Never benchmark async code in a debug
build; the numbers describe a different program.

The `SetStateMachine` member exists for exactly this transition. When the
struct is boxed, the builder needs a reference to the *boxed* copy, not the
stack one, and `SetStateMachine` is the callback that hands it over. You will
never call it; you will see it in decompiled output and in stack traces, and
now you know what it is for.

## Performance notes

The async machinery is cheap but not free. Per suspension you pay: one boxing
allocation for the state machine (once per invocation, not once per await), one
`Action` delegate, one `MoveNextRunner` in some paths, and a queue operation.
Per *non-suspending* invocation you pay a branch and possibly a cached task.

The optimisations that actually move numbers, in order:

- **Preserve the synchronous path.** Cache hits, buffered reads, and short-
  circuit returns should not suspend. `IsCompleted` does the rest.
- **Cache completed tasks** for common results: `Task.CompletedTask`, static
  `Task<bool>` for true/false, `Task.FromResult` hoisted to a field.
- **Return `ValueTask<T>`** from APIs that usually complete synchronously —
  the next sector — but only after measuring.
- **Shrink hoisted state.** Scope large locals so they die before the await;
  pass small structs rather than capturing whole closures.
- **Avoid `Task.Run` on servers.** Every hop is a queue and a cache miss.

The number worth remembering: an awaited-and-suspended async call is on the
order of tens of nanoseconds of overhead plus an allocation. Utterly
irrelevant next to a 2 ms database call; very relevant in a parser called ten
million times, which is precisely the shape that should not be async at all.

## When not to reach for this machinery

Not everything deserves to be async. A method that never waits on anything
external should be synchronous: making it async adds a state machine, a task
and a suspension point in exchange for nothing. `async` over CPU-bound work is
a lie — the work still needs a thread, and hiding that behind a `Task`-returning
signature just moves the decision of where it runs to a caller who has less
information.

Nor should you hand-roll awaiters casually. The exercise here is educational,
and there are real cases — integrating a native event source, a game-engine
frame scheduler, a deterministic virtual clock — but a custom awaiter that gets
`ExecutionContext` capture or exception propagation subtly wrong produces bugs
that look like cosmic rays. When you need a promise, `TaskCompletionSource` is
the boring, correct answer; when you need a pooled promise,
`ManualResetValueTaskSourceCore<T>` is the next sector's boring, correct
answer.

Finally, resist the urge to "optimise" by removing `async` and returning the
inner task directly. `return InnerAsync();` instead of `return await
InnerAsync();` does save a state machine, but it also removes your method's
frame from the exception stack trace and — the sharp edge — changes the
lifetime semantics inside `using` and `try`/`finally`: the `using` disposes
when your method returns, which is now *before* the inner task completes. The
elision is safe only when there is no enclosing `try`, `using`, or `lock`.
That trade — a few dozen bytes against a disposed-object bug — is almost never
worth taking outside a measured hot path.
