## Exercise 1 - the cache-first ValueTask

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB02_ValueTaskPooling/Ex1.cs`.

`Store` holds a `Dictionary<string, int>` cache and a
`Func<string, Task<int>> loader` supplied to its constructor.

- `Store.GetAsync(string key)` returns `ValueTask<int>`. On a cache hit it must
  return a **synchronously completed** value — `GetAsync(k).IsCompletedSuccessfully`
  is `true` immediately, and `loader` is not called. On a miss it delegates to a
  private `async Task<int>` core that calls `loader`, stores the result and
  returns it.
- `Store.LoadCount` counts how many times `loader` was invoked.
- `Store.TryPeek(string key, out int value)` reads the cache without loading.

Example: with `loader` returning `key.Length`, `await store.GetAsync("abc")` is
`3` and `LoadCount` is `1`; a second `GetAsync("abc")` returns
`IsCompletedSuccessfully == true` and leaves `LoadCount` at `1`.

The gate calls `GetAsync` and inspects the returned `ValueTask<int>` before
awaiting it, so the fast path has to be genuinely synchronous.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb02_valuetask_pooling ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The gate inspects the returned value *before* awaiting. That single sentence
rules out one implementation entirely: if `GetAsync` is an `async` method, the
work still happens synchronously on a hit, but you have paid for a builder on
every single call — and, more to the point, the exercise is about the shape
that avoids it.

So: what does a method returning `ValueTask<int>` look like when it is not
`async`?

## Hint 2

```csharp
public ValueTask<int> GetAsync(string key)
{
    if (cache.TryGetValue(key, out int hit))
        return new ValueTask<int>(hit);        // no Task, no state machine

    return new ValueTask<int>(LoadCoreAsync(key));
}

private async Task<int> LoadCoreAsync(string key) { /* ... */ }
```

Two constructors do the work: `ValueTask<T>(T result)` for a value you already
have, and `ValueTask<T>(Task<T> task)` for one you do not. The miss path
allocates exactly as much as plain `Task<int>` would.

## Hint 3

Worth being precise about what you saved. On a hit: no `Task<int>`, no builder,
no state machine — the struct carries the `int` and awaiting it is a branch. On
a miss: everything you would have paid before, plus a slightly larger return
value. That asymmetry is the entire design.

The decision left to you is what the core does about caching a failed load. The
reference stores only successful results, which means a transient failure is
retried next call — usually right. Caching failures ("negative caching") is a
real technique with real uses, but it needs a separate expiry policy and it
should be a decision, not an accident of where you put the `cache[key] = ...`
line.

Note also that this class is not thread-safe. Sector 7 fixes that properly;
here it would only obscure the point.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it from the profiler's side. Imagine this method is called four million
times a second by a serialiser, with a 98% hit rate. Count the heap objects per
call for the naive `async Task<int>` version, then for the version you are
about to write.

The number you are trying to get to on the hit path is zero. Anything that
allocates on a hit — including the state machine's task — is what you are
removing.

## Hint 2

A quick way to check whether your fast path is truly synchronous, without a
gate: assign the return value and look at it.

```csharp
ValueTask<int> v = store.GetAsync("warm");
Debug.Assert(v.IsCompletedSuccessfully);      // must hold before any await
int value = v.Result;                          // legal ONLY because of the line above
```

`.Result` on a `ValueTask` is legal exactly when it has already completed
successfully, and undefined otherwise. Never write the second line without the
first.

## Hint 3

Once it passes, try the variation that teaches the most: mark `GetAsync` as
`async ValueTask<int>` and make the body `if (hit) return value; return await
LoadCoreAsync(key);`. It still passes a value test, and
`IsCompletedSuccessfully` is still true on a hit — because an async method that
never suspends completes synchronously.

What you lost is the allocation-free part: the builder runs, and for
`AsyncValueTaskMethodBuilder` a synchronous completion is cheap but not free,
and every miss now allocates a state machine box *plus* the inner task. The
split version has one state machine on the miss path and none on the hit path.

That comparison — same observable behaviour, different cost — is why this
optimisation is measured rather than argued about.

## Exercise 2 - consume once, or preserve

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB02_ValueTaskPooling/Ex2.cs`.

- `Once.SumTwiceWrong(ValueTask<int> value)` is the broken shape, written on
  purpose so you can see it: `await value + await value`. It compiles and it is
  a contract violation.
- `Once.SumTwiceRight(ValueTask<int> value)` returns the same arithmetic
  without consuming the input twice — it must call `Preserve()` (or await once
  into a local) and explain nothing to the runtime.
- `Once.Materialize(ValueTask<int> value)` returns a `ValueTask<int>` that is
  safe to await any number of times.
- `Once.SafeSnapshot(ValueTask<int> value)` returns a `Task<int>` for handing to
  `Task.WhenAll` and friends.
- `Once.DescribeState(ValueTask<int> value)` returns `"sync"` when the value is
  already successfully completed, `"faulted"`, `"cancelled"`, or `"pending"` —
  and must not await or consume it.

Example: `Once.DescribeState(new ValueTask<int>(3))` is `"sync"`;
`Once.DescribeState(new ValueTask<int>(pendingTask))` is `"pending"`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb02_valuetask_pooling ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Read `SumTwiceWrong` and ask what would have to be true for it to work. It
would need the `ValueTask` to still be answerable the second time — which is
true for a `Task`-backed one and false for a pooled one. Code that works only
for some implementations of an interface is broken code that happens to pass.

The fix in `SumTwiceRight` is one line, and there are two acceptable versions.

## Hint 2

```csharp
int v = await value;      // one consumption, then use the int twice
return v + v;
```

or, if you genuinely need a re-awaitable value:

```csharp
ValueTask<int> safe = value.Preserve();
return await safe + await safe;
```

`Preserve()` returns a `ValueTask<T>` backed by a `Task<T>`, which is why the
repeat is legal — and why it allocates.

For `DescribeState`, look at the three properties that report status without
touching the result: `IsCompletedSuccessfully`, `IsFaulted`, `IsCanceled`.

## Hint 3

The distinction to keep straight is between `AsTask()` and `Preserve()`.

`AsTask()` consumes the `ValueTask` and gives you a `Task<T>` — after calling
it, the original struct must not be used again. `Preserve()` gives you a new
`ValueTask<T>` that is task-backed and re-awaitable, and is itself safe to call
on a value nobody has consumed yet. In both cases you have converted a
zero-allocation value into an allocation; there is no free re-awaitability.

Left to you: whether `DescribeState` should exist at all in production code.
Reading status without consuming is legal and useful for fast paths
(`if (v.IsCompletedSuccessfully) return v.Result;`), but a method whose whole
job is to *report* the state of somebody else's `ValueTask` usually means the
value is being passed around more than the contract wants.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Frame the exercise as writing documentation you can execute. Each method is one
sentence from the `ValueTask` contract:

- "await at most once" — `SumTwiceWrong` breaks it, `SumTwiceRight` respects it
- "convert if you need more" — `Materialize`, `SafeSnapshot`
- "you may inspect without consuming" — `DescribeState`

If you can state the sentence before writing the body, the body is two lines.

## Hint 2

Here is the failure this rule prevents, concretely. A pooled source looks like:

```
op 17 completes -> awaiter reads result -> core.Reset() -> Version becomes 18
                -> the same object is handed out for op 18
```

Your second `await` on the value from op 17 arrives with token 17 against an
object now serving op 18. A validating core throws
`InvalidOperationException`; a non-validating one hands you op 18's result. Now
imagine op 17 was "read user 4001's balance" and op 18 was somebody else's.

That is why the rule is absolute rather than "avoid where possible".

## Hint 3

There is a fourth state worth noticing while writing `DescribeState`: a
`default(ValueTask<int>)`. It is a *successfully completed* value task whose
result is `default(int)` — zero. That is a deliberate design choice so that a
struct field with no initialisation behaves like `Task.FromResult(0)` rather
than throwing.

It has a practical consequence: you cannot distinguish "no value was set" from
"the value is zero" by inspecting a `ValueTask<int>`, so do not use one as an
optional field. And it is a nice trick for an implementer — returning
`default` from a `ValueTask`-returning method is the cheapest possible
"nothing to do here", which is exactly what a no-op `DisposeAsync` should
return.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 - combining without WhenAll

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB02_ValueTaskPooling/Ex3.cs`. There is no
`ValueTask.WhenAll`, and the reason is the contract: `WhenAll` stores its
inputs. Write the pattern the BCL uses instead.

- `Combine.SumAsync(ValueTask<int>[] items)` returns `ValueTask<int>` with the
  total. When **every** input is already successfully completed it must return
  a synchronously completed result and allocate no list and no task — the gate
  asserts `IsCompletedSuccessfully` on the return value.
- When some are pending, only those may be converted with `AsTask()`, and the
  method returns a `ValueTask<int>` wrapping the continuation.
- `Combine.CompletedCount(ValueTask<int>[] items)` returns how many are already
  successfully completed, without consuming any of them.
- `Combine.FirstResultAsync(ValueTask<int> a, ValueTask<int> b)` returns
  whichever completes first, converting both exactly once.

Example: `SumAsync([new(1), new(2), new(3)])` returns a value task that is
already complete with `6`, having touched no heap.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb02_valuetask_pooling ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two passes, not one. First walk the array asking each item "are you already
done successfully?" — that question is free and does not consume anything.
Accumulate those. Only the leftovers need converting.

If the leftovers list is still null at the end, you never allocated it and you
can return a plain value.

## Hint 2

```csharp
int total = 0;
List<Task<int>>? pending = null;

foreach (ValueTask<int> item in items)
{
    if (item.IsCompletedSuccessfully) total += item.Result;
    else (pending ??= []).Add(item.AsTask());
}

if (pending is null) return new ValueTask<int>(total);
return new ValueTask<int>(FinishAsync(pending, total));
```

`??=` allocates the list lazily, which is the whole point — a warm cache never
touches it. `item.Result` is legal here *only* because the line above proved it
is complete.

## Hint 3

Two details that are easy to get wrong.

`IsCompletedSuccessfully` and not `IsCompleted`: a faulted or cancelled value
is "completed", and reading `.Result` on it throws immediately, which would
turn a fan-out into a fail-fast without you deciding to. Letting the faulted
ones go through `AsTask()` and into the continuation means the failure surfaces
where you expect it.

And `AsTask()` consumes: call it once per item, store the result. A loop that
calls `item.AsTask()` twice — once to test something, once to add — is the same
double-consumption bug in a new hat.

For `FirstResultAsync`, `Task.WhenAny` needs `Task`s, so convert both exactly
once, and remember that the loser keeps running. Whether that matters is a
design question this sector does not answer for you; the cancellation sector
does.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about the shape of the data rather than the API. In the workload this
exists for — a serialiser reading fields, a cache fan-out — the array is
usually *entirely* complete. The interesting optimisation is not "handle mixed
efficiently"; it is "make the all-complete case cost nothing".

Write the all-complete path first, with no list at all, and only then add the
fallback.

## Hint 2

A test you can run in your head: for `SumAsync([new(1), new(2)])`, how many
objects does your implementation put on the heap?

The target is zero. A `List<Task<int>>` you allocated but never filled is one.
A `Task<int>` from an unconditional `AsTask()` is two more. A closure capturing
`total` for a continuation is another. Each of those is a line you can point at
and delete.

## Hint 3

Worth knowing what the framework itself does here. `System.IO.Pipelines`,
`Channel`, and the `Socket` async APIs all use this exact two-pass shape, and
several of them go further: rather than a `List<Task<int>>`, they hold a small
inline array or reuse a rented buffer, because the fallback path is still worth
optimising in a networking core.

You should not do that. The two-pass shape is the readable 95% of the benefit;
rented buffers in a summing helper is the kind of code that gets a comment
saying "do not touch" and then rots. Keep the optimisation proportional to the
call rate you actually have — which for most of us means writing
`await Task.WhenAll(...)` over `Task<int>` and never opening this file again.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 - implementing IValueTaskSource

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB02_ValueTaskPooling/Ex4.cs`. Build a reusable promise:
one object that can represent operation after operation without allocating a
new one each time.

```csharp
public sealed class ReusableOperation : IValueTaskSource<int>
{
    public ValueTask<int> Start();                 // hands out (this, current version)
    public void Complete(int value);
    public void Fail(Exception error);
    public short Version { get; }
    public int Completions { get; }                // how many operations have been consumed
}
```

Back it with a `ManualResetValueTaskSourceCore<int>` field (not `readonly` —
it is a mutable struct). Implement the three interface members by forwarding to
the core, and `Reset()` the core inside `GetResult` so the instance is
immediately reusable.

Required behaviour:

- `Start()` twice in a row without completing in between is an
  `InvalidOperationException` — one operation at a time.
- After a full cycle (`Start`, `Complete`, `await`), `Version` has changed and
  the object can be used again.
- Awaiting a `ValueTask<int>` from a *previous* cycle throws
  `InvalidOperationException` — the core's token check catches it.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb02_valuetask_pooling ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

You are not writing the hard parts. `ManualResetValueTaskSourceCore<T>` already
handles continuation storage, the race between "the awaiter registers" and "the
result arrives", `ExecutionContext` flow, and the version check. Your three
interface members are one line each.

The design work is deciding where `Reset()` goes, and guarding "one operation
at a time".

## Hint 2

```csharp
private ManualResetValueTaskSourceCore<int> core;   // NOT readonly

public ValueTaskSourceStatus GetStatus(short token) => core.GetStatus(token);

public void OnCompleted(Action<object?> continuation, object? state, short token,
    ValueTaskSourceOnCompletedFlags flags) =>
    core.OnCompleted(continuation, state, token, flags);

public int GetResult(short token)
{
    try { return core.GetResult(token); }
    finally { core.Reset(); }     // next Version; instance free for reuse
}
```

`Start()` is `new ValueTask<int>(this, core.Version)`, and completion is
`core.SetResult(value)` / `core.SetException(error)`.

The `finally` matters: reset even when `GetResult` throws, or a failed
operation permanently retires the object.

## Hint 3

The `readonly` trap is worth dwelling on, because the compiler does not warn
you. If you write

```csharp
private readonly ManualResetValueTaskSourceCore<int> core = new();
```

then every call to a mutating member operates on a defensive *copy*. `SetResult`
writes to a temporary that is thrown away, the awaiter never completes, and
nothing anywhere reports an error. This is the single most common bug in
hand-written `IValueTaskSource` implementations, and it is why the BCL's own
guidance spells out "must not be readonly".

`core.RunContinuationsAsynchronously = true` in the constructor is the other
line worth adding — it is the same decision as sector 1's
`RunContinuationsAsynchronously`, applied here, and for the same reason: do not
let whoever calls `Complete` end up running the awaiter's code.

Left to you: whether "one at a time" should throw or be a documented
precondition. The BCL's own sources generally use a field flag and throw,
because a violated precondition in a pooled promise is unrecoverable.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start by drawing the object's life as a cycle: idle → in flight → completed →
consumed → idle again, with the version incrementing on the last edge. Every
method you write belongs to exactly one transition.

That picture also tells you where the errors live: `Start` from "in flight" is
an error, and `GetResult` with a version from a previous lap is an error.

## Hint 2

Compare what you are building with a `TaskCompletionSource<int>`:

| | `TaskCompletionSource<int>` | `IValueTaskSource<int>` |
|---|---|---|
| allocation per operation | one TCS + one Task | none after the first |
| await twice | fine | undefined |
| reusable | no | yes, via version tokens |
| you must implement | nothing | three members |

Reuse is the whole feature, and the version token is what makes reuse
detectable rather than silently wrong. If you understand that trade, the code
writes itself.

## Hint 3

Once the gate passes, try the experiment that makes the token real: hold a
`ValueTask<int>` from cycle one, complete and consume it, start cycle two, and
then await the old value again. You should get an `InvalidOperationException`
from the core.

Now imagine the core did not check. You would get cycle two's result, delivered
to cycle one's caller, with no exception and no log line. That is the failure
the entire "await once" rule exists to prevent, and seeing the check fire is
the fastest way to stop treating the rule as pedantry.

The other thing worth trying: set `RunContinuationsAsynchronously` to `false`
and observe which thread the awaiting code runs on after `Complete`. It is the
completer's — sector 1's hijacking, reproduced exactly, in a different
primitive.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 - the failure and cancellation states

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB02_ValueTaskPooling/Ex5.cs`. A `ValueTask` can be born
already failed or already cancelled, and those states have their own rules.

- `States.Failed(string message)` returns a `ValueTask<int>` already faulted
  with an `InvalidOperationException` carrying `message` — returned, not
  thrown.
- `States.Cancelled(CancellationToken token)` returns a `ValueTask<int>` in the
  cancelled state for that token.
- `States.Classify(ValueTask<int> value)` returns `"ok"`, `"faulted:<Type>"`,
  `"cancelled"` or `"pending"` **without** consuming the value.
- `States.ReadOrDefaultAsync(ValueTask<int> value, int fallback)` returns the
  result, or `fallback` when the value faulted, and lets cancellation through
  untouched — an `OperationCanceledException` must escape.
- `States.EagerGuard(int[]? values)` returns `ValueTask<int>`; a null argument
  throws `ArgumentNullException` **at the call site**, not on the returned
  value.

Example: `Classify(States.Failed("boom"))` is `"faulted:InvalidOperationException"`;
`await ReadOrDefaultAsync(States.Failed("boom"), 9)` is `9`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb02_valuetask_pooling ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Every state you need has a static factory, and they mirror the `Task` ones from
sector 1 exactly. Look at `ValueTask.FromResult`, `ValueTask.FromException<T>`
and `ValueTask.FromCanceled<T>`.

For `Classify`, remember that the status properties may be read freely — that
is not consumption. Consumption is awaiting or reading `.Result`.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public static ValueTask<int> Failed(string message) =>
    ValueTask.FromException<int>(new InvalidOperationException(message));
```

For `ReadOrDefaultAsync`, the ordering of your catch clauses is the exercise:
`OperationCanceledException` derives from `Exception`, so a bare
`catch (Exception)` written first eats it. Catch cancellation explicitly and
rethrow, or use a filter:

```csharp
catch (Exception ex) when (ex is not OperationCanceledException)
```

For `EagerGuard`, `ValueTask<T>`-returning methods split exactly like the
`Task` ones in sector 1: a non-async wrapper validates, an async core does the
work.

## Hint 3

The detail that catches people: getting the exception *type name* out of a
faulted `ValueTask` without consuming it. There is no `Exception` property on
`ValueTask<T>` — the status properties are all it exposes.

So `Classify` can report `"faulted"` from `IsFaulted` alone, but to name the
type it has to look at the underlying task. `value.AsTask().Exception` gives it
to you, at the cost of consuming the value and allocating — which is exactly
why the reference answer preserves first:

```csharp
Task<int> task = value.Preserve().AsTask();
```

That is a legitimate use of `Preserve`: you want to inspect *and* the caller
still holds their copy.

Left to you: whether a classifier that has to allocate to answer is a good API.
It is fine in diagnostics and a bad idea in a hot path — which is a fair
summary of a lot of `ValueTask` reflection code.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Sort the five methods by which side of the "consumption" line they sit on.
`Failed`, `Cancelled` and `EagerGuard` *produce* values; `Classify` inspects
without consuming; `ReadOrDefaultAsync` consumes exactly once. Writing that
list first prevents the usual mistake of awaiting inside a classifier.

## Hint 2

The cancellation requirement in `ReadOrDefaultAsync` is not decoration. In a
real service, a cancelled operation means the caller went away; converting that
into a fallback value means you compute and return a result nobody wanted, and
your metrics show success for a request that was abandoned.

Write the method so a reviewer can see the intent:

```csharp
catch (OperationCanceledException) { throw; }
catch (Exception) { return fallback; }
```

Two clauses, in that order, is clearer than one clever filter — and it is the
version that survives someone adding a third case later.

## Hint 3

A subtlety about `ValueTask.FromCanceled<T>(token)`: like `Task.FromCanceled`,
it requires a token that is already cancelled. A live token throws
`ArgumentOutOfRangeException`, which is an odd-looking error until you realise
what it is protecting — a "cancelled" result that nobody actually cancelled
would be a lie the status system cannot represent.

And note the asymmetry worth remembering: `IsCanceled` on a value task is true
only for that genuine cancelled state. A value faulted with a hand-made
`OperationCanceledException` reports `IsFaulted`, not `IsCanceled`. Retry
policies, logging filters and `WhenAll` all branch on the status rather than on
the exception type, so producing the wrong one produces the wrong behaviour
three layers away.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 - the interface that forced the design

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB02_ValueTaskPooling/Ex6.cs`. `IAsyncEnumerator<T>`
returns `ValueTask<bool>` from `MoveNextAsync` and `ValueTask` from
`DisposeAsync`. Implement one by hand and you will see why.

- `BufferedSequence` implements `IAsyncEnumerable<int>`, constructed with
  `int[][] pages` and a `Func<int, Task<int[]>>`-free design: it holds the pages
  already, but yields them one item at a time from an internal buffer, refilling
  the buffer via `Task.Yield()` between pages so a page boundary genuinely
  suspends.
- `BufferedSequence.Enumerator.MoveNextAsync()` must return a **synchronously
  completed** `ValueTask<bool>` for every item within a page (the gate asserts
  `IsCompletedSuccessfully` before awaiting) and may suspend only at page
  boundaries.
- `DisposeAsync()` returns `default` when there is nothing to clean up.
- `BufferedSequence.SyncMoves` counts how many `MoveNextAsync` calls completed
  synchronously.

Example: pages `[[1,2,3],[4,5]]` enumerated fully yields `1,2,3,4,5` with three
of the five item-moves synchronous within the first page.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb02_valuetask_pooling ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Count the calls before you write anything. Enumerating a thousand-item buffered
source calls `MoveNextAsync` a thousand times, and all but a handful have the
answer sitting in an array already.

If that method returned `Task<bool>`, that is a thousand allocations per
enumeration. Now you know why the interface is shaped the way it is — and your
implementation's job is to preserve the property.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public ValueTask<bool> MoveNextAsync()
{
    if (index + 1 < buffer.Length)
    {
        index++;
        return new ValueTask<bool>(true);      // synchronous, no allocation
    }

    return new ValueTask<bool>(AdvancePageAsync());   // the rare slow path
}

private async Task<bool> AdvancePageAsync() { /* ... */ }
```

Same split as ex1: a non-async method with a fast path and an async core. For
`DisposeAsync` with nothing to clean up, `default` is a completed `ValueTask` —
cheaper than `ValueTask.CompletedTask` and identical in behaviour.

## Hint 3

Two implementation details that the gate will notice.

`GetAsyncEnumerator(CancellationToken)` is the interface member, and the token
parameter is there for a reason the next-but-one sector covers; here you may
accept and ignore it, but do not omit it — the signature is part of the
contract.

And the enumerator must return `false` from `MoveNextAsync` *after* the last
item, not throw. `await foreach` calls it exactly once more than there are
items, and a source that throws on exhaustion breaks every consumer.

Left to you: whether `Current` should throw before the first move. The BCL's
own enumerators mostly return `default` and document it, because a check on
every access costs more than the mistake is worth — but for a type used by
strangers, throwing is defensible.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Approach it as a state machine you write by hand — which is precisely what
`yield return` would have generated for you. Two indices: which page, which
item inside it. `MoveNextAsync` advances the second, and when it runs out,
advances the first.

Writing it manually once is worth more than reading about it, because it makes
the shape of every async iterator you use afterwards obvious.

## Hint 2

Here is the equivalent written with `yield`, so you can compare afterwards:

```csharp
public async IAsyncEnumerable<int> ItemsAsync()
{
    foreach (int[] page in pages)
    {
        await Task.Yield();          // page boundary
        foreach (int item in page) yield return item;
    }
}
```

The compiler generates a class implementing both `IAsyncEnumerable<int>` and
`IAsyncEnumerator<int>`, with a `ManualResetValueTaskSourceCore<bool>` inside
it — exactly what you built in ex4, generated. That is not a coincidence; the
async-iterator builder was one of the reasons `IValueTaskSource` exists.

## Hint 3

The trap in the whole design is that `ValueTask<bool>` from `MoveNextAsync` is
consumed by `await foreach` and by nobody else. That is what makes it safe.

The moment you write a helper that takes an `IAsyncEnumerator<T>` and stores
the `ValueTask<bool>` — say, to race two enumerators against each other — you
are outside the contract, and against a compiler-generated enumerator (which
*is* pooled, via its own source) you will get wrong answers rather than
exceptions.

If you need to race async streams, the honest approach is to pump each into a
`Channel<T>` and race the channels — sector 6. It allocates more and it is
correct, which is usually the right trade when the alternative is undefined
behaviour.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 - pooling the state machine

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB02_ValueTaskPooling/Ex7.cs`.

- `Pooled.SumAsync(Task<int>[] work)` is an `async ValueTask<int>` method
  annotated with
  `[AsyncMethodBuilder(typeof(PoolingAsyncValueTaskMethodBuilder<>))]`. It sums
  the results, awaiting each in turn.
- `Pooled.PlainAsync(Task<int>[] work)` is the identical method with no
  annotation, for comparison.
- `Pooled.NoBuilderAsync(Task<int>[] work)` returns `ValueTask<int>` with no
  `async` keyword at all: it returns a completed value when every input is
  already completed successfully, and delegates to `PlainAsync` otherwise.
- `Pooled.Describe()` returns a one-line string naming which of the three
  allocates on the all-complete path: exactly `"NoBuilderAsync"`.

Both async versions must produce identical results; the annotation changes
allocation behaviour, not semantics.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb02_valuetask_pooling ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The attribute goes on the method, and it needs the *open generic* builder type:

```csharp
[AsyncMethodBuilder(typeof(PoolingAsyncValueTaskMethodBuilder<>))]
public static async ValueTask<int> SumAsync(Task<int>[] work) { /* ... */ }
```

`using System.Runtime.CompilerServices;` for the attribute, and the builder
lives there too. The body is an ordinary loop.

## Hint 2

Be clear about what each version costs on the *all-complete* path, because that
is what `Describe` is asking about:

- `SumAsync` — the pooled builder still runs; no suspension means no box to
  pool, and the builder returns a completed `ValueTask<int>`.
- `PlainAsync` — same, with the standard builder.
- `NoBuilderAsync` — no builder at all, because the method is not `async`.

The third is the only one that skips the machinery entirely, which is the
answer `Describe` wants. Note this is the ex1 lesson again, one level up:
pooling optimises the suspending path; splitting optimises the synchronous one.
They are complementary, not alternatives.

## Hint 3

What pooling actually pools: the boxed state machine (`AsyncStateMachineBox`),
kept in a small per-thread cache plus a limited global one. It does **not** pool
the `ValueTask` (a struct), the `Task` your inner awaits create, or anything
your method allocates itself.

So the win applies to methods that suspend often, in a tight loop, where that
box was surviving long enough to be promoted. The published measurements show
solid gains there and a small regression elsewhere — which is why it is opt-in
per method, or per process via
`DOTNET_SYSTEM_THREADING_POOLASYNCVALUETASKS=1`.

Left to you: whether you would ever ship the attribute. A defensible position
is "no, and I know it exists so I can recognise it and so I can flip the
environment variable during an investigation". That answer is better received
in an interview than enthusiasm.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about who is allowed to make this choice. The attribute changes the code
the compiler generates for *your* method only; callers cannot see it and cannot
opt out. That makes it a local, reversible decision — unlike changing a return
type from `Task<T>` to `ValueTask<T>`, which is a breaking change to everyone.

That asymmetry is a useful lens: prefer optimisations that are invisible at
the boundary.

## Hint 2

If you want to see it rather than take it on faith, the measurement that works
is allocated-bytes, not time:

```csharp
long before = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
for (int i = 0; i < 10_000; i++) await SumAsync(pending);
long after = GC.GetAllocatedBytesForCurrentThread();
```

Run it against a set of tasks that genuinely suspend, in release mode, on a
single thread. In debug the state machine is a class and the numbers describe a
different program — the same warning as sector 1.

## Hint 3

There is a third builder worth knowing about even though you will not use it
here: `[AsyncMethodBuilder(typeof(AsyncTaskMethodBuilder))]` and friends are
what let library authors implement *custom awaitable types* end to end — UniTask
in Unity, and the `IAsyncEnumerable` machinery in the BCL, both do this.

The language feature is deliberately general: the compiler performs the
transformation and delegates every semantic decision — how the promise is
created, where continuations run, whether anything is pooled — to a builder
type you can supply. It is the same duck-typing philosophy as the awaiter
pattern in sector 1, applied to the other end of the method.

Knowing that changes how you read an unfamiliar async API: the question is
never "is this magic", it is "which builder and which awaiter".

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 - the counter-case

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB02_ValueTaskPooling/Ex8.cs`. Not every method should
return `ValueTask<T>`. Write both versions of one that should not, and encode
the decision rule.

- `Remote.FetchValueTaskAsync(Func<Task<int>> call)` returns `ValueTask<int>`
  wrapping the call. This is the wrong choice: the method always awaits real
  I/O, so a task is allocated regardless.
- `Remote.FetchTaskAsync(Func<Task<int>> call)` returns `Task<int>` — the right
  choice for the same work.
- `Remote.FanOutAsync(Func<Task<int>>[] calls)` runs them concurrently and sums
  the results, and must take the `Task`-returning version because `WhenAll`
  needs tasks. Converting `ValueTask`s here would allocate an extra object per
  call.
- `Remote.ShouldUseValueTask(bool hotPath, bool usuallySynchronous, bool measured)`
  returns `true` only when all three are `true`.
- `Remote.Rationale()` returns the one-line rule as a string, exactly:
  `"hot path + usually synchronous + measured"`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb02_valuetask_pooling ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Write `FanOutAsync` first, using the `Task`-returning fetch. Then try to write
it using the `ValueTask`-returning one and count how many `AsTask()` calls you
need. That count is the argument.

The other three methods are almost trivial; the exercise is the reasoning they
encode.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public static ValueTask<int> FetchValueTaskAsync(Func<Task<int>> call) =>
    new(call());        // the task was allocated anyway; the struct adds copying

public static Task<int> FetchTaskAsync(Func<Task<int>> call) => call();
```

For the fan-out, `Task.WhenAll` over an array of `Task<int>` is direct:

```csharp
int[] results = await Task.WhenAll(calls.Select(c => c()));
```

Watch the laziness — `Select` is deferred, so materialise once with `ToArray()`
if you enumerate it more than once, or hand it straight to `WhenAll`, which
enumerates exactly once.

## Hint 3

The rule in `ShouldUseValueTask` deserves defending rather than memorising.

**Hot path** — if the method is called a hundred times a request, the
allocation is noise next to everything else the request does. **Usually
synchronous** — if it always waits, `ValueTask` saves nothing and costs struct
copying. **Measured** — because allocation profiles are consistently
counter-intuitive, and gen0 collection is cheap enough that most "obvious"
allocation wins do not show up at all.

The three-way conjunction also matters as an interview answer: it demonstrates
that you know the optimisation has a cost, which is the part that separates
"I read a blog post" from "I have used this".

Left to you: whether a public API should ever return `ValueTask<T>` when you do
not control the callers. There is a good argument for "only if it is
documented and the type is in the name of what you are optimising" — and the
BCL's own choices are a decent guide to where that line sits.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Invert the exercise: assume someone has already changed every `Task<T>` in a
codebase to `ValueTask<T>` because it sounded faster. List what breaks or gets
worse. You should get at least: `WhenAll` sites now allocate, some caller
stored one in a field, a retry helper awaits twice, struct copying went up
everywhere, and nothing on the slow path got faster.

Then write the four methods as the antidote to that list.

## Hint 2

There is a clean way to see the "always allocates anyway" point. For a method
that always awaits I/O, the objects per call are:

- `Task<T>` version: one task (from the inner call) + one state machine box.
- `ValueTask<T>` version: one task + one state machine box + a larger return
  value copied at every frame.

The struct never removed anything, because there was nothing synchronous to
remove. This is the single most common misapplication of the type, and being
able to state it in two lines is worth more than the code.

## Hint 3

One more consideration that rarely makes the blog posts: **diagnostics**.
`Task<T>` is visible to a lot of tooling — the debugger's Tasks window,
`TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException`, ETW events, async call stacks in dumps.
A `ValueTask` backed by a pooled `IValueTaskSource` is much harder to inspect
after the fact: there is no task object, the source has been recycled, and the
async stack is not reconstructible from a dump the way a `Task` chain is.

For a hot networking primitive that is an acceptable price. For your service's
business logic, it means the day you need to debug a production hang is the day
you find out what you traded away. That is a legitimate reason to keep `Task<T>`
even where the allocation argument is marginal — and it is a good thing to say
out loud when someone proposes a sweeping change.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge - an allocation-free buffered reader

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB02_ValueTaskPooling/Challenge.cs`. Build the shape the
whole sector has been circling: a reader that answers from a buffer with no
allocation, and uses a **reusable** promise when it genuinely has to wait.

```csharp
public sealed class PullReader : IValueTaskSource<int>
{
    public PullReader(int[] source, int chunkSize);
    public ValueTask<int> ReadAsync(Memory<int> destination);
    public void Release();          // makes the next chunk available
    public int SyncReads { get; }
    public int AsyncReads { get; }
}
```

Behaviour:

- `ReadAsync` copies up to `destination.Length` items from the current chunk
  and returns the count **synchronously** when the buffer has data — the gate
  checks `IsCompletedSuccessfully` before awaiting, and asserts that repeated
  buffered reads allocate no new promise object.
- When the buffer is empty and the source is not exhausted, `ReadAsync` returns
  a `ValueTask<int>` backed by `this`, pending until `Release()` refills the
  buffer.
- At end of source, `ReadAsync` returns `0` synchronously, forever.
- One outstanding asynchronous read at a time; a second is
  `InvalidOperationException`.
- The same `PullReader` instance serves every pending read — no
  `TaskCompletionSource`, no per-read allocation.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb02_valuetask_pooling challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two halves that barely interact. The buffered half is ex1's shape: check, copy,
`return new ValueTask<int>(count)`. The waiting half is ex4's shape: hand out
`new ValueTask<int>(this, core.Version)` and complete it from `Release()`.

Write and test them separately. The only shared state is "how much is in the
buffer", and the only shared decision is which half a given call goes down.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public ValueTask<int> ReadAsync(Memory<int> destination)
{
    if (available > 0 || exhausted)
    {
        SyncReads++;
        return new ValueTask<int>(CopyOut(destination));
    }

    if (pending) throw new InvalidOperationException("read already in flight");
    pending = true;
    this.destination = destination;      // remember where to copy on Release
    AsyncReads++;
    return new ValueTask<int>(this, core.Version);
}
```

`Release()` refills the buffer and, if a read is pending, copies into the
remembered destination and calls `core.SetResult(count)`.

Remember `GetResult(short)` must `Reset()` the core in a `finally` so the next
asynchronous read gets a fresh version.

## Hint 3

The sharp edges, in the order they will bite.

**Holding a `Memory<int>` across the wait.** It is a struct pointing at
someone's array; storing it in a field is legal (unlike `Span<T>`) but it means
the caller must not reuse that buffer until the read completes. That is exactly
the contract `Stream.ReadAsync` has, so you are in good company — but write the
line deliberately, not by accident.

**End of source.** Once exhausted, every read returns `0` synchronously and
must never pend again, or a consumer loop `while (await ReadAsync(buf) > 0)`
hangs at the end instead of finishing.

**`Release()` with no pending read.** Must be a no-op refill, not a
`SetResult` on a core nobody is waiting on — that would complete a version
nobody holds and then the *next* reader would find the core already completed.

Left to you: whether to validate the "one at a time" rule with a flag and a
throw, or to document it and let the core's token check catch violations. The
BCL does the former for readers and the latter in a few hot paths; the former
is the right default.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Write the consumer loop first, on paper:

```csharp
int[] buffer = new int[4];
while (true)
{
    int n = await reader.ReadAsync(buffer);
    if (n == 0) break;
    // use buffer[0..n]
}
```

Now walk your implementation against it for a source of 10 items and a chunk of
3. How many of those `ReadAsync` calls should be synchronous? How many promise
objects should exist by the end? The answers — most, and one — are the
specification.

## Hint 2

A useful decomposition: separate "what does the reader know" from "what does a
read do".

State: the source array, the chunk size, how far into the source we have
released, the current buffer window, whether we are exhausted, whether a read
is pending, and the destination of the pending read.

Operations: `ReadAsync` (fast or slow), `Release` (refill, maybe complete),
`GetResult` (deliver and reset).

If a piece of state does not appear in exactly one operation's precondition and
one's postcondition, you probably do not need it.

## Hint 3

Compare what you have built with the two obvious alternatives, because the
comparison is the point of the challenge.

**A `TaskCompletionSource` per pending read** — correct, simple, and allocates
two objects per wait. Perfectly fine for a reader called a thousand times a
second, and what you should write first in real life.

**A `Channel<int[]>`** — even simpler, handles backpressure for free, and
allocates more. Sector 6's answer, and the right one for most producer/consumer
problems.

**This** — allocates nothing steady-state, imposes the await-once contract on
every caller, and needs the token check to make violations detectable. It is
what `System.IO.Pipelines` and `SslStream` do, and the reason they can saturate
a network card.

Being able to name all three, and say when each is right, is the actual skill.
Writing the third one is how you earn the right to say the first two are
usually better.

exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 - the misuse audit

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB02_ValueTaskPooling/Review1.cs`. Four signatures, four
misuses, one repair each. No new APIs — this is about recognising the shapes at
a glance, which is what code review actually requires.

- `Audit.Classify(string usage)` maps a described misuse to its rule, exactly:
  - `"stored"` → `"do not store a ValueTask"`
  - `"double-await"` → `"consume a ValueTask at most once"`
  - `"blocking"` → `"never block on an incomplete ValueTask"`
  - `"always-async"` → `"return Task when the method always waits"`
  - anything else → `"unknown"`
- `Audit.RepairedStore(ValueTask<int> value)` returns a `Task<int>` safe to
  keep in a field.
- `Audit.RepairedDoubleAwait(ValueTask<int> value)` returns the value twice
  over (`$"{v}/{v}"`) with one consumption.
- `Audit.RepairedBlocking(ValueTask<int> value)` returns the result without
  blocking — an `async` method — and must work whether or not the input has
  already completed.
- `Audit.RepairedAlwaysAsync(Func<Task<int>> call)` returns `Task<int>`.

Example: `Audit.Classify("double-await")` is `"consume a ValueTask at most
once"`; `await Audit.RepairedDoubleAwait(new ValueTask<int>(4))` is `"4/4"`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb02_valuetask_pooling review1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Each repair is one line, and each one is a different escape from the same
contract. Before writing them, say which rule each broken shape violated —
that mapping is `Classify`, and the repairs follow from it.

The only one with a choice in it is the double-await, where "await once into a
local" and "`Preserve()` then await twice" are both correct for different
reasons.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public static Task<int> RepairedStore(ValueTask<int> value) => value.AsTask();

public static async Task<string> RepairedDoubleAwait(ValueTask<int> value)
{
    int v = await value;
    return $"{v}/{v}";
}
```

For `RepairedBlocking`, the entire repair is deleting `.Result` and adding
`await`. For `RepairedAlwaysAsync`, the repair is the return type — the body is
`call()`.

`Classify` is a `switch` expression over the four strings with a default.

## Hint 3

The one worth arguing about is `RepairedStore`. `AsTask()` allocates, and
somebody will ask whether the allocation was avoidable.

It was not. Storage means "consumable later, possibly more than once, possibly
from another thread" — every property `ValueTask` explicitly does not have. The
allocation is not overhead you failed to optimise away; it is the cost of the
guarantees you actually need. Being able to say that clearly is the difference
between a review comment that lands and one that starts an argument.

Left to you: whether `Preserve()` or `AsTask()` is the better repair. `AsTask`
when the destination is a task-shaped API or a field of type `Task<T>`;
`Preserve` when you want to keep the `ValueTask` type in the signature and only
need repeat-awaitability. Both allocate exactly once.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Read this as a review checklist rather than an exercise, and make the checklist
short enough to hold in your head while scrolling a diff:

1. Does a `ValueTask` get awaited more than once on any path?
2. Does one get stored in a field, list, or dictionary?
3. Is `.Result` / `.GetAwaiter().GetResult()` called without an
   `IsCompletedSuccessfully` check immediately above it?
4. Does the method ever complete synchronously? If not, why is it not `Task`?

Four questions catch essentially every real misuse.

## Hint 2

Question 3 is the one with a legitimate exception, and it is worth being precise
about so you do not flag good code:

```csharp
if (value.IsCompletedSuccessfully) return value.Result;   // fine
return await value;                                        // fine
```

That pattern appears throughout the BCL and is exactly right — the check is
what makes `.Result` defined. What you are looking for in review is `.Result`
with no such check on the line above, especially inside a helper where the
check happened in a different method and might not still hold.

## Hint 3

Question 4 is the one that finds the most code and starts the most arguments,
because "return `Task` when the method always waits" reads like a style
preference until you cost it out.

A useful way to frame the review comment: ask for the number. "What fraction of
calls complete synchronously, and how many calls per second?" If the author has
those numbers, the `ValueTask` is probably justified and you have learned
something about the system. If they do not, the answer is `Task<T>` and you have
saved every future caller a class of bug in exchange for an allocation the GC
will never notice.

That is also, more or less, how to disagree productively about any
micro-optimisation: not "this is premature" but "what does the profile say".

lessons.title: V3·CB2 — ValueTask, pooling, and when the optimization pays
lessons.summary: ValueTask exists to remove one allocation from methods that usually finish without waiting. It buys that with a much stricter contract: consume it once, never block on it, never store it. This sector covers the three things a ValueTask can wrap, IValueTaskSource, pooling, and the honest cost/benefit.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·CB2 — ValueTask, pooling, and when the optimization pays

The previous sector ended on the fast path: an async method whose awaits are
already complete never boxes its state machine and never queues a continuation.
One allocation survives that optimisation — the `Task<T>` itself. For most code
that is irrelevant. For `Stream.ReadAsync` on a buffered stream, called a
million times a second, where 99% of calls are served from the buffer, it is
the entire cost of the call.

`ValueTask<T>` is the answer to exactly that shape: **a method that returns
`Task<T>` but usually already has the answer.**

**What it actually is.** `ValueTask<T>` is a readonly struct with three fields:
an object, a `T`, and a short. The object is `null`, a `Task<T>`, or an
`IValueTaskSource<T>`. So it can be in one of three states:

- **A result already in hand.** `new ValueTask<int>(42)` stores the 42 in the
  struct. No heap allocation at all — the struct rides in registers or on the
  stack, and awaiting it is a branch plus a field read.
- **A wrapped `Task<T>`.** For the slow path, when the method genuinely has to
  wait: you allocate a task like before, and the struct just carries it. You
  have paid the struct's size (16-24 bytes of copying) on top. Slightly worse
  than `Task<T>` alone.
- **An `IValueTaskSource<T>`.** A reusable, poolable object that implements the
  promise protocol itself, with a version token so it can be recycled between
  operations. This is how `Socket.ReceiveAsync` manages to be async and
  allocation-free per call even when it does suspend.

**The contract you accept in return.** `Task<T>` is a well-behaved immutable
value: await it as many times as you like, from as many places as you like,
years later, block on it, hand it to `WhenAll`. `ValueTask<T>` guarantees none
of that. The rules, and they are hard rules:

1. **Await it at most once.** A pooled source may already have been recycled
   for another operation by the time you await again, and you will silently get
   somebody else's result.
2. **Never `.Result` or `.GetAwaiter().GetResult()` on one that is not
   complete.** There is no blocking support; the behaviour is undefined.
3. **Do not store it in a field, a list, or a dictionary.** Storage implies
   later use, which implies a second consumption.
4. **Do not pass it to `WhenAll`/`WhenAny`.** They take `Task`; converting via
   `AsTask()` is allowed and allocates, which tells you something.

If you need to break any of those, `.Preserve()` converts the `ValueTask<T>`
into one backed by a `Task<T>` that *is* safe to await repeatedly, and
`.AsTask()` gives you the task itself. Both allocate. That is the deal: the
allocation comes back the moment you want `Task`'s freedoms.

**Why the rules are so sharp.** Because the whole point is reuse. An
`IValueTaskSource<T>` implementation hands out `(source, token)` pairs; every
operation on `GetResult` bumps the token, and any awaiter holding a stale token
is — by contract — a bug that the source is allowed to detect or to ignore.
`ManualResetValueTaskSourceCore<T>` is the BCL's ready-made core for this, and
writing one with it is a genuinely reasonable thing to do in a networking
library and a genuinely unreasonable thing to do in a web app.

**Pooling.** .NET 5 added an opt-in pooled builder:
`[AsyncMethodBuilder(typeof(PoolingAsyncValueTaskMethodBuilder<>))]` on a
method, or `DOTNET_SYSTEM_THREADING_POOLASYNCVALUETASKS=1` for the whole
process. It pools the *state machine box* for methods that do suspend, so a
consistently-suspending `ValueTask` method stops allocating too. It is off by
default because pooling has its own costs — a rented object that is never
returned is worse than an allocation, and the GC is extremely good at
short-lived objects.

**The honest verdict, up front.** Return `Task<T>` unless you have measured a
problem. `ValueTask<T>` is a *library author's* tool for hot APIs where the
synchronous path dominates. Using it everywhere buys you nothing on the slow
path, costs you struct copying, and hands every caller a landmine. The BCL uses
it in exactly the places that fit: `Stream.ReadAsync`, `IAsyncEnumerator<T>`,
`ChannelReader<T>`, `SemaphoreSlim`, `Socket`. Those all share one property —
called constantly, usually already have the answer.

**Where the saving actually is, arithmetically.** A `Task<int>` is about 24-32
bytes plus header. Gen0 allocation in .NET is a pointer bump and gen0
collection of an object that died immediately is close to free, so one task per
call is genuinely nothing — until the call rate is high enough that allocation
*rate* pushes survivors into gen1 through sheer volume, or until the method is
inside something like a serialiser's inner loop where the surrounding work is
measured in nanoseconds rather than milliseconds. Against the saving you pay a
larger return value: 8 bytes of reference becomes 16-24 bytes of struct, copied
at every return and every parameter pass. For a method called a thousand times
a second the copy costs more than the allocation saved. For one called ten
million times a second with a 95% synchronous rate, the allocation wins
decisively. That crossover is why "measure" is not a hedge in this sector; it
is the deciding input.

**How to read a `ValueTask` in somebody else's signature.** When you see one,
three things are being told to you. The author expects this to be called a lot;
the author expects it usually not to wait; and the author has moved a class of
bug from their code to yours. That last part is the reason this sector spends
as much time on the rules as on the mechanism — you will consume far more
`ValueTask`s than you produce, and the consuming rules are the ones that will
bite.

Everything in this sector is deterministic and allocation-observable: the gates
count how many times a factory ran, compare object identity, and check states,
rather than timing anything.

# Reading - csharp/v3cb02_valuetask_pooling

## Notes

**The struct layout is the whole story.** `ValueTask<T>` holds
`object? _obj`, `T? _result`, `short _token`, `bool _continueOnCapturedContext`.
When `_obj` is null the result is right there in the struct. When it is a
`Task<T>`, the struct is a thin wrapper. When it is an `IValueTaskSource<T>`,
`_token` says which operation you are asking about. Everything about the
contract falls out of that third case.

**"At most once" is not a style guideline.** A pooled source that has been
recycled will either throw `InvalidOperationException` (if it validates the
token) or return the wrong operation's result (if it does not, for speed). The
second failure mode is the reason the rule is stated so absolutely: it is a
silent data-corruption bug in a concurrency primitive, which is the worst
possible place for one.

**`AsTask()` vs `Preserve()`.** `AsTask()` gives you a `Task<T>` and *consumes*
the `ValueTask` — you must not use the original afterwards. `Preserve()`
returns a new `ValueTask<T>` backed by a task, which you may await repeatedly,
and it is safe to call on an already-consumed-by-nobody value. Use `Preserve`
when you have to hold on to a result; use `AsTask` when you are handing it to
task-shaped APIs.

**There is no `ValueTask.WhenAll`.** The design is deliberate: `WhenAll` stores
its inputs, and storage is exactly what the contract forbids. The idiomatic
pattern is to check `IsCompletedSuccessfully` first and harvest completed ones
without allocating, converting only the ones still pending.

**`IsCompletedSuccessfully` is the property to reach for.** `IsCompleted` is
true for faulted and cancelled too. In a fast path you want "finished, with a
result, no exception to rethrow", which is the narrower one.

**Pooling is not free.** `PoolingAsyncValueTaskMethodBuilder` keeps a per-thread
and a global pool of state-machine boxes. It wins when the method suspends
often and the object would otherwise be promoted out of gen0. It loses when
allocation was already cheap, and it can hurt badly if a rented box is held
past its lifetime by a buggy awaiter. Measure, and prefer to fix the algorithm
first.

**`ValueTask` (non-generic) exists too**, for methods that return no value:
`DisposeAsync`, `WriteAsync`. Same rules, same three states, minus the result
field.

## ex1

The cache-first shape is the canonical `ValueTask` case, and the structure to
memorise is: a non-async method that returns `new ValueTask<T>(cached)` on the
hit and delegates to a private `async Task<T>` core on the miss. The wrapper
does not need a state machine at all, which is where the saving comes from —
marking the wrapper `async` reintroduces the builder on every call and undoes
most of the point.

Note the miss path returns `new ValueTask<T>(task)`, which allocates the task
just as before. `ValueTask` never makes the slow path faster; it makes the fast
path free.

## ex2

Double-await is the rule everybody nods at and then breaks by accident, usually
by writing a helper that both logs and returns:

```csharp
var v = source.GetAsync();
logger.LogDebug("got {Value}", await v);
return await v;                 // second consumption
```

With a `Task<T>`-backed `ValueTask` that happens to work, which is worse than
failing — it works in your tests and breaks in production against a pooled
implementation. `Preserve()` exists precisely so you can opt into re-awaitable
semantics when you need them, and the allocation it costs is the honest price.

## ex3

Combining `ValueTask`s is where people reach for `Task.WhenAll` and hit the
type system. The pattern in the reference answer — harvest the completed ones
synchronously, convert the rest — is what `System.IO.Pipelines` and the BCL's
own helpers do. On a workload where most inputs are already complete, it
allocates only for the stragglers.

Notice the subtlety in the harvest: you must call `.Result` only when
`IsCompletedSuccessfully` is true. On a faulted `ValueTask`, `.Result` throws
the original exception, which is fine — but on an *incomplete* one it is
undefined behaviour, not a block.

## ex4

`ManualResetValueTaskSourceCore<T>` is a struct you embed in your own class,
and it does the hard parts: continuation storage, `ExecutionContext` capture,
`SynchronizationContext` posting, and result/exception storage. You supply
`GetResult`, `GetStatus` and `OnCompleted` as three-line forwarders, plus
`Reset()` when you want to reuse the instance.

The version token is the part to understand rather than copy. `core.Version`
increases on every `Reset()`; every method takes the token the caller was
handed and the core throws if it does not match. That check is what turns "you
must not await twice" from a documentation sentence into a runtime error, and
it is why implementing this yourself without the core is a bad idea.

## ex5 - ex8

The failure states are where `ValueTask` and `Task` diverge least — the same
three-state model, the same `Canceled`-is-not-`Faulted` distinction — and that
is exactly why they are worth checking. A cancelled `ValueTask` produced by
faulting with a hand-made `OperationCanceledException` reports `IsFaulted`, and
every retry policy downstream will treat an abandoned request as an error.

The hand-written enumerator in ex6 is the sector's argument in a single
interface. `MoveNextAsync` returning `ValueTask<bool>` is not a
micro-optimisation nobody asked for: `await foreach` over a buffered source
calls it once per element, and `Task<bool>` would have meant an allocation per
element, forever, in a language feature. Notice also who consumes that value —
the `foreach` desugaring, exactly once — which is what makes the strict
contract safe there.

Pooling in ex7 is the complement of everything else in the sector. Splitting a
wrapper from an async core optimises the *synchronous* path;
`PoolingAsyncValueTaskMethodBuilder` optimises the *suspending* one by
recycling the state-machine box. They are orthogonal, and neither is a default.
The counter-case in ex8 is the one to carry away: a method that always waits
gains nothing from either, because the allocation it would have saved was never
avoidable.

## Further reading

- [Understanding the Whys, Whats, and Whens of ValueTask](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/understanding-the-whys-whats-and-whens-of-valuetask/) — Stephen Toub's canonical piece; read it twice.
- [`ValueTask<TResult>`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.tasks.valuetask-1) — the API surface and the usage rules, stated by the docs themselves.
- [`IValueTaskSource<TResult>`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.tasks.sources.ivaluetasksource-1) — the protocol.
- [`ManualResetValueTaskSourceCore<TResult>`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.tasks.sources.manualresetvaluetasksourcecore-1) — the reusable core.
- [Async ValueTask pooling in .NET 5](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/async-valuetask-pooling-in-net-5/) — what the pooling builder does and what it costs.
lessons.fullReadme:
# V3·CB2 — ValueTask, pooling, and when the optimization pays

`ValueTask<T>` is a targeted optimisation with a sharp contract. This sector is
about knowing the target, the contract, and — most importantly — when not to
reach for it.

## Concept 1 — three states in one struct

```csharp
public readonly struct ValueTask<TResult>
{
    internal readonly object? _obj;      // null | Task<TResult> | IValueTaskSource<TResult>
    internal readonly TResult? _result;
    internal readonly short _token;
    internal readonly bool _continueOnCapturedContext;
}
```

- `_obj == null` — the result is in `_result`. Zero allocations.
- `_obj is Task<TResult>` — the slow path; a task was allocated anyway.
- `_obj is IValueTaskSource<TResult>` — a poolable promise, identified by
  `_token`.

## Concept 2 — the canonical shape

```csharp
public ValueTask<byte[]> GetAsync(string key)          // NOT async
{
    if (cache.TryGetValue(key, out byte[]? hit))
        return new ValueTask<byte[]>(hit);             // no allocation

    return new ValueTask<byte[]>(LoadAsync(key));      // slow path allocates
}

private async Task<byte[]> LoadAsync(string key) { /* ... */ }
```

The wrapper is deliberately not `async`. An `async ValueTask<T>` method still
builds a state machine and, when it suspends, still allocates — you keep only
the task allocation on the synchronous path, which is a smaller win than
splitting.

## Concept 3 — the rules, and the escape hatches

```csharp
ValueTask<int> v = GetAsync();

int a = await v;
int b = await v;            // WRONG: may return another operation's result

ValueTask<int> safe = GetAsync().Preserve();
int c = await safe;
int d = await safe;         // fine: Preserve() is Task-backed

Task<int> t = GetAsync().AsTask();     // fine, allocates, consumes the original
```

Also forbidden: storing a `ValueTask` in a field or collection; calling
`.Result` when `IsCompleted` is false; passing one to `Task.WhenAll`.

## Concept 4 — combining without WhenAll

```csharp
public static ValueTask<int> SumAsync(ValueTask<int>[] items)
{
    int total = 0;
    List<Task<int>>? pending = null;

    foreach (ValueTask<int> item in items)
    {
        if (item.IsCompletedSuccessfully) total += item.Result;   // free
        else (pending ??= []).Add(item.AsTask());                 // only now allocate
    }

    if (pending is null) return new ValueTask<int>(total);
    return new ValueTask<int>(FinishAsync(pending, total));
}
```

When everything is already complete — the common case for a warm cache — this
allocates nothing, not even the list.

## Concept 5 — IValueTaskSource and reuse

```csharp
public sealed class Operation : IValueTaskSource<int>
{
    private ManualResetValueTaskSourceCore<int> core;    // mutable struct field

    public ValueTask<int> Start() => new(this, core.Version);

    public void Complete(int value) => core.SetResult(value);

    public int GetResult(short token)
    {
        int result = core.GetResult(token);
        core.Reset();                       // next Version; instance reusable
        return result;
    }

    public ValueTaskSourceStatus GetStatus(short token) => core.GetStatus(token);

    public void OnCompleted(Action<object?> c, object? s, short token,
        ValueTaskSourceOnCompletedFlags flags) => core.OnCompleted(c, s, token, flags);
}
```

The `core` field must not be `readonly`: it is a mutable struct and the methods
mutate it in place. That is one of the few places in modern C# where a mutable
struct field is the correct design, and the compiler will happily let you get
it wrong by copying.

## Concept 6 — pooling the state machine

```csharp
[AsyncMethodBuilder(typeof(PoolingAsyncValueTaskMethodBuilder<>))]
public async ValueTask<int> HotPathAsync() { /* ... */ }
```

This pools the boxed state machine for calls that suspend. Process-wide, the
same thing is `DOTNET_SYSTEM_THREADING_POOLASYNCVALUETASKS=1`. It is opt-in
because the GC handles short-lived gen0 objects extremely well, and a pool that
is misused is worse than no pool.

## Worked example — counting the allocations

Take a cache with a 95% hit rate, called two million times a second by a
serialiser. Per call:

| implementation | hit | miss |
|---|---|---|
| `async Task<byte[]>` | task + state machine box | task + box + inner task |
| `async ValueTask<byte[]>` | state machine box | box + inner task |
| split wrapper + async core | nothing | box + inner task |

The third row is the design this sector teaches, and the interesting column is
the first one: at a 95% hit rate, 1.9 million of those two million calls stop
allocating entirely. The 5% that miss are unchanged — they were always going to
allocate, because they were always going to wait.

Now change the hit rate to zero, which is what a "fetch from the database"
method looks like. Every row becomes identical except that the `ValueTask` rows
copy a bigger struct at every frame. That is the counter-case, and it is why
the same optimisation is right in one method and wrong in the one next to it.

## Worked example — how a misuse fails

```csharp
ValueTask<int> v = reader.ReadAsync(buffer);
if (v.IsCompletedSuccessfully) log.Debug("fast path");
int n = await v;          // fine so far
retryBuffer.Add(v);       // stored: the contract is broken here
// ... later, from another method
int again = await retryBuffer[0];    // asks a recycled source about a dead operation
```

Against a `Task`-backed value this runs correctly and ships. Against a pooled
`IValueTaskSource` — the same interface, a different implementation, perhaps a
framework upgrade away — the last line either throws
`InvalidOperationException` from the token check or, in a source that skips the
check for speed, returns another operation's result with no error at all.
There is no partial credit here, which is why the rules are stated as
absolutes rather than as guidance.

## Common mistakes

1. **Awaiting twice.** Works against a `Task`-backed value, corrupts against a
   pooled one.
2. **`async ValueTask<T>` everywhere.** You keep the state machine and gain
   almost nothing; the win comes from the non-async wrapper.
3. **Storing one in a field** so it can be "awaited later by whoever needs it".
4. **`.Result` on an incomplete `ValueTask`.** Not a block — undefined.
5. **Returning `ValueTask<T>` from a method that always does I/O.** Pure cost:
   you allocate the task anyway and copy a larger struct.
6. **A readonly `ManualResetValueTaskSourceCore<T>` field.** Every call
   mutates a copy; nothing works and nothing warns you.
7. **Assuming `IsCompleted` means success.** It includes faulted and cancelled.

## Interview angle

> "When would you return `ValueTask<T>` instead of `Task<T>`?"

When the method is called very often *and* usually completes synchronously — a
buffered read, a cache hit, a semaphore that is not contended — and I have
measured that the `Task` allocation matters. The saving is the allocation on
the synchronous path only; the slow path still allocates, plus a bigger struct
copy. In exchange the caller accepts a stricter contract: await once, do not
block, do not store, do not hand it to `WhenAll`. For anything else, `Task<T>`,
because it is immutable and safe to pass around.

Good follow-ups to be ready for: what the three internal states are; what
`Preserve()` is for; why there is no `ValueTask.WhenAll`; and what
`IValueTaskSource`'s version token protects against.

## Check yourself

1. Name the three things a `ValueTask<T>` can wrap.
2. Which of those makes the "await once" rule mandatory?
3. What does `Preserve()` do, and what does it cost?
4. Why is there no `ValueTask.WhenAll`?
5. Why should the cache-hit wrapper not be marked `async`?
6. What is the difference between `IsCompleted` and `IsCompletedSuccessfully`?
7. What happens if you call `.Result` on an incomplete `ValueTask<T>`?
8. Why must a `ManualResetValueTaskSourceCore<T>` field not be `readonly`?
9. What does the version token in `IValueTaskSource` protect against?
10. What exactly does `PoolingAsyncValueTaskMethodBuilder` pool?
11. Give one BCL API that returns `ValueTask<T>` and say why it fits.
12. Give a signature where `ValueTask<T>` is the wrong choice, and why.
13. Does `ValueTask` help a method that awaits a database call? Explain.
lessons.fullReading:
# Reading - csharp/v3cb02_valuetask_pooling

## Where it came from

`ValueTask<T>` arrived in .NET Core 2.0 for one concrete customer:
`Stream.ReadAsync`. Streams are read in loops, and buffered streams answer most
reads from memory. Every one of those synchronous answers allocated a
`Task<int>` whose only job was to carry an integer that was already known.
`Task.FromResult` caching helps for a handful of values, but a read returns a
byte count, and caching every plausible byte count is absurd.

The non-generic `ValueTask` came later, in .NET Core 2.1, together with
`IValueTaskSource`, because the same argument applied to `DisposeAsync`,
`WriteAsync` and — crucially — to operations that *do* suspend but happen
constantly, like socket receives. A server doing a million receives per second
cannot afford a promise object per receive, even when every one of them is
genuinely asynchronous. `IValueTaskSource` solved that by making the promise
reusable, which is the piece people miss when they think `ValueTask` is only
about synchronous completion.

`IAsyncEnumerator<T>.MoveNextAsync` returning `ValueTask<bool>` is the same
reasoning applied to language design: an async stream over a buffered source
answers most `MoveNextAsync` calls immediately, and a `Task<bool>` per item
would have made `await foreach` allocate per element forever.

## How the reuse protocol works

A source hands out `new ValueTask<T>(this, token)` where `token` is its current
version. The awaiter calls `GetStatus(token)`, then either `GetResult(token)`
or `OnCompleted(..., token, flags)`. The core compares the token to its version
and throws if they differ. When the operation is consumed, `Reset()` bumps the
version, and the instance is free to represent the next operation.

The consequence is the contract: an awaiter that keeps its `ValueTask` and asks
again after a `Reset` is asking about an operation that no longer exists. If the
core validates, you get an `InvalidOperationException` with a message about the
value task; if a hand-rolled source skips validation for speed, you get another
caller's data. Both outcomes are the same bug, and only one of them is
survivable.

`ValueTaskSourceOnCompletedFlags` carries `UseSchedulingContext` and
`FlowExecutionContext`, which is how the previous sector's context rules get
honoured by a hand-written source. Forgetting to flow `ExecutionContext` is the
classic hand-rolled-source bug: correlation ids vanish, and nobody connects it
to the networking layer somebody optimised last quarter.

## Performance notes, with numbers to reason about

The saving from a synchronous `ValueTask<T>` is one small heap allocation —
roughly 24 to 32 bytes plus the GC's eventual sweep. Gen0 allocation in .NET is
a pointer bump; collection of a gen0 object that died immediately is close to
free. So the arithmetic only becomes interesting at very high call rates, or
when allocation rate is pushing objects into gen1 and gen2 through sheer
volume.

Against that, `ValueTask<T>` costs you struct copying at every return and
parameter pass — 16 to 24 bytes instead of 8 — plus a branch on every await.
For a method called a thousand times a second the copy costs more than the
allocation saved. For a method called ten million times a second with a 95%
synchronous rate, the allocation dominates decisively.

The rule of thumb that survives contact with profilers: **`Task<T>` by default;
`ValueTask<T>` when the method is on a hot path, usually completes
synchronously, and the profile shows allocation.** Two of three is not enough.

Pooling shifts the second half of that. `PoolingAsyncValueTaskMethodBuilder`
recycles state-machine boxes so that even consistently-suspending methods stop
allocating. The published measurements show meaningful gains on tight async
loops and slight losses on everything else, which is exactly why it is opt-in
rather than default. Turning it on process-wide is a benchmark-and-see
decision, not a best practice.

## What the language had to add to make it work

`ValueTask<T>` could not simply be "a struct that is awaitable" — several
pieces of the language and runtime had to move to accommodate it, and knowing
which ones explains some otherwise arbitrary API shapes.

The awaiter had to be a struct too (`ValueTaskAwaiter<T>`), or every await
would have allocated the thing the type exists to avoid. `ConfigureAwait` had
to return yet another struct (`ConfiguredValueTaskAwaitable<T>`), which is why
the `_continueOnCapturedContext` flag lives inside the value itself rather than
in an awaiter wrapper. `IValueTaskSource<T>`'s `OnCompleted` takes an
`Action<object?>` plus a state object rather than a plain `Action`, precisely so
that a continuation can be registered without allocating a closure — the same
trick you see on `CancellationToken.Register` and on `Timer`.

And the async method builders had to be pluggable, which is the
`[AsyncMethodBuilder]` mechanism from sector 1. `AsyncValueTaskMethodBuilder<T>`
knows how to complete synchronously without ever creating a `Task`; the pooling
variant knows how to rent and return boxes. None of this required a change to
`await` itself, because `await` was duck-typed from the start. That decision,
made in C# 5 for reasons that had nothing to do with allocation, is what made
the whole `ValueTask` design possible seven years later.

## When not to use it

Do not return `ValueTask<T>` from:

- **A method that always does real I/O.** The task is allocated regardless; you
  have added struct copying and a caller-facing hazard for nothing.
- **A public API whose callers you do not control**, unless the performance
  case is strong and documented. Every caller now has four ways to write a
  silent bug.
- **Anything that will be composed.** If callers naturally want `WhenAll`,
  `ContinueWith`, caching or fan-out, you will spend your saving on `AsTask()`
  calls and then some.
- **An interface you expect people to implement casually.** Implementers get
  the same hazards, plus the temptation to hand-roll a source.

And do not hand-write an `IValueTaskSource<T>` without
`ManualResetValueTaskSourceCore<T>`. The core handles continuation storage,
context flow, the race between `OnCompleted` and `SetResult`, and the token
check. Those are exactly the four things that are easy to get subtly wrong and
impossible to debug from a bug report.

One more place to stop and think before reaching for it: **anything you will
want to test in isolation**. A `Task<T>`-returning seam is trivial to fake —
`Task.FromResult`, `Task.FromException`, a `TaskCompletionSource` you complete
when the test decides. All of that works for `ValueTask<T>` too, but the fake
is now `Task`-backed while production is source-backed, so the exact hazard
you most want a test to catch — a double consumption somewhere in the code
under test — is the one your fake cannot reproduce. Tests pass, production
returns the wrong customer's balance. If you do ship a `ValueTask`-returning
interface, it is worth writing at least one deliberately pooled fake so the
contract is exercised.

There is a broader lesson here that outlives `ValueTask`. This is an
optimisation that moves cost from one place (the allocator, which is very good
at its job) to another (the programmer's attention, which is not). That trade
is correct in a networking stack shipped to millions of processes and wrong in
the service you are writing this week. Knowing the mechanism is valuable
whether or not you ever type the keyword — because when you see `ValueTask` in
someone else's signature, you now know what they were optimising, what they
promised, and what you are not allowed to do with the thing they handed you.
