exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 - checking before you work

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB03_Cancellation/Ex1.cs`.

- `Cooperative.ProcessAsync(IReadOnlyList<int> items, CancellationToken token)`
  returns the running total of the items, checking the token **before** each
  item so an already-cancelled call does no work at all. It throws
  `OperationCanceledException` when cancelled.
- `Cooperative.Processed` counts how many items were handled across all calls.
- `Cooperative.CountUntilCancelled(IReadOnlyList<int> items, CancellationToken token)`
  returns how many items it managed to process before the token fired, instead
  of throwing — for the caller who wants partial progress.
- `Cooperative.IsPointless(CancellationToken token)` returns `true` when the
  token can never be cancelled (`CancellationToken.None`), so a hot path can
  skip its checks entirely.

Example: with a token cancelled up front, `ProcessAsync` throws and `Processed`
stays at `0`. Cancelling after two items makes `CountUntilCancelled` return
`2`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb03_cancellation_timeouts ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

"Before each item" is doing real work in that sentence. A loop that processes
then checks does one unit of work per cancellation — fine for adding integers,
not fine when the unit is a payment.

Put the check at the top of the loop body, and note that this also handles the
already-cancelled case for free: the first iteration throws before touching
anything.

## Hint 2

```csharp
foreach (int item in items)
{
    token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested();
    total += item;
    Processed++;
}
```

`ThrowIfCancellationRequested()` builds the exception with the right token
attached, which is what makes the resulting task end `Canceled` rather than
`Faulted`.

For the partial-progress version, do not throw: poll
`token.IsCancellationRequested` and `break`. Those are the two different
consumption styles, and the choice between them is a contract decision, not a
preference.

## Hint 3

`IsPointless` is about `CanBeCanceled`, which is `false` only for
`CancellationToken.None` (and `default`). It exists so hot code can avoid
registering callbacks it will never need:

```csharp
if (!token.CanBeCanceled) return FastPath();
```

You will see that check inside the BCL constantly, and almost never in
application code, where the branch costs more than it saves.

Left to you: whether partial progress should be a separate method or a flag.
Two methods is usually right — a caller who wants "all or nothing" and a caller
who wants "as much as possible" are asking different questions, and a boolean
parameter that changes whether a method throws is a design smell that survives
into every call site.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about it as a contract question first: when a caller cancels, what should
they get back? There are exactly two defensible answers, and this exercise asks
you to implement both.

"Throw" means the operation had no meaningful partial result — a transaction,
a parse, a request. "Return what I got" means progress is itself the answer — a
batch import, a scan, a drain. Match the shape to the meaning and the code
follows.

## Hint 2

A detail worth internalising: the two idioms produce different *task statuses*,
and downstream code branches on those.

```csharp
Task t1 = ProcessAsync(items, cancelled);         // ends Canceled
Task t2 = Task.Run(() => CountUntilCancelled(items, cancelled));  // ends RanToCompletion
```

`WhenAll`, ASP.NET Core's logging filters and every retry library treat those
two completely differently. Returning a partial result is *not* signalling
cancellation, and if the caller needed to know the difference, you have hidden
it from them.

## Hint 3

Once it passes, consider the granularity question that this exercise papers
over. Checking once per item is right when items are roughly equal and
individually short. It is wrong in two directions:

- **Items that take minutes.** A check between them means cancellation takes
  minutes to take effect. You need checks *inside* the unit, which means the
  token has to be passed into `Process`.
- **Items that take nanoseconds.** A million checks in a tight loop is a
  measurable cost for a signal that arrives once. Check every N iterations, or
  restructure into chunks.

The general rule: cancellation latency should be roughly the granularity of
your checks, so pick the granularity from the latency you promised.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 - timeout or cancellation?

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB03_Cancellation/Ex2.cs`. The same
`OperationCanceledException` arrives whether the caller gave up or your own
budget expired, and those mean opposite things.

- `Budget.CallAsync(Task<int> work, TimeSpan limit, TimeProvider time, CancellationToken token)`
  returns the work's result; throws `TimeoutException` when `limit` expires
  first, and `OperationCanceledException` when `token` fires first. The
  distinction must be reliable, not incidental.
- `Budget.Classify(Exception error, CancellationToken caller)` returns
  `"cancelled"` for an `OperationCanceledException` when `caller` was
  cancelled, `"timeout"` for a `TimeoutException`, `"failed"` otherwise.
- `Budget.Describe(TaskStatus status)` maps `RanToCompletion`/`Canceled`/
  `Faulted` to `"ok"`/`"cancelled"`/`"failed"`, anything else to `"pending"`.

The gate drives time with a `FakeTimeProvider`: it advances past `limit`
without any real waiting, and separately cancels the token, and checks that the
two paths produce different exception types.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb03_cancellation_timeouts ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The framework will classify for you if you let it. There is an overload of
`Task.WaitAsync` that takes both a `TimeSpan` and a `CancellationToken` — and a
.NET 8 overload that also takes a `TimeProvider`, which is how the gate can
advance the clock instead of waiting.

Look at what it throws in each case before writing any `catch`.

## Hint 2

```csharp
return await work.WaitAsync(limit, time, token);
```

`TimeoutException` when `limit` elapses; `OperationCanceledException` (actually
`TaskCanceledException`) when `token` fires. Two types, two meanings, no
inspection required.

`Classify` then becomes a `switch` on the exception with a `when` clause on the
caller's token — and the ordering matters, since the cancellation case must be
tested before any general `Exception` case.

## Hint 3

Why the alternative implementation is worse, and worth knowing anyway:

```csharp
using var budget = new CancellationTokenSource(limit, time);
using var linked = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(token, budget.Token);
try { return await work.WaitAsync(linked.Token); }
catch (OperationCanceledException) when (!token.IsCancellationRequested)
{
    throw new TimeoutException();
}
```

Same behaviour, four times the code, and one subtle hazard: the exception
carries the *linked* token, so testing `ex.CancellationToken == token` fails.
Filter on `token.IsCancellationRequested` instead.

That version does have a real advantage though — `linked.Token` can be passed
*into* the work so the callee stops too. `WaitAsync` only stops your wait.
Decide which you need; the sector's challenge needs the second.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from operations rather than from code. Write down what should happen in
your monitoring for each case:

- Caller cancelled: no log, no metric, no retry, no alert. A user closed a tab.
- Your budget expired: a counter, probably a circuit-breaker signal, possibly a
  retry, definitely a log at warning.

Two completely different responses. If your code cannot tell them apart, you
will pick one and be wrong half the time — usually by alerting on abandoned
requests, which trains everyone to ignore the alert.

## Hint 2

A test for your own understanding: which token is attached to the exception in
each of these?

```csharp
await work.WaitAsync(token);                       // token
await work.WaitAsync(limit, token);                 // token, or TimeoutException
await work.WaitAsync(linked.Token);                 // linked.Token, always
```

The third is the trap. `linked.Token` is neither of the parents, so any code
downstream comparing `ex.CancellationToken` to the caller's token gets `false`
even when the caller cancelled. Filter on the source's state, not the
exception's token.

## Hint 3

`Describe` looks like filler and is not. Status-based classification is what
`WhenAll`, hosting, and logging actually use, and the mapping is exactly where
people introduce bugs by treating `Canceled` as a kind of `Faulted`.

Worth knowing precisely: `TaskStatus` has seven values, three of which are
terminal (`RanToCompletion`, `Canceled`, `Faulted`) and four of which are not
(`Created`, `WaitingForActivation`, `WaitingToRun`, `Running`,
`WaitingForChildrenToComplete` — five, in fact, which is itself a reason to use
`IsCompleted`/`IsCanceled`/`IsFaulted` rather than switching on the enum in
production code).

The exercise asks for the enum switch so that you have looked at it once. In
real code, prefer the boolean properties: they are stable, unambiguous, and do
not require you to remember which of the non-terminal states exist.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 - linked sources, and disposing them

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB03_Cancellation/Ex3.cs`.

- `Linked.RunAsync(Func<CancellationToken, Task<int>> work, TimeSpan limit, TimeProvider time, CancellationToken caller)`
  creates its own budget source, links it with `caller`, and passes the
  **linked** token into `work` so the work itself can stop. Both sources are
  disposed before the method returns, on every path.
- `Linked.Registrations(CancellationToken token)` returns how many callbacks
  are currently registered on a token — implement it by keeping your own
  counter around `Register`/`Dispose` in `Linked.Watch(CancellationToken)`,
  which returns an `IDisposable` that unhooks.
- `Linked.LeakDemo(CancellationToken longLived, int count)` creates `count`
  linked sources **without** disposing them and returns the count — the shape
  the gate uses to show the leak.
- `Linked.NoLeak(CancellationToken longLived, int count)` does the same and
  disposes each one.

The gate holds a long-lived source, calls both, and compares how many
registrations remain attached to it afterwards: `count` versus zero.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb03_cancellation_timeouts ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The `using` in `using var linked = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(...)`
is not decoration. Creating the linked source *registers a callback on every
parent*, and disposing it is what removes them.

So the leak is not the source object itself — it is the entry the parent token
now holds, which roots that object and everything it captures.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public static async Task<int> RunAsync(
    Func<CancellationToken, Task<int>> work, TimeSpan limit,
    TimeProvider time, CancellationToken caller)
{
    using var budget = new CancellationTokenSource(limit, time);
    using var linked = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(caller, budget.Token);
    return await work(linked.Token).ConfigureAwait(false);
}
```

Two `using`s: the first also disposes a timer, the second unhooks two
registrations. `LeakDemo` is the same loop with the `using` removed, which is
the point.

## Hint 3

The reason this is the most common cancellation leak in production: the parent
is usually something that lives for the whole process.
`IHostApplicationLifetime.ApplicationStopping`, a connection-scoped token, a
long-poll session. Each undisposed child adds an entry to a list that is never
walked until shutdown, and each entry roots a request-scoped object graph.

The profile is unmistakable once you know it: memory climbing in a straight
line under steady load, a heap dump full of `CancellationTokenSource` and
`CancellationCallbackInfo`, and a GC root path back to one token created at
startup.

Left to you: whether to use `using` or `try`/`finally`. `using` is right almost
always; the exception is when the source must outlive the method — a long poll,
a subscription — and then the object owning it becomes responsible for
disposal, which usually means it needs to implement `IDisposable` itself. A
`CancellationTokenSource` stored in a field is a disposal obligation, and the
compiler will not remind you.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Approach it by asking what a token actually holds. It is a struct wrapping a
reference to the source; the source holds state plus a list of registrations.
"Linking" means "put an entry in the parent's list that cancels me".

Once you see it as a list, the leak is obvious: things go into lists and, unless
something takes them out, they stay.

## Hint 2

`Watch` is where the exercise stops being about theory. The shape you need:

```csharp
public static IDisposable Watch(CancellationToken token)
{
    Interlocked.Increment(ref registered);
    CancellationTokenRegistration reg = token.Register(static () => { });
    return new Unhook(reg);        // Dispose: reg.Dispose(); Interlocked.Decrement(...)
}
```

Note the `static` lambda: with no captures, the delegate is cached and the
registration costs nothing extra. `Register` has state-taking overloads for the
same reason — the API is designed for hot paths that must not allocate.

## Hint 3

Two facts about `CancellationTokenRegistration.Dispose()` that are worth having
before you need them.

It **blocks** if the callback is currently executing on another thread, until
that callback finishes. That is deliberate — after `Dispose` returns you are
guaranteed the callback is not running — and it is a real synchronisation point
that can deadlock if the callback is waiting for the disposing thread. .NET 8
added `Unregister()`, which removes without waiting, precisely for that case.

And registering on an **already-cancelled** token invokes the callback
immediately, synchronously, on the registering thread, before `Register`
returns. If you register while holding a lock, that callback runs under your
lock. Both facts point the same direction: keep cancellation callbacks tiny,
non-blocking, and free of locks.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 - registering callbacks

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB03_Cancellation/Ex4.cs`. `Register` is the bridge to APIs
that have never heard of `CancellationToken`.

- `Bridge.WaitAsync(TaskCompletionSource<int> source, CancellationToken token)`
  returns the source's task, but cancels the returned task when `token` fires —
  implemented with `token.Register`, not `Task.WaitAsync`. The registration must
  be disposed on both paths.
- `Bridge.Registered` counts live registrations; the gate asserts it returns to
  zero after each call, cancelled or not.
- `Bridge.RunsImmediately(CancellationToken cancelled, List<string> log)`
  registers a callback that appends `"fired"` on an **already-cancelled** token
  and returns `true` if the callback had already run by the time `Register`
  returned.
- `Bridge.NoClosure(TaskCompletionSource<int> source, CancellationToken token)`
  registers using the state-taking overload with a `static` lambda, so no
  closure is allocated.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb03_cancellation_timeouts ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The pattern has three parts and all three matter: register a callback that
completes something, await, and dispose the registration in a `finally`.

Miss the `finally` and a successful call leaves a callback attached to the
token — which is fine for a request-scoped token and a leak for anything
longer-lived.

## Hint 2

```csharp
CancellationTokenRegistration registration = token.Register(
    static state => ((TaskCompletionSource<int>)state!).TrySetCanceled(), source);

try { return await source.Task.ConfigureAwait(false); }
finally { registration.Dispose(); }
```

`TrySetCanceled` rather than `SetCanceled`, because the real result and the
cancellation can race and only one may win.

The `static` lambda plus the state argument is the no-closure form: the
delegate has no captures, so the compiler caches a single instance.

## Hint 3

`RunsImmediately` demonstrates the behaviour that surprises people: registering
on a token that is *already* cancelled does not add anything to a list. It
invokes your callback synchronously, on your thread, before `Register` returns.

That is usually what you want — otherwise an already-cancelled token would be
silently ignored — but it has a consequence: if you register while holding a
lock, the callback runs under your lock. Combined with the fact that `Cancel()`
also runs callbacks inline on the cancelling thread, the rule becomes: **cancellation
callbacks must be short, non-blocking, and must not take locks.**

Left to you: `Dispose()` versus `Unregister()`. `Dispose` blocks until a
currently-running callback finishes, which gives you a strong guarantee and an
opportunity to deadlock. `Unregister()` (.NET 8) removes without waiting.
Prefer `Dispose` unless you have a specific reason, and know why the reason
exists.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Frame it as: how do you make something cancellable that was written before
cancellation existed? A file handle, a native callback, an event, a
`TaskCompletionSource` somebody else completes.

The answer is always the same shape — you cannot stop the operation, so you
give the *waiter* a way out and you leave the operation running. Write that
sentence in the method's doc comment; it is the honest description of what your
method does.

## Hint 2

Compare what you are writing with what `Task.WaitAsync(token)` does internally.
It is almost exactly this: a `TaskCompletionSource`-like promise, a
registration on the token, a continuation on the original task, and disposal of
the registration when either wins.

Writing it once tells you two things the docs do not emphasise: the original
task is untouched, and the composed task's completion is a race that
`TrySet*` must arbitrate. Both facts explain behaviour you will see later —
notably that a cancelled `WaitAsync` leaves the original running and, if it
later faults, produces an unobserved task exception.

## Hint 3

The allocation angle in `NoClosure` is worth taking seriously, because it is
the same pattern as `IValueTaskSource.OnCompleted` in the previous sector and
`ThreadPool.UnsafeQueueUserWorkItem`.

```csharp
token.Register(() => source.TrySetCanceled());              // closure: 1 object
token.Register(static s => ((TaskCompletionSource<int>)s!).TrySetCanceled(), source);  // 0
```

The BCL threads this "callback plus state object" shape through every hot
registration API precisely so infrastructure code can register without
allocating. In application code the closure is irrelevant. Recognising *why*
the two-argument overload exists is the useful part — it tells you which layer
of the framework you are looking at.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 - wrapping something that cannot be cancelled

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB03_Cancellation/Ex5.cs`. Some work simply does not accept
a token — a legacy client, a native call, a third-party SDK. You can still give
the caller a way out, as long as you are honest about what you did.

- `Abandon.WaitOrAbandonAsync(Task<int> work, CancellationToken token)` returns
  the work's result, or throws `OperationCanceledException` when the token
  fires first. The name says what happens to `work`: nothing.
- `Abandon.Abandoned` counts how many calls returned by abandoning work that
  was still running.
- `Abandon.ObserveFailures(Task<int> work)` attaches a continuation that
  observes an abandoned task's exception, so a later fault does not become an
  unobserved task exception.
- `Abandon.StillRunning(Task<int> work)` returns `true` when the abandoned task
  has not completed — the fact the method's caller most needs to know.

Example: cancel while `work` is pending, and `WaitOrAbandonAsync` throws while
`StillRunning(work)` is `true`. Completing `work` afterwards still succeeds.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb03_cancellation_timeouts ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

There is no trick that stops the work. Accept that first, then design around
it: your method's job is to stop *waiting* and to leave the system in a state
where the still-running work does not cause a second problem later.

Two problems to head off: an exception nobody observes, and a caller who
believes the work stopped.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public static async Task<int> WaitOrAbandonAsync(Task<int> work, CancellationToken token)
{
    try
    {
        return await work.WaitAsync(token).ConfigureAwait(false);
    }
    catch (OperationCanceledException)
    {
        Abandoned++;
        ObserveFailures(work);      // the orphan may still fault
        throw;
    }
}
```

`ObserveFailures` is a continuation that touches `task.Exception`:

```csharp
_ = work.ContinueWith(static t => _ = t.Exception,
    TaskContinuationOptions.OnlyOnFaulted | TaskContinuationOptions.ExecuteSynchronously);
```

## Hint 3

Why observing matters. A faulted task whose exception is never read used to
crash the process at finalisation in .NET 4.0; since 4.5 it raises
`TaskScheduler.UnobservedTaskException` and is otherwise swallowed. Either way,
an abandoned task that later fails is an error nobody logged — and in a service
with a retry loop that is how a dependency outage becomes invisible.

The bigger design point is in the naming. A method called `WaitOrAbandonAsync`
tells its caller what really happened; one called `CancelAsync` lies. If your
API abandons work, say so in the name or the doc comment, because the caller's
next decision — retry? compensate? assume nothing was written? — depends
entirely on it.

Left to you: whether to abandon at all. The alternatives are to refuse
cancellation for that operation (honest, sometimes correct) or to push the
token down into the dependency by replacing it (expensive, always better).
Abandoning is the pragmatic middle, and it should feel slightly uncomfortable.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what the *system* looks like one second after your method throws. There is
a connection still open, a query still running, possibly a write about to
commit. Your caller has moved on and may already be retrying.

That picture is the exercise. The code is six lines; the judgement is knowing
which six.

## Hint 2

Here is the failure mode that makes this worth practising. A payment call is
abandoned on timeout; the caller retries; both calls eventually reach the
provider; the customer is charged twice. Nothing in the code was wrong except
the assumption that a cancelled wait meant an undone operation.

The mitigations are all outside the token system: idempotency keys, a
`Conditional` write, a reconciliation job. When you write an abandoning
wrapper, that is the conversation you are starting.

## Hint 3

A subtlety with `StillRunning`: it is a snapshot, and by the time the caller
reads it the answer may have changed. That is not a flaw to fix — it is the
nature of the question — but it does mean the method should be used for
diagnostics and decisions like "log this", not for control flow like "if it is
still running, do X".

The general shape of that rule: any predicate about concurrent state is stale
the instant it returns. Sector 7 makes this precise for collections; here it is
enough to notice that `IsCompleted`, `Count`, `IsCancellationRequested` and
friends all answer "was it true a moment ago". Code that branches on them needs
to be correct for both answers anyway.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 - the chain is only as good as its weakest link

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB03_Cancellation/Ex6.cs`. A three-layer call chain, one of
which drops the token. Repair it.

- `Chain.HandleAsync(int[] ids, CancellationToken token)` — the entry point;
  sums `LoadAsync` over each id, checking the token between ids.
- `Chain.LoadAsync(int id, CancellationToken token)` — calls `FetchAsync` and
  must forward the token.
- `Chain.FetchAsync(int id, CancellationToken token)` — awaits
  `Chain.Source(id)` (a `Func<int, Task<int>>` field the gate sets) with the
  token honoured.
- `Chain.Broken(int id)` is left in the file as the counter-example: it calls
  `FetchAsync(id, CancellationToken.None)`, swallowing the caller's intent.
  Leave it, and implement `Chain.UsesNone(Delegate call)` returning `true` for
  it — the gate checks you can name the smell.
- `Chain.Depth` counts how many layers actually observed a cancellation.

With a token cancelled before the call, `HandleAsync` must throw without
invoking `Source` at all.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb03_cancellation_timeouts ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The rule is boring and absolute: every method that takes a token passes it to
every method it calls that accepts one. A chain works only if there are no
gaps.

Write the three real methods with the token threaded through and check the
requirement at the top: an already-cancelled token means `Source` is never
invoked, which means the check must happen before the first call, not after.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public static async Task<int> HandleAsync(int[] ids, CancellationToken token)
{
    int total = 0;
    foreach (int id in ids)
    {
        token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested();
        total += await LoadAsync(id, token).ConfigureAwait(false);
    }

    return total;
}
```

Each inner layer does the same: accept, forward, and let the innermost one do
the actual honouring with `WaitAsync(token)` or by passing it to something that
understands it.

`UsesNone` can be as simple as comparing `call.Method.Name` against the known
broken method's name — the gate is checking recognition, not reflection
prowess.

## Hint 3

Where chains break in real code, in order of frequency:

1. **An overload without a token.** Someone adds `LoadAsync(int id)` as a
   convenience and it passes `CancellationToken.None`. Every caller who takes
   the convenience overload has silently opted out.
2. **A cached wrapper.** A memoising layer awaits the inner call without a
   token because "it's just a cache".
3. **A `Task.Run`.** The delegate captures the token or it does not; nothing
   forces the issue.
4. **An interface defined without a token parameter.** The most expensive one,
   because fixing it is a breaking change.

That last one is why the guidance is to put a `CancellationToken` on every
async interface method from the beginning, even when today's implementation
ignores it. Adding one later means changing every implementer and every caller.

Left to you: whether to give the parameter a `= default`. On a public API it is
kind; on an internal one it is how gap number one gets introduced. Prefer
non-optional internally.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Come at it as a code reviewer with a grep. What would you search for to find
broken links in an unfamiliar codebase?

`CancellationToken.None`, `default)` at a call site that has a token in scope,
and async methods with no token parameter at all. Those three searches find
almost every gap, and running them once on a real repository is more
educational than this exercise.

## Hint 2

There is a compiler-assisted version of this discipline worth knowing: analyzer
rule **CA2016**, "Forward the CancellationToken parameter to methods that take
one". Turn it on and it flags exactly the gap this exercise is about, at build
time, with a code fix.

It does not catch the case where a method has no token parameter at all —
that is a design review question, not an analyzer one — but it removes the
mechanical mistakes, which are the majority.

## Hint 3

The subtle case that neither the analyzer nor this exercise covers: a token
forwarded correctly but *ignored* by the innermost layer.

```csharp
public static async Task<int> FetchAsync(int id, CancellationToken token)
{
    return await Source(id);          // token accepted, never used
}
```

Every layer forwards, the analyzer is happy, and cancellation still does
nothing. The only defence is a test: cancel the token and assert that the
operation throws `OperationCanceledException` rather than completing. That test
is cheap, it is deterministic, and it is the one people skip — which is why
"cancellation is wired up but does not work" is such a common finding.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 - retry and backoff without waiting

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB03_Cancellation/Ex7.cs`. Write a retry policy whose tests
run in microseconds.

- `Retry.RunAsync(Func<int, Task<int>> attempt, int maxAttempts, TimeProvider time, CancellationToken token)`
  calls `attempt(n)` for `n` from `0`; on failure it waits
  `2^n` seconds via `Task.Delay(delay, time, token)` and tries again, up to
  `maxAttempts`. The last failure is rethrown, not wrapped.
- `OperationCanceledException` from an attempt is **not** retried — it goes
  straight out.
- `Retry.Delays` records the delays actually requested, in order, so the gate
  can assert the schedule is `1s, 2s, 4s`.
- `Retry.Attempts` counts attempts made.
- `Retry.NextDelay(int attempt)` returns the delay for a given attempt number,
  as a pure function.

The gate uses a `FakeTimeProvider`, advancing it after each failure, so a
policy with a one-hour maximum backoff is tested instantly.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb03_cancellation_timeouts ex7
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start with what you want the test to look like:

```csharp
var time = new FakeTimeProvider();
Task<int> run = Retry.RunAsync(FailTwiceThenSucceed, 3, time, token);
time.Advance(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1));
time.Advance(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2));
Assert.Equal(42, await run);
Assert.Equal([1s, 2s], Retry.Delays);
```

Every line of that is impossible with a real clock and trivial with an injected
one. Design the method so that test can exist.

## Hint 2

Note where the token appears: not only in the attempt, but in the *delay*. A
retry that ignores cancellation while sleeping will happily wait sixty seconds
after the caller has gone away, holding whatever the operation held.

`Task.Delay(delay, time, token)` throws `TaskCanceledException` when the token
fires during the wait — which is the correct behaviour and, note, will be
caught by a bare `catch` if you put one before the cancellation clause. This is
the third time in this sector that clause ordering has been the bug; that
repetition is the lesson.

## Hint 3

Worth knowing what the ecosystem does so you can decide when to write your own.
Polly (now `Microsoft.Extensions.Resilience`) gives you retry, timeout, circuit
breaker, hedging and rate limiting as composable strategies, all
`TimeProvider`-aware, all with the jitter and predicate support this exercise
skips.

The reason to write one by hand once is that resilience policies are the
easiest place in a system to be confidently wrong. A retry without a cap
amplifies an outage. A retry on a non-idempotent write duplicates data. A
retry that swallows cancellation keeps working for a caller that has gone. You
should be able to name each of those failure modes before you configure a
library that hides them.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 - draining, with a hard deadline

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB03_Cancellation/Ex8.cs`. Shutdown in three phases: stop
accepting, finish what is in flight, and give up honestly when the grace period
runs out.

```csharp
public sealed class Drain
{
    public bool TryAccept(Task<int> work);        // false once stopping
    public Task<string> ShutdownAsync(TimeSpan grace, TimeProvider time);
}
```

- `TryAccept` adds the task to the in-flight set and returns `true` — until
  shutdown has begun, after which it returns `false` without adding.
- `ShutdownAsync` stops accepting, waits for the in-flight set with `grace` as
  a hard deadline, and returns `"drained: <n>"` when everything finished or
  `"forced: <n>"` naming how many were still running when the deadline passed.
- `Drain.InFlight` reports the current count.
- Cleanup must not use the stopping signal as its own deadline — the grace
  period is a separate budget.

Example: two accepted tasks, one completes, `ShutdownAsync` with the fake clock
advanced past `grace` returns `"forced: 1"`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb03_cancellation_timeouts ex8
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Think about who reads the return value. A container orchestrator sees an exit
code; an operator sees a log line; a dashboard sees a metric. All three need to
know whether the shutdown was clean, because that is the difference between "a
normal deploy" and "we dropped work on the floor".

So `"drained"` versus `"forced"` is not string formatting — it is the shutdown's
only output. Design it as the signal it is.

## Hint 2

The concurrency detail that makes `TryAccept` interesting: there is a race
between "check the flag" and "add to the set". If shutdown begins between those
two operations, you have added work that nobody will wait for.

The whole method needs to be atomic with respect to the flag flip:

```csharp
lock (gate)
{
    if (stopping) return false;
    inFlight.Add(work);
    return true;
}
```

Sector 7 covers why that is the right shape and what the alternatives cost.
Here, notice only that "check then act" across two pieces of shared state is
never safe without something making it one step.

## Hint 3

Real hosts formalise all of this and it is worth knowing the names, because
your code will live inside one.

ASP.NET Core's generic host gives every `IHostedService` a `StopAsync(CancellationToken)`
whose token is already bounded by `HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout` — 30 seconds by
default, and very frequently too short for a real drain. `IHostApplicationLifetime`
exposes `ApplicationStopping` (start draining) and `ApplicationStopped` (it is
over). Kubernetes adds `SIGTERM`, `terminationGracePeriodSeconds`, and the
readiness probe you must fail *first* so the load balancer stops sending you
requests before you start refusing them.

The whole sequence is the same three phases as your `Drain`, with the load
balancer as phase zero. Getting phase zero wrong is the most common cause of
"we see 502s during every deploy" — the pod stops accepting before the traffic
stops arriving.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge - retry with a per-attempt timeout and an overall deadline

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB03_Cancellation/Challenge.cs`. Combine everything: two
budgets, three outcomes, and no leaks.

```csharp
public static Task<string> RunAsync(
    Func<CancellationToken, Task<int>> attempt,
    TimeSpan perAttempt,
    TimeSpan overall,
    int maxAttempts,
    TimeProvider time,
    CancellationToken caller);
```

Rules:

- Each attempt gets its own timeout of `perAttempt`, expressed as a linked
  token so the attempt itself stops — not merely the wait.
- The whole call gets `overall` as a deadline, also linked with `caller`.
- Returns `"ok: <value>"` on success.
- An attempt that times out is retried, as long as the overall deadline has not
  passed and attempts remain.
- Exhausting attempts returns `"failed: <last exception type name>"`.
- Exceeding the overall deadline returns `"deadline"`.
- `caller` cancelling throws `OperationCanceledException` out of the method —
  it is never reported as a failure.
- Every `CancellationTokenSource` you create is disposed, including one per
  attempt.

The gate drives a `FakeTimeProvider` and asserts on all five outcomes plus a
registration count that must return to zero.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb03_cancellation_timeouts challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two budgets means two sources, at two different scopes. The overall one is
created once, outside the loop, linked with the caller. The per-attempt one is
created inside the loop, linked with the overall one — so an attempt stops when
its own timeout fires *or* when the overall deadline passes *or* when the
caller gives up.

Draw that three-level tree first; the code is then a transcription of it.

## Hint 2

```csharp
using var deadline = new CancellationTokenSource(overall, time);
using var outer = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(caller, deadline.Token);

for (int n = 0; n < maxAttempts; n++)
{
    using var perAttemptSource = new CancellationTokenSource(perAttempt, time);
    using var inner = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(outer.Token, perAttemptSource.Token);

    try { return $"ok: {await attempt(inner.Token)}"; }
    catch (OperationCanceledException) when (caller.IsCancellationRequested) { throw; }
    catch (OperationCanceledException) when (deadline.IsCancellationRequested) { return "deadline"; }
    catch (OperationCanceledException) { /* this attempt timed out: retry */ }
    catch (Exception ex) when (n + 1 < maxAttempts) { last = ex; }
}
```

Four clauses in that order. Each one asks a *source* whether it fired, never
the exception's token — the exception carries `inner.Token`, which matches
nothing.

## Hint 3

The classification order is the whole challenge, and it is worth stating why
each position is forced.

`caller` first: a caller who gave up outranks everything, and reporting their
cancellation as a timeout would put a non-event in your error metrics.
`deadline` second: the overall budget is a real outcome the caller asked for,
distinct from a single attempt's failure. Per-attempt third: the only one that
retries. General failure last, and only when attempts remain.

Get the order wrong and each mistake has a specific production signature:
caller-cancellations logged as timeouts, deadline exceeded reported as
`"failed"`, or — worst — a retry loop that keeps going after the caller has
gone away.

Left to you: whether "deadline" should also carry the last exception. There is
a good argument for `"deadline after 3 attempts, last: TimeoutException"`,
because a deadline with no context is the least actionable log line in any
system. The gate wants the plain string; your production version should not.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Enumerate the outcomes before writing a line, because a method with five of
them is a method whose tests you want to write first:

1. success
2. attempt timed out, retry available → loop
3. attempts exhausted → `"failed: T"`
4. overall deadline → `"deadline"`
5. caller cancelled → throw

Then ask, for each: which source is cancelled at that moment? That question
produces your catch clauses directly, and in the right order.

## Hint 2

The disposal requirement is not busywork. Count the sources created for three
attempts: one deadline, one outer link, and three attempt sources plus three
inner links — eight objects, each holding registrations on its parents.

Without `using` inside the loop, the outer token accumulates registrations for
the life of the call, and if the caller's token is application-scoped, the
outer source accumulates on *it* for the life of the process. This is the leak
from ex3, one nesting level deeper, which is exactly where it hides in real
code.

## Hint 3

One design question the exercise deliberately leaves open: should a retried
attempt be *abandoned* or *stopped*?

Because you pass `inner.Token` into `attempt`, a well-behaved attempt stops on
its own timeout, which is the good case — no orphaned work, no double writes.
But `attempt` is somebody else's delegate, and if it ignores the token, your
timeout only stopped your wait. You are then retrying an operation that is
still in flight.

Production answers: require idempotency keys for anything retried, or hedge
deliberately (issue attempt two *while* one is running and take the first
answer, which is a technique, not an accident). What you must not do is assume
the first attempt stopped because you asked. That assumption, applied to a
payment API, is a well-documented way to charge people twice.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 - four broken snippets

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB03_Cancellation/Review1.cs`. Four cancellation bugs, each
one you will meet in a real review. Name them, then write the repaired version.

- `Audit.Diagnose(string symptom)` maps a symptom to its cause, exactly:
  - `"cancelled requests appear as errors"` → `"catch clause ordering"`
  - `"memory grows under load"` → `"undisposed linked source"`
  - `"cancellation does nothing"` → `"token not forwarded"`
  - `"every later call times out"` → `"CancelAfter on a shared source"`
  - anything else → `"unknown"`
- `Audit.RepairedCatch(Task<int> work, CancellationToken token)` returns
  `"ok: <n>"` or `"failed: <Type>"`, and lets `OperationCanceledException` out.
- `Audit.RepairedLink(Func<CancellationToken, Task<int>> work, TimeSpan limit, TimeProvider time, CancellationToken caller)`
  is ex3's shape with correct disposal.
- `Audit.RepairedForward(Func<int, CancellationToken, Task<int>> inner, int id, CancellationToken token)`
  forwards rather than passing `CancellationToken.None`.
- `Audit.RepairedTimeout(TimeSpan limit, TimeProvider time)` returns a **fresh**
  source per call rather than calling `CancelAfter` on a shared one.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb03_cancellation_timeouts review1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Read the four symptoms as a triage list. Each one is a thing an operator says
before anyone has looked at code, and each maps to exactly one mistake from
this sector. Getting from symptom to cause without reading the code is the
skill being tested.

The repairs are then one or two lines each; you have written every one of them
already in this sector.

## Hint 2

The fourth symptom is the one that needs explaining. `CancelAfter` on a shared,
long-lived `CancellationTokenSource` sets a timer *on that source*. Once it
fires, the source is cancelled permanently — a `CancellationTokenSource` is
one-shot — so every future operation using that token starts already cancelled.

```csharp
// wrong: shared source, now permanently cancelled after the first timeout
sharedSource.CancelAfter(limit);

// right: a fresh source per operation
return new CancellationTokenSource(limit, time);
```

That "every later call times out instantly" symptom is unmistakable once you
have seen it, and baffling before.

## Hint 3

For `RepairedCatch`, the clause order that keeps cancellation out of the error
path:

```csharp
try { return $"ok: {await work.ConfigureAwait(false)}"; }
catch (OperationCanceledException) { throw; }
catch (Exception ex) { return $"failed: {ex.GetType().Name}"; }
```

The equivalent single-clause form is
`catch (Exception ex) when (ex is not OperationCanceledException)`, which is
more compact and, in my view, slightly worse — the two-clause version makes the
rethrow visible, and the rethrow is the behaviour a reviewer needs to see.

Left to you: which style to standardise on. Pick one and apply it everywhere;
the failure mode is a codebase with both, where the third pattern somebody adds
gets it wrong and nobody notices because there was no pattern to violate.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Try writing the *tests* for these four repairs before the repairs. Each one has
a one-line assertion that would have caught it:

1. cancel the token, assert the method throws rather than returning `"failed"`
2. run the operation 1000 times, assert the parent's registration count is zero
3. cancel the token, assert `inner` observed a cancelled token
4. call twice, assert the second call is not already cancelled

None of these are hard tests. All four bugs ship regularly, because nobody
writes them.

## Hint 2

A different lens on the same four: each is a *lifetime* mistake.

- Clause ordering: an exception's meaning has a lifetime — it must not be
  reclassified on the way up.
- Undisposed link: a registration outlives the operation that created it.
- Not forwarding: intent fails to propagate down a call's lifetime.
- Shared `CancelAfter`: a one-shot signal applied to an object with a longer
  life than the operation.

Cancellation bugs are almost always about something living longer or shorter
than it should. That framing catches the fifth one you have not seen yet.

## Hint 3

The one that deserves a permanent place in your review checklist is number
four's general form: **`CancellationTokenSource` is single-use**. There is no
reset. Once cancelled, always cancelled; `Token.IsCancellationRequested` stays
true for ever.

That means any source stored in a field is a source that can be permanently
poisoned by one timeout, one shutdown signal, or one `Cancel()` from a code
path you forgot about. Sources belong to operations, and operations are
usually shorter than the objects that run them.

The corollary shows up when people try to build a "restartable" component: you
cannot reuse the source, so you replace it — and now you have the generation-swap
problem from sector 1's challenge, with the same `Interlocked.CompareExchange`
answer. Recognising that these are the same problem is a good sign you have
internalised both.

lessons.title: V3·CB3 — Cancellation, timeouts and cooperative shutdown
lessons.summary: Nothing in .NET can stop running code from outside. Cancellation is a signal plus a discipline, timeouts are cancellation with a clock attached, and graceful shutdown is both applied to a whole process. This sector covers linked sources, registration leaks, TimeProvider and draining.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·CB3 — Cancellation, timeouts and cooperative shutdown

`Thread.Abort` was removed from .NET Core, and its removal is the premise of
this sector. Killing a thread mid-operation leaves locks held, files half
written, static state half updated, and `finally` blocks unreliable — the
runtime cannot know what invariants the thread was between. So .NET has no way
to stop running code from outside. What it has instead is a signal, and a set
of conventions for code that wants to listen.

That single fact generates everything else. **A `CancellationToken` cancels
nothing.** It is a flag with a callback list. Code that checks it can stop;
code that does not will run to completion no matter how urgently you cancel.
When you `await work.WaitAsync(token)` and the token fires, you have stopped
*waiting* — the work carries on, holding its connection, finishing its write,
eventually completing into a task nobody is holding. Understanding that
sentence is the difference between using this API and believing in it.

**The shape of the API.** `CancellationTokenSource` is the producer: it owns
`Cancel()`, `CancelAfter(delay)`, and — since .NET 8 — `CancelAsync()`.
`CancellationToken` is the consumer's read-only view: `IsCancellationRequested`,
`ThrowIfCancellationRequested()`, `Register(callback)`, `CanBeCanceled`,
`WaitHandle`. `CancellationTokenRegistration` is what `Register` hands back, and
disposing it is how you unhook — a detail that turns into a memory leak the
moment a short-lived operation registers against a long-lived token.

**Two idioms cover almost everything.** When you control the loop, check
between units of work:

```csharp
foreach (Item item in items)
{
    token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested();
    Process(item);
}
```

When you are waiting on somebody else's task, stop the wait:

```csharp
Result r = await work.WaitAsync(token);       // .NET 6+
```

Both raise `OperationCanceledException`. That type gets special treatment
throughout the framework: a task that ends with one whose token matches is
`TaskStatus.Canceled` rather than `Faulted`; ASP.NET Core does not log it as an
error; retry policies do not retry it. Producing a plain exception where a
cancellation was meant, or catching cancellation and reporting it as failure,
breaks all three behaviours at once.

**Timeouts are cancellation with a clock.** `new CancellationTokenSource(delay)`
and `source.CancelAfter(delay)` fire the same signal a timer thread later. That
means a timeout arrives at the awaiting code as `OperationCanceledException`,
indistinguishable from the caller giving up — unless you keep the two sources
separate and check which one fired. `ex.CancellationToken` tells you, and
`Task.WaitAsync(TimeSpan)` avoids the question entirely by throwing
`TimeoutException` instead. The distinction matters because the two mean
opposite things operationally: a caller cancelling is a non-event, and your own
timeout expiring is a signal about the dependency you were calling.

**Linked sources join two lifetimes.** `CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(a, b)`
gives a source that fires when either input does — the standard way to combine
"the caller gave up" with "my own budget expired". It also registers callbacks
on both inputs, which is why it is `IDisposable` and why *not* disposing it is
a real leak: an undisposed linked source stays attached to the parent token for
as long as the parent lives, and a long-lived parent plus a per-request child
means unbounded growth. `using var linked = ...` every single time.

**One-shot, always.** A `CancellationTokenSource` cannot be reset. Once
cancelled it stays cancelled, and every token handed out from it is cancelled
for ever after. That single property explains a whole family of bugs: a source
stored in a field and given a `CancelAfter` will, after its first timeout,
start every subsequent operation already cancelled. Sources belong to
operations, and operations are almost always shorter-lived than the objects
running them.

**Graceful shutdown is the same mechanism at process scale.** A host signals a
stopping token; components stop accepting new work, finish what is in flight,
and get a bounded grace period before the process exits anyway. Each of those
three phases is a different use of the same primitives, and the interesting
engineering is in the third: deciding what "abandon" means for work you cannot
finish, and making sure the decision is deliberate rather than a `kill -9`.

**The discipline that makes all of it work.** Cancellation is the one feature
in this course that is only as good as its least careful call site. A token
that reaches nine layers and is dropped by the tenth cancels nothing, and the
symptom — "we wired up cancellation and it does nothing" — points at no
particular line. So the conventions are worth adopting wholesale rather than
case by case: the token is the last parameter, it is named consistently, it is
non-optional on internal methods, every async interface method takes one from
the day it is written, and analyzer rule CA2016 is on so the compiler catches
the mechanical omissions. The design mistakes it cannot catch — an interface
defined without a token, a convenience overload that passes
`CancellationToken.None` — are the expensive ones, because fixing them later
means changing every implementer.

**And one asymmetry to hold on to.** Accepting a token is cheap and forwarding
it is free, but *honouring* it costs design work: you have to decide what a
half-finished operation leaves behind. A cancelled read leaves nothing. A
cancelled write might leave a row, a file, a charge. That is why "is this
cancellable?" is a question about your data model rather than about your
plumbing, and why some operations should accept a token and deliberately
ignore it, with a comment saying so.

The gates here never sleep. Cancellation is driven by an explicit `Cancel()`,
timeouts by an injected `TimeProvider` you control, and every assertion is
about state — which exception type came out, what the task's status is, how
many items were processed before the signal. Real time in a test is a flake
waiting to happen, and `TimeProvider` exists precisely so it never has to be.

# Reading - csharp/v3cb03_cancellation_timeouts

## Notes

**`OperationCanceledException` vs `TaskCanceledException`.** The second derives
from the first. `Task.Delay`, `WaitAsync` and most BCL waits throw
`TaskCanceledException`; `ThrowIfCancellationRequested` throws the base. Catch
`OperationCanceledException` and stop thinking about it. The one time the
distinction matters is when you are matching on `ex.CancellationToken` to work
out *whose* cancellation it was.

**Status follows the token, not the type.** A task ends `Canceled` only when it
completes with an `OperationCanceledException` whose `CancellationToken` equals
the one the task was associated with. Throw an `OperationCanceledException`
carrying a token nobody asked about, and the task ends `Faulted`. That is why
`ThrowIfCancellationRequested()` — which builds the exception with the right
token — is preferable to `throw new OperationCanceledException()`.

**Cancelling a wait is not cancelling work.** `WaitAsync(token)` composes a new
task that completes when either the original completes or the token fires. The
original keeps running. If it holds a connection, the connection stays held. If
you need the work itself to stop, the token has to reach the code doing the
work — which is the whole reason for the "pass the token down" discipline.

**Registrations are the leak.** `token.Register(callback)` adds an entry to the
token's callback list and returns a `CancellationTokenRegistration` whose
`Dispose` removes it. With a per-request token nothing bad happens; with a
long-lived application-lifetime token and a per-operation registration, the
list grows without bound. Everything you register, you dispose — usually with
`using`, occasionally in a `finally`.

**Linked sources leak the same way, doubled.** They register on every parent.
`using var linked = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(token)` is
not a style preference; the version without `using` is a bug that only shows up
under load.

**`CancelAsync` in .NET 8.** `Cancel()` runs registered callbacks
synchronously, on the cancelling thread — the same hijacking pattern as sector
1's `TaskCompletionSource`. `CancelAsync()` returns a `Task` and runs them
without blocking the caller, which matters when a shutdown path cancels a
source with hundreds of registrations.

**`TimeProvider`.** .NET 8's abstraction over the clock, timers, and
`Task.Delay`. Inject it, and a test can use `FakeTimeProvider` from
`Microsoft.Extensions.TimeProvider.Testing` to advance time instantly and
deterministically. Every timeout, retry and backoff you write should take one.

## ex1

The reason to check *before* the work rather than after is that an already-
cancelled request should do zero work. A loop that processes then checks does
one unit of work per cancellation, which sounds trivial until the unit is a
database write.

`ThrowIfCancellationRequested()` also reads better than the `if` it replaces,
and it produces the right exception with the right token — two things a
hand-written `if (token.IsCancellationRequested) throw new OperationCanceledException()`
gets wrong more often than not.

## ex2

Telling a timeout from a cancellation is the exercise most people have never
done, and it shows up in production as "we retried a request the user had
already abandoned". The mechanics: keep the two sources separate, link them,
and when the exception arrives ask `ex.CancellationToken` — or, more robustly,
ask `callerToken.IsCancellationRequested` first, since the linked token is the
one that will actually be attached.

The alternative design is to not use cancellation for your own timeout at all:
`await work.WaitAsync(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2), token)` throws
`TimeoutException` for the budget and `OperationCanceledException` for the
caller, and the types do the classification for you. When it fits, it is the
cleaner answer.

## ex3

The linked source pattern is four lines and three of them are important:

```csharp
using var budget = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(5));
using var linked = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(token, budget.Token);
await DoWorkAsync(linked.Token);
```

Both `using`s are required. The first disposes a timer; the second unhooks two
registrations. Drop either and you have a leak that scales with your request
rate — the classic profile is a service whose memory climbs steadily and whose
heap is full of `CancellationTokenSource` objects rooted by a token created at
startup.

## ex4

`Register` is the bridge to code that has never heard of `CancellationToken`:
legacy APIs, native handles, `TaskCompletionSource`. The pattern — register a
callback that completes a source, dispose the registration in a `finally` — is
the standard way to make anything cancellable from the outside.

Use the state-taking overload, `Register(static (state) => ..., obj)`, when the
call is hot: it avoids a closure allocation, exactly like
`IValueTaskSource.OnCompleted` in the previous sector. And remember that a
callback registered on an already-cancelled token runs *immediately, on the
registering thread*, which is a surprise if you registered while holding a
lock.

## ex5 - ex8

Abandoning work you cannot cancel is the honest middle ground, and the naming
carries the honesty. A method called `WaitOrAbandonAsync` tells its caller that
a connection is still open and an operation may still commit; one called
`CancelAsync` lies about the same code. The follow-on obligations — observe the
orphan's exception, and never assume a retried operation is not still in
flight — are what turn "we added a timeout" into "we added a timeout and did
not start double-charging customers".

The retry exercise is where `TimeProvider` earns its place. A backoff schedule
tested against a real clock is either slow or flaky and usually both; injected,
it is a microsecond test you can assert an exact schedule on. Note where the
token appears in that loop: in the attempt *and* in the delay, because a retry
that keeps sleeping after the caller has gone is holding resources for nobody.

The drain in ex8 is the whole sector applied to a process. Its one non-obvious
rule is that cleanup must not use the token that told you to stop — pass the
stopping token into your flush and the flush is cancelled the instant it
begins, losing data during the one shutdown where you had every chance to save
it.

## Further reading

- [Cancellation in managed threads](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/threading/cancellation-in-managed-threads) — the cooperative model in full.
- [`CancellationTokenSource`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.cancellationtokensource) — including `CancelAfter` and .NET 8's `CancelAsync`.
- [`TimeProvider`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.timeprovider) — the testable clock, and `Task.Delay` overloads that take one.
- [Recommended patterns for CancellationToken](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/premier-developer/recommended-patterns-for-cancellationtoken/) — the guidance most teams end up rediscovering.
- [Graceful shutdown in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/fundamentals/host/generic-host) — how `IHostApplicationLifetime` and the stopping token fit together.

# V3·CB3 — Cancellation, timeouts and cooperative shutdown

Cancellation in .NET is a signal, not a weapon. Everything else in this sector
follows from that.

## Concept 1 — the three types

```csharp
using var source = new CancellationTokenSource();   // the producer
CancellationToken token = source.Token;              // the read-only view
CancellationTokenRegistration reg = token.Register(() => Cleanup());  // the hook
source.Cancel();                                     // fires callbacks, sets the flag
reg.Dispose();                                       // unhook
```

`CancellationToken.None` is a token that can never be cancelled;
`token.CanBeCanceled` is `false` for it, which lets hot paths skip registration
entirely.

## Concept 2 — the two consumption idioms

```csharp
// you own the loop: check between units of work, before doing any
foreach (Item item in items)
{
    token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested();
    await ProcessAsync(item, token);          // and pass it down
}

// you are waiting on someone else: stop the wait, not the work
Result r = await work.WaitAsync(token);
```

The second one is worth reading twice: the work is still running afterwards.

## Concept 3 — timeouts

```csharp
// A: my own budget, expressed as cancellation
using var budget = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2));
using var linked = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(token, budget.Token);
await CallAsync(linked.Token);       // OperationCanceledException either way

// B: my own budget, expressed as a timeout
await CallAsync(token).WaitAsync(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(2), token);
// TimeoutException for the budget, OperationCanceledException for the caller
```

B classifies for you and is usually what you want at a call site. A is what you
want when the token must reach the callee so the *work* stops, not just the
wait.

## Concept 4 — telling them apart

```csharp
catch (OperationCanceledException) when (caller.IsCancellationRequested)
{
    throw;                     // the caller gave up: not our problem, not an error
}
catch (OperationCanceledException)
{
    throw new TimeoutException("upstream call exceeded its budget");
}
```

Filter on the *caller's* token rather than on `ex.CancellationToken`, because
the exception usually carries the linked token, not either parent.

## Concept 5 — testable time

```csharp
public sealed class Retrier(TimeProvider time)
{
    public async Task<T> RunAsync<T>(Func<Task<T>> call, CancellationToken token)
    {
        for (int attempt = 0; ; attempt++)
        {
            try { return await call(); }
            catch (Exception) when (attempt < 2)
            {
                await Task.Delay(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(1 << attempt), time, token);
            }
        }
    }
}
```

In production, `TimeProvider.System`. In tests, `FakeTimeProvider` plus
`Advance(TimeSpan)` — no sleeping, no flakes, and a backoff schedule you can
assert on.

## Concept 6 — cooperative shutdown

Three phases, three different uses of the same token:

1. **Stop accepting.** The moment the stopping token fires, refuse new work.
2. **Drain.** Wait for in-flight work, with a hard deadline.
3. **Abandon.** Past the deadline, stop waiting and report what was left. Do
   not pretend it finished.

## Worked example — a cancellable operation, end to end

```csharp
public async Task<Report> BuildAsync(int[] ids, CancellationToken token)
{
    // 1. our own budget, linked with the caller's intent
    using var budget = new CancellationTokenSource(TimeSpan.FromSeconds(30), time);
    using var linked = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(token, budget.Token);

    var rows = new List<Row>(ids.Length);
    foreach (int id in ids)
    {
        // 2. check between units, before doing any work
        linked.Token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested();

        // 3. forward - so the callee stops too, not just our wait
        rows.Add(await repository.LoadAsync(id, linked.Token).ConfigureAwait(false));
    }

    return new Report(rows);
}
```

Four decisions in twelve lines: the budget exists and is disposed, the caller
outranks it, the check happens before the work, and the token reaches the layer
that does the I/O. Remove any one and the method still compiles and still looks
cancellable.

## Worked example — the leak, in profile

```csharp
// startup
CancellationToken appStopping = lifetime.ApplicationStopping;

// per request, 500 times a second
var linked = CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(appStopping, requestAborted);
await HandleAsync(linked.Token);      // no using
```

Each call adds a registration to `appStopping`'s callback list. The list is
never walked until shutdown, and every entry roots the linked source, which
roots the closure, which roots the request scope. Memory climbs linearly under
constant load; a heap dump shows tens of thousands of
`CancellationTokenSource` instances with a GC root path to a single token
created at startup. The fix is the word `using`.

## Common mistakes

1. **Believing cancellation stops work.** It stops waiting. The work stops only
   if the work checks.
2. **Not passing the token down.** One layer that drops it breaks the chain.
3. **Not disposing linked sources or registrations.** Steady memory growth
   under load, rooted by a long-lived token.
4. **`catch (Exception)` before the cancellation clause.** Turns a user closing
   a tab into an error log and an alert.
5. **Throwing `OperationCanceledException` with the wrong token.** The task
   ends `Faulted`, and every downstream policy behaves differently.
6. **`CancelAfter` on a shared, long-lived source.** You have just given every
   future user of that source a deadline.
7. **Real `Task.Delay` in tests.** Slow and flaky; inject `TimeProvider`.
8. **Treating your own timeout as the caller's cancellation.** Opposite
   operational meanings.

## Concept 7 — the source is single-use

```csharp
var source = new CancellationTokenSource();
source.Cancel();
source.Token.IsCancellationRequested;    // true, for ever
```

There is no `Reset`. A cancelled source is spent, which means:

- A source in a field is one `Cancel()` away from poisoning every future
  operation that uses it.
- `CancelAfter` on a shared source is a permanent booby trap: after the first
  timeout, every later call starts cancelled.
- A "restartable" component must *replace* its source, which brings back the
  generation-swap problem from sector 1 — and the same
  `Interlocked.CompareExchange` answer.

The rule that avoids all three: sources belong to operations, tokens belong to
call chains, and fields hold neither unless the field's lifetime genuinely is
the operation's lifetime.

## Interview angle

> "How do you cancel a running task?"

You do not. You signal an intent with a `CancellationToken` and the code
decides. Cooperative cancellation exists because forcibly aborting a thread
leaves locks held and invariants broken — which is why `Thread.Abort` was
removed. In practice: check `ThrowIfCancellationRequested` between units of
work you control, use `WaitAsync(token)` to stop waiting on work you do not,
and pass the token to everything you call. `WaitAsync` stops your wait; the
underlying work keeps running until it checks its own token.

Follow-ups: how a timeout differs from a cancellation and how you would tell
them apart; why a linked source must be disposed; what makes a task `Canceled`
rather than `Faulted`; and how you would test a 30-second timeout without
waiting 30 seconds.

## Check yourself

1. Why was `Thread.Abort` removed, and what replaced it?
2. What does `await work.WaitAsync(token)` do to `work` when the token fires?
3. Which exception type do `ThrowIfCancellationRequested` and `Task.Delay`
   throw, and how are they related?
4. What makes a task end `Canceled` instead of `Faulted`?
5. Why must a linked `CancellationTokenSource` be disposed?
6. Where does a callback registered on an already-cancelled token run?
7. How do you distinguish "the caller gave up" from "my own budget expired"?
8. What does `Task.WaitAsync(TimeSpan)` throw, and why is that useful?
9. What is `CancellationToken.None` for, and what does `CanBeCanceled` buy you?
10. What does `CancelAsync()` fix compared to `Cancel()`?
11. Sketch a graceful drain with a hard deadline. What do you report?
12. How would you test a retry policy with exponential backoff in under a
    millisecond of wall-clock time?
13. Why is a `CancellationTokenSource` in a field a disposal obligation?
14. Why should cleanup code not use the token that requested the shutdown?
15. What does analyzer rule CA2016 catch, and what does it miss?

# Reading - csharp/v3cb03_cancellation_timeouts

## Why it is cooperative

.NET Framework had `Thread.Abort`, which injected a `ThreadAbortException` at
an arbitrary instruction boundary in another thread. It was used, it appeared
to work, and it was a disaster in slow motion. An abort could land between
acquiring a lock and entering the `try` that would have released it. It could
land inside a `finally`, or in a static constructor, leaving a type permanently
unusable for the life of the process. It could interrupt a two-field update and
leave an object in a state its invariants said was impossible.

.NET Core removed it: calling `Thread.Abort` throws
`PlatformNotSupportedException`. What replaced it is not a weaker version of
the same idea but a different idea — the running code is the only thing that
knows when it is safe to stop, so the running code decides. Everything awkward
about cancellation in .NET is downstream of that being correct.

The same reasoning explains why there is no "cancel this task" method on
`Task`. A task is a promise, not a process; there is frequently no thread to
interrupt and no work to stop, because the pending thing is a network read the
kernel is holding. The only meaningful cancellation is at the layer that issued
the operation, which is exactly where the token needs to arrive.

## The mechanics, in more detail than the docs give you

A `CancellationTokenSource` holds a state integer and a partitioned list of
registrations. `Cancel()` transitions the state and then walks the list,
invoking callbacks **synchronously on the cancelling thread**, in reverse order
of registration. If a callback throws, `Cancel()` aggregates and keeps going
(`Cancel(throwOnFirstException: true)` changes that). Because callbacks run
inline, a `Cancel()` under a lock runs foreign code under that lock — the same
hazard as sector 1's `SetResult`, and the reason .NET 8 added `CancelAsync()`.

`Register` on an already-cancelled token does not add to the list; it invokes
the callback immediately, on the registering thread, before returning. Code
that registers while holding a lock therefore has two ways to run a callback
under that lock, not one.

`CancellationTokenRegistration.Dispose()` removes the registration and, if the
callback is currently running on another thread, **blocks until it finishes** —
a small, real, and occasionally surprising synchronisation point.
`Unregister()` is the non-blocking alternative added in .NET 8.

`CreateLinkedTokenSource` registers on every parent token and cancels the child
when any fires. The child is a full source with its own registration list, its
own timer if you call `CancelAfter`, and its own disposal requirement. A common
production leak: a long-lived `IHostApplicationLifetime.ApplicationStopping`
token, and a per-request linked source that nobody disposes. The registrations
accumulate on the application token, each rooting a request-scoped object
graph, and memory climbs in a straight line until restart.

## Timeouts, and why the type matters

A timeout implemented as cancellation is convenient and lossy: at the catch
site, "I gave up" and "you gave up" look identical. That distinction is not
academic. A caller cancelling is a non-event — no log, no metric, no retry. A
timeout expiring is a statement about a dependency, and it belongs in a
counter, probably in a circuit breaker, and possibly in an alert.

Three ways to keep the information, in increasing order of preference:

1. **Inspect `ex.CancellationToken`.** Works, but the exception usually carries
   the linked token, so you must compare against the parents rather than test
   equality with either.
2. **Filter on the caller's token.** `catch (OperationCanceledException) when
   (callerToken.IsCancellationRequested)` is direct and reads correctly.
3. **Use `WaitAsync(TimeSpan, token)`.** The framework throws
   `TimeoutException` for the budget and `OperationCanceledException` for the
   token. The types classify for you, which means the catch sites downstream
   cannot get it wrong.

The cost of option 3 is that it only stops the wait — the callee never learns
about the deadline. When the callee should stop too, you need the linked-source
version, and then you need option 2 to classify.

## Testing time without spending it

`TimeProvider`, added in .NET 8, is the abstraction the ecosystem had been
hand-rolling for a decade. It supplies `GetUtcNow()`, `CreateTimer(...)`,
`GetTimestamp()` and — through overloads — `Task.Delay(delay, timeProvider,
token)` and `CancellationTokenSource(delay, timeProvider)`.

Inject it into anything with a schedule: retry policies, backoff, caches with
expiry, rate limiters, circuit breakers, drain deadlines. In tests, use
`FakeTimeProvider` and call `Advance(TimeSpan.FromMinutes(5))`; every timer due
in that window fires synchronously, so a test of a five-minute backoff runs in
microseconds and never flakes.

The alternative — real delays in tests — is worse than slow. It is
*non-deterministic*, so the test fails once a fortnight on a loaded CI machine,
gets marked flaky, gets retried automatically, and eventually stops testing
anything. A retry policy whose test suite has been quarantined is a retry
policy nobody can safely change.

## The cost of a token, and why it is small

People occasionally worry about the overhead of threading a
`CancellationToken` through everything. The numbers say not to. The token is a
struct wrapping one reference, so passing it costs a register.
`IsCancellationRequested` is a volatile read of an integer.
`ThrowIfCancellationRequested` is that read plus a branch that is never taken
in the normal case, and the JIT predicts it perfectly.
`CancellationToken.None` makes `CanBeCanceled` false, which lets a hot path
skip registration entirely — the BCL uses that check constantly.

What does cost is `Register`: an allocation for the registration node, a
lock-free insert into a partitioned list, and a matching removal on dispose.
That is why hot loops check the flag rather than registering, and why the
registration-based bridges in this sector are written once, at the edge, rather
than per iteration. The rule of thumb: **checking is free, registering is not**,
so check in loops and register only when you must wake something up.

## When not to cancel

Not everything should be cancellable, and forcing a token through everything
has costs.

**Operations that must complete for correctness.** A two-phase commit, an audit
write, a compensating action after a failure — cancelling those halfway is
worse than finishing them. Accept the token, ignore it deliberately, and
document why. The shape to reach for is `CancellationToken.None` passed
explicitly at the call site, which reads as a decision rather than an omission.

**Very short operations.** Threading a token through a method that takes
microseconds adds a parameter, a check, and a branch for no benefit. The
convention is that anything doing I/O or looping takes a token; pure
computation on small inputs does not.

**Shutdown paths themselves.** Cancelling your cleanup because shutdown was
requested is a classic self-inflicted wound: the stopping token fires, the
drain logic passes it to the flush call, the flush is cancelled, and data is
lost during an *orderly* shutdown. Cleanup gets its own budget, usually a
separate source with a hard deadline, never the token that told you to stop.

And a note on style that becomes a rule at scale: the token goes last in the
parameter list, it is named `cancellationToken` or `token` consistently, and it
defaults to `default` only on public APIs where the caller genuinely may not
have one. Internal methods should take it non-optionally, because an optional
token is a token somebody will forget to pass, and a broken link in the chain
is invisible until the day you need it.
