# Reading - csharp/v3cb04_async_exceptions

## The design problem, and the two answers

When the TPL shipped in .NET 4.0, `Task` had to answer a question synchronous
code never asks: what happens when one operation produces several failures? A
`Parallel.For` over a thousand items can fail a hundred times. A `WhenAll` over
ten calls can fail ten. There is no single exception to throw, so
`AggregateException` was created — a container with `InnerExceptions`, thrown
by `Wait()`, `Result`, and `Parallel`'s methods.

Then C# 5 added `await`, and `AggregateException` became wrong for the common
case. Nobody wants to write `catch (AggregateException ex) when
(ex.InnerException is IOException)` around every network call. So `await` took
the other answer: rethrow the first exception, preserving its stack trace with
`ExceptionDispatchInfo`, and leave the complete set on the task for anyone who
wants it.

Both answers are still there, and which one you get depends on how you consume
the task. That is the whole story behind the most-asked async interview
question, and it is a history lesson rather than a design flaw.

## ExceptionDispatchInfo, and what a good stack trace costs

`throw ex;` sets `ex.StackTrace` to the current location, erasing where the
exception came from. In synchronous code you avoid it with a bare `throw;`,
which preserves the trace because the runtime knows you are rethrowing in the
same frame.

Across an async boundary neither works: the exception is stored on a task,
possibly for milliseconds, then raised on a completely different stack.
`ExceptionDispatchInfo.Capture(ex)` snapshots the trace and the watson buckets;
`.Throw()` re-raises with the original trace intact and a marker line —
`--- End of stack trace from previous location ---` — separating the two
halves. Every `await` does this for you, which is why async stack traces are
readable at all.

It is also why you should reach for `ExceptionDispatchInfo` in your own code
whenever you store an exception and rethrow it later: a retry loop keeping the
last failure, a custom awaiter's `GetResult`, a result type that carries an
error. The alternative is a stack trace pointing at your rethrow statement, and
a colleague who cannot find the bug.

## The deadlock, precisely

```
UI thread: var r = SomeAsync().Result;   // blocks the UI thread
SomeAsync: await httpCall;                // captured the UI SynchronizationContext
httpCall completes on an IO thread
  -> continuation posted to the UI message queue
  -> UI thread is blocked in .Result and never pumps
  -> the task never completes
  -> .Result never returns
```

Two properties are required: a `SynchronizationContext` that runs
continuations on one specific thread, and a blocking wait on that thread. Old
ASP.NET had one (a per-request context with a limited concurrency lock), WPF
and WinForms have one, and Unity has one. **ASP.NET Core does not**, which is
why the same code that deadlocked in 2015 merely wastes a thread today.

`ConfigureAwait(false)` breaks the cycle by declining to capture the context,
so the continuation goes to the pool and completes regardless of what the UI
thread is doing. Library authors apply it everywhere because a library cannot
know whether its caller has a context. Application authors on ASP.NET Core
generally do not need it, and the honest summary is: it is noise in an app and
insurance in a library.

## async void, in more detail than you want

`AsyncVoidMethodBuilder` has nowhere to put a failure. Its `SetException` calls
`SynchronizationContext.Post` to rethrow on the captured context, or — with no
context — queues the rethrow to the thread pool, where an unhandled exception
crashes the process by design (a deliberate .NET Core change from 4.x's
swallow-and-continue).

The practical results: `try { EventHandlerAsync(); } catch { }` at the call
site catches nothing; a unit test calling an `async void` method finishes
before the method does, and the assertion failure surfaces in an unrelated
test; and a background `async void` method that throws takes the service down.

The only place it is unavoidable is an event handler, because the delegate's
signature demands `void`. Even there the body should be
`try { await ... } catch { log }` from top to bottom, so the failure never
reaches the builder.

`ICommand` implementations, `IHostedService` background loops, and message
handlers all *look* like they need `async void` and do not: they need
`async Task` plus a caller that awaits, or an explicit fire-and-forget helper
that observes.

## Reading an async stack trace

Async traces look corrupted the first time you meet one, and they are not. A
failure that crosses three awaits carries three
`--- End of stack trace from previous location ---` markers, because at each
await boundary the exception was stored on a task and re-raised on a new stack.

Read them top-down as "closest to the throw" outward. The frames above the
first marker are where the exception was originally raised. Each marker below
moves you one await boundary towards the consumer. People routinely read them
backwards, conclude the trace is meaningless, and start adding logging instead
of reading.

Two things make them shorter and more useful.
`[StackTraceHidden]` — used on `ArgumentNullException.ThrowIfNull` and the
other throw helpers — omits the helper's own frame, so you see your call site
rather than the BCL's. And the async state machine's `MoveNext` frames are
displayed with the original method name rather than the mangled
`<LoadAsync>d__4.MoveNext` in modern runtimes, which was a genuine quality-of-
life change around .NET Core 2.1.

If a trace still looks empty, suspect one of three things: a release build with
inlining, an exception constructed but never thrown (its `StackTrace` is null
until it is thrown), or a `throw ex;` upstream.

## When not to catch

Two anti-patterns are worth naming because they look responsible.

**The catch-all wrapper.** `try { ... } catch (Exception ex) { log; return
default; }` around an operation converts every failure into a plausible-looking
success. Downstream code then makes decisions on a default value it believes is
data. Catch what you can handle; let the rest travel.

**The cancellation swallow.** `catch (Exception)` above any cancellation clause
turns an abandoned request into an error, and at scale that is the alert nobody
trusts. If you catch broadly, filter:
`catch (Exception ex) when (ex is not OperationCanceledException)`.

There is a third, subtler one: catching in order to add context and rethrowing
with `throw new WrapperException(msg, ex)`. That is fine when the wrapper adds
information the caller needs to act on, and harmful when it is applied
mechanically at every layer — you end up with six nested exceptions whose
`InnerException` chain is the only useful part, and logs that print the least
specific message at the top.

## Disposal, elision, and the bug that hides in a using

```csharp
public Task<string> ReadAsync(string path)
{
    using var stream = File.OpenRead(path);
    return ReadCoreAsync(stream);        // BUG
}
```

Removing `async`/`await` from a method that returns a task is a real
optimisation — one fewer state machine — and it is safe **only** when there is
no enclosing `using`, `try`, `catch`, `finally`, or `lock`. Here the `using`
disposes the stream when the method returns, which is before the returned task
completes. The core then reads from a disposed stream, usually intermittently,
usually in production.

The same applies to exception handling: an elided method's frame is absent from
the stack trace, and a `try`/`catch` around the elided call cannot catch what
the inner task carries, because the exception is not raised until somebody
awaits. Write `return await` inside any protective construct, and reserve
elision for the trivial pass-through case where you can see the whole method at
once.

## Exercise 1 - your first async iterator

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB05_AsyncStreams/Ex1.cs`.

- `Pages.ItemsAsync(Func<int, Task<int[]>> fetchPage, int pageCount)` is an
  `async IAsyncEnumerable<int>` that fetches page `0` through `pageCount - 1`
  and yields each page's items in order.
- `Pages.Fetches` counts how many pages were actually fetched.
- `Pages.SumAsync(IAsyncEnumerable<int> source)` consumes a stream with
  `await foreach` and returns the total.
- `Pages.StartedYet(IAsyncEnumerable<int> source)` returns `false` —
  demonstrating that merely *calling* an async-iterator method runs none of its
  body. Implement it by returning whether `Fetches` is still zero.

Example: with pages `[[1,2],[3]]`, `SumAsync(ItemsAsync(fetch, 2))` is `6` and
`Fetches` is `2`. Calling `ItemsAsync(fetch, 2)` without enumerating leaves
`Fetches` at `0`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb05_async_streams ex1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Three ingredients make a method an async iterator: the `async` modifier, at
least one `yield return`, and a return type of `IAsyncEnumerable<T>`. No
`return` statement, no `Task`.

Write the outer loop over pages, await the fetch, then yield each item of the
page in an inner loop.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public static async IAsyncEnumerable<int> ItemsAsync(
    Func<int, Task<int[]>> fetchPage, int pageCount)
{
    for (int page = 0; page < pageCount; page++)
    {
        Fetches++;
        int[] items = await fetchPage(page).ConfigureAwait(false);
        foreach (int item in items) yield return item;
    }
}
```

Note the two levels: one await per page, then several yields with no awaiting
at all. That is why `MoveNextAsync` returns a `ValueTask<bool>` — most calls
have the answer already.

`SumAsync` is a plain `await foreach` accumulating into a local.

## Hint 3

`StartedYet` is making a point that is easy to skim past: the method body has
not run. Calling `ItemsAsync(...)` constructs the state machine, sets its state
to "not started", and returns it. The first `MoveNextAsync` — issued by
`await foreach` — is what executes your first line.

Two consequences follow, and both bite in real code. Argument validation inside
an async iterator does not run until enumeration, so the same non-async-wrapper
split from sector 1 applies. And a stream created but never enumerated does
nothing at all — no fetch, no connection, no side effect — which is either a
useful property or a silent no-op depending on whether you meant it.

Left to you: whether `Fetches` should be a static counter at all. It is a test
seam here; in production a counter shared across every call of a static method
is exactly the shared mutable state sector 7 is about.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start from the consumer and work backwards. Write `SumAsync` first — it is four
lines and it forces you to type `await foreach`, which makes the producer's
required shape obvious.

Then ask: what does the loop call, in what order, and what must my method
return for that to compile?

## Hint 2

A useful comparison to draw once, on paper: the same function written three
ways.

```csharp
Task<int[]> All();                    // fetch everything, then return
IEnumerable<int> Lazy();              // lazy, but every fetch blocks a thread
IAsyncEnumerable<int> Streaming();    // lazy and non-blocking
```

The middle one is the option people forget exists and then implement by
accident — a synchronous iterator that calls `.Result` inside. It has the
memory profile of the third and the thread profile of the worst possible first.
If you see `yield return` next to `.Result`, that is what happened.

## Hint 3

Once it passes, try removing the `await` from the loop body and see what the
compiler says. Without any await, `async IAsyncEnumerable<T>` is legal but
warns — you have built an asynchronous sequence that never suspends, which is
usually a sign the method should have been an ordinary `IEnumerable<T>`.

The reverse case is more interesting: a method with awaits and no `yield`
cannot return `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` at all, because there is nothing to
enumerate. Those two errors together define the shape precisely, and hitting
them deliberately once is faster than remembering the rule.

## Exercise 2 - the attribute everybody forgets

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB05_AsyncStreams/Ex2.cs`.

- `Tokens.HonouredAsync(Func<int, Task<int>> load, int count, [EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken token = default)`
  yields `load(i)` for `i` in `0..count-1`, checking the token before each
  item, and honours a token supplied by `WithCancellation` at enumeration time.
- `Tokens.IgnoredAsync(Func<int, Task<int>> load, int count, CancellationToken token = default)`
  is the identical method **without** the attribute — left in as the
  counter-example.
- `Tokens.ConsumeAsync(IAsyncEnumerable<int> source, CancellationToken token, int stopAfter)`
  enumerates with `WithCancellation(token)`, counts items, and returns the
  count; cancellation propagates out.
- `Tokens.Produced` counts how many items the producer actually generated.

The gate enumerates each version with a token it cancels after two items:
`HonouredAsync` stops producing, `IgnoredAsync` keeps going until the consumer
stops it.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb05_async_streams ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The two methods differ by one attribute and behave completely differently.
Before writing them, work out *why* a token parameter alone is not enough —
the answer is in when the parameter's value is fixed.

An async-iterator method returns a factory. The token you passed to the factory
was chosen when the sequence was created; `WithCancellation` supplies one when
it is enumerated, and those can be different moments and different callers.

## Hint 2

```csharp
using System.Runtime.CompilerServices;

public static async IAsyncEnumerable<int> HonouredAsync(
    Func<int, Task<int>> load,
    int count,
    [EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken token = default)
{
    for (int i = 0; i < count; i++)
    {
        token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested();
        Produced++;
        yield return await load(i).ConfigureAwait(false);
    }
}
```

The attribute tells the compiler: the token given to `GetAsyncEnumerator`
belongs in this parameter. It *combines* it with whatever the caller passed at
creation, so both work.

## Hint 3

The compiler is on your side here and people ignore it. **CS8425** —
"asynchronous iterator has one or more parameters of type `CancellationToken`
but none of them is decorated with the `EnumeratorCancellation` attribute" — is
a warning, and it fires exactly on `IgnoredAsync`.

Treat warnings as errors in any project that streams, and this class of bug
becomes impossible rather than merely rare.

Note also what the attribute does *not* do. It does not add a check to your
loop — you still have to call `ThrowIfCancellationRequested` or pass the token
into whatever you await. It only makes the token *arrive*. A stream that
receives the token and never looks at it is the second-most-common version of
this bug, and no analyzer catches it.

Left to you: whether to also pass `token` into `load`. Here `load` does not
take one; in real code it would, and forwarding it is what stops an in-flight
fetch rather than merely stopping the loop.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Try predicting the gate's numbers before you run it. With a token cancelled
after two items and a source of ten:

- `HonouredAsync`: how many items does the producer generate?
- `IgnoredAsync`: how many?

Write both numbers down. The gap between them is the entire cost of a missing
attribute, and seeing it as a number is more persuasive than any explanation.

## Hint 2

There are two ways for a consumer to supply a token, and they are not
equivalent:

```csharp
await foreach (int x in Stream(load, 10, token)) { }              // creation time
await foreach (int x in Stream(load, 10).WithCancellation(token)) { }  // enumeration time
```

The first works with or without the attribute — it is an ordinary parameter.
The second works *only* with the attribute. Since the second is the form that
composes (a method returning a stream, enumerated by somebody else who has the
token), the attribute is what makes streams usable across component
boundaries.

## Hint 3

One more subtlety worth knowing before you meet it in review: the attribute is
on the *parameter*, and it can be applied to only one parameter per method. If
a method has two `CancellationToken` parameters — rare, but it happens with
"creation token plus per-item token" designs — you must choose which one
receives the enumeration-time token, and the other is an ordinary parameter.

And when you write an enumerator by hand (as sector 2's ex6 did), none of this
applies: you get the token in `GetAsyncEnumerator` and it is your job to link
it with any stored one, and to dispose the linked source in `DisposeAsync`.
That is three lines of work the compiler does for you, and forgetting the
disposal is sector 3's leak all over again.

## Exercise 3 - proving laziness

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB05_AsyncStreams/Ex3.cs`.

- `Lazy.NumbersAsync(int count, List<int> produced)` yields `0..count-1`,
  appending each value to `produced` as it is generated, with an `await` per
  item.
- `Lazy.TakeAsync(IAsyncEnumerable<int> source, int n)` returns the first `n`
  items as a `List<int>`, stopping the enumeration with `break`.
- `Lazy.FirstMatchAsync(IAsyncEnumerable<int> source, Func<int, bool> match)`
  returns the first matching item, or `-1`, and must not pull any item after
  the match.
- `Lazy.RanAhead(List<int> produced, int consumed)` returns `true` when the
  producer generated more items than the consumer took — for a correct
  implementation it never does.

Example: `TakeAsync(NumbersAsync(1000, produced), 3)` returns `[0,1,2]` and
leaves `produced` with exactly three entries.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb05_async_streams ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The producer runs only between `MoveNextAsync` calls. So the question "how many
items were produced" is answered entirely by how many times the consumer asked.

`break` in an `await foreach` stops asking. Nothing else is needed — no flag,
no cancellation, no cooperation from the producer.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public static async Task<List<int>> TakeAsync(IAsyncEnumerable<int> source, int n)
{
    var taken = new List<int>(n);
    await foreach (int item in source.ConfigureAwait(false))
    {
        taken.Add(item);
        if (taken.Count == n) break;
    }

    return taken;
}
```

For `FirstMatchAsync`, `return` directly out of the loop — the desugaring's
`finally` still runs `DisposeAsync`, so the producer is cleaned up properly.

## Hint 3

The exact count is worth predicting rather than measuring. Taking three items
from a stream of a thousand causes:

- three `MoveNextAsync` calls that return `true`
- three items produced
- **zero** further calls, because `break` exits before asking again
- one `DisposeAsync`, which resumes the producer at its `yield return` so its
  `finally` blocks run

The producer never generates item four. If your implementation produces one
extra, you asked one time too many — usually by structuring the loop as
"ask, then check whether we wanted it".

Left to you: whether `TakeAsync` should be an operator returning
`IAsyncEnumerable<int>` instead of a `List<int>`. The lazy version composes and
never materialises; the eager one is easier to test. Ex6 writes the lazy
version, so leave it eager here and compare them afterwards.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Draw the interleaving before coding. For `TakeAsync(source, 2)` over a producer
that logs each item:

```
consumer: MoveNextAsync -> producer runs to first yield -> "0"
consumer: takes 0, MoveNextAsync -> producer resumes -> "1"
consumer: takes 1, count == n, break
consumer: DisposeAsync -> producer resumes at yield, runs finally, ends
```

Four consumer actions, two producer resumptions, two items. Once you can write
that trace, the code is transcription.

## Hint 2

The property being demonstrated has a name worth knowing: **demand-driven
evaluation**, and it is the same property that makes synchronous LINQ's
`First()` cheap over a huge sequence. The async version adds one thing —
between demands, the producer is suspended rather than blocked, so it costs no
thread.

That combination is unusual and valuable: a paged HTTP source that a consumer
abandons after three items makes exactly one HTTP request, holds no thread
while waiting for it, and cleans up its client on the `break`.

## Hint 3

The dark side of the same property, which the exercise deliberately does not
exercise: **the producer cannot run ahead**. If each item costs a 50 ms network
call and each item takes 50 ms to process, a stream takes 100 ms per item —
strictly sequential — where a producer running one item ahead would take 50.

That is not a flaw in `IAsyncEnumerable`; it is what pull-based means. When you
want overlap you need a buffer between the two, which is a `Channel` with a
small bound: the producer runs ahead by exactly the bound, and stops when the
buffer is full. Sector 6 builds that. Recognising which of the two problems you
have — "I want to stop early and cheaply" versus "I want producer and consumer
overlapped" — is the design decision, and the answer is a different type in
each case.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 - disposal, and what an early break really does

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB05_AsyncStreams/Ex4.cs`.

- `Cleanup.Resource` is a small `IAsyncDisposable` class recording
  `"disposed"` into a supplied log when `DisposeAsync` runs.
- `Cleanup.ReadAsync(List<string> log, int count)` is an async iterator that
  opens a `Resource` with `await using`, appends `"opened"`, wraps its loop in
  `try`/`finally` appending `"finally"`, and yields `0..count-1`.
- `Cleanup.TakeAsync(IAsyncEnumerable<int> source, int n)` takes `n` items and
  breaks.
- `Cleanup.Abandon(IAsyncEnumerable<int> source)` calls `GetAsyncEnumerator`,
  pulls one item, and returns **without** disposing — the leak, left in on
  purpose.
- `Cleanup.Order(List<string> log)` returns the log joined with `","`.

After `TakeAsync(ReadAsync(log, 10), 2)` the log is exactly
`"opened,finally,disposed"`. After `Abandon`, it is `"opened"` — nothing else
ran.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb05_async_streams ex4
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Predict the log for four scenarios before writing any code:

1. the consumer takes all 10 items
2. the consumer breaks after 2
3. the consumer's body throws on item 1
4. nobody disposes the enumerator

Three of the four produce identical logs. The fourth is the bug. Being able to
say which is which is the whole exercise.

## Hint 2

A useful diagnostic for real systems: if a `finally` inside an async iterator
is not running, the enumerator was not disposed. That happens in exactly three
ways —

- hand-rolled `GetAsyncEnumerator` without `await using`
- storing an enumerator in a field and never disposing the owner
- a process that exits while a stream is suspended

— and the symptom is always a leaked connection, file handle or transaction
that a heap dump will show you as a suspended state machine holding a live
resource.

## Hint 3

One rule this exercise should leave you with: **never hold a lock across
`yield return`.**

You are suspended at that point for as long as the consumer takes, which is
unbounded — they might be writing to a slow socket, or might `break` and go
away entirely. A lock held across a yield is a lock held for the consumer's
processing time, and a deadlock the first time a consumer's body touches the
same lock.

The same argument applies, more mildly, to transactions and to anything with a
server-side timeout. If your iterator holds something whose lifetime matters,
either buffer a chunk and release it before yielding, or accept that the
consumer's speed is now your resource-hold time and design the consumer
accordingly.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 - the enumerator, written by hand

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB05_AsyncStreams/Ex5.cs`. `yield return` generates a
class; write that class yourself once, and every async stream afterwards is
transparent.

- `Manual.Range(int count, Func<int, Task<int>> load)` returns an
  `IAsyncEnumerable<int>` implemented without `yield`.
- Its `GetAsyncEnumerator(CancellationToken)` must **link** the token it is
  given with a token supplied at construction, and dispose the linked source in
  `DisposeAsync`.
- `MoveNextAsync` returns `ValueTask<bool>` and completes synchronously when
  the next value is already known.
- `Current` is a plain property; `DisposeAsync` returns `default` when there is
  nothing to release.
- `Manual.SyncMoves` counts synchronously completed moves.

Example: `Range(3, load)` enumerated with `WithCancellation(token)` yields
`load(0), load(1), load(2)` and stops when the token fires.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb05_async_streams ex5
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Write the interfaces out longhand before implementing them — there are only
four members total, and seeing them together tells you where each piece of
state lives:

```
IAsyncEnumerable<T>: GetAsyncEnumerator(CancellationToken)
IAsyncEnumerator<T>: MoveNextAsync() -> ValueTask<bool>
                     Current { get; }
                     DisposeAsync() -> ValueTask   (from IAsyncDisposable)
```

Anything you need across calls belongs on the enumerator, not the enumerable —
which is also why enumerating twice creates two cursors and re-runs everything.

## Hint 2

Compare your finished class with what the compiler emits for the equivalent
`yield` version. Decompile it, or just note the differences you can predict:

- the compiler's version implements all three interfaces on one object, so a
  first enumeration allocates nothing extra
- it uses `ManualResetValueTaskSourceCore<bool>` internally, so per-item
  promises are pooled
- it handles the "enumerate twice" case by allocating a fresh state machine on
  the second `GetAsyncEnumerator`

Your version is simpler and allocates a little more. That is the correct trade
for hand-written code, and it is why you should reach for `yield return`
whenever it fits.

## Hint 3

The reason to have done this once shows up when you read someone else's
streaming API. You will now recognise, at a glance:

- whether their `MoveNextAsync` has a synchronous fast path
- whether they linked the enumeration token or dropped it
- whether `DisposeAsync` actually releases anything
- whether the enumerable is re-enumerable or one-shot

All four are visible in twenty lines, and all four are things that will
otherwise surprise you at runtime. Reading an implementation is much faster
than discovering its behaviour empirically — and for streaming code, the
behaviour that matters is rarely documented.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 - operators that stay lazy

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB05_AsyncStreams/Ex6.cs`. The base library ships no LINQ
for async streams. Write three operators that preserve laziness and
cancellation.

- `Operators.SelectAwait<TIn, TOut>(this IAsyncEnumerable<TIn> source, Func<TIn, ValueTask<TOut>> selector, [EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken token = default)`
- `Operators.Where<T>(this IAsyncEnumerable<T> source, Func<T, bool> predicate, [EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken token = default)`
- `Operators.Take<T>(this IAsyncEnumerable<T> source, int count, [EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken token = default)`

Requirements for all three:

- Lazy: nothing runs until the result is enumerated, and each operator pulls
  exactly one item from its source per item it produces.
- Cancellation flows: each forwards the token with `WithCancellation`.
- `Take(0)` pulls nothing at all from the source — not even one item.
- `Operators.Pulled` counts items pulled from the innermost source.

Example: `NumbersAsync(1000).Where(IsEven).SelectAwait(DoubleAsync).Take(2)`
consumed fully pulls exactly four items from the source (`0,1,2,3`).

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb05_async_streams ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Each operator is an async iterator that consumes one stream and produces
another. The body is an `await foreach` over the source with a `yield return`
inside — which automatically gives you laziness, because nothing runs until
somebody enumerates the result.

Write `Where` first; it is the shortest and the other two follow the same
skeleton.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public static async IAsyncEnumerable<T> Where<T>(
    this IAsyncEnumerable<T> source,
    Func<T, bool> predicate,
    [EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken token = default)
{
    await foreach (T item in source.WithCancellation(token).ConfigureAwait(false))
        if (predicate(item)) yield return item;
}
```

`SelectAwait` is the same with `yield return await selector(item)`. `Take` is
the same with a counter and a `yield break` — or a `break` — once it reaches
`count`.

## Hint 3

`Take(0)` is the requirement that separates a correct implementation from a
plausible one. Consider:

```csharp
int taken = 0;
await foreach (T item in source...)      // pulls one item before the check
{
    if (taken++ >= count) yield break;
    yield return item;
}
```

That pulls one item even for `Take(0)`, because entering the loop *is* a pull.
Guard before the loop:

```csharp
if (count <= 0) yield break;
```

The same class of off-by-one applies to any operator with a limit, and it
matters when a pull costs a network round trip.

Left to you: whether `SelectAwait` should take `Func<T, ValueTask<TOut>>` or
`Func<T, CancellationToken, ValueTask<TOut>>`. The second forwards cancellation
into the selector itself, which is what `System.Linq.Async` offers as
`SelectAwaitWithCancellation`. The naming is ugly and the behaviour is right.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Test your understanding of composition before writing: for
`source.Where(even).Take(2)` over `0,1,2,3,4,...`, how many items does the
*source* produce?

The answer is 3 (`0`, `1`, `2`), because `Take` stops asking once it has two
and `Where` only pulls when asked. If you predicted 5, you are thinking of the
eager version; if you predicted 2, you forgot that `Where` discards.

Getting this right in your head is what "lazy composition" means concretely.

## Hint 2

A structural point worth noticing: each operator adds one layer of state
machine, and a chain of five operators means five `MoveNextAsync` calls per
item delivered. That is a real cost — synchronous LINQ has the same property
and is famously fine, but the async version's per-call cost is higher.

For a chain over a million small items, a single hand-written loop beats five
composed operators by a wide margin. For a chain over paged network results,
the difference is unmeasurable. Compose freely at the edges; write the loop by
hand in the inner ten percent, when a profile says so.

## Hint 3

There is one operator you should deliberately *not* write, and knowing why is
worth more than the three you did: **`Merge`**, which interleaves two streams
by whichever produces first.

You cannot express it with `await foreach` and `yield return`, because a single
async iterator pulls from one source at a time. Doing it properly means holding
a `ValueTask<bool>` from each enumerator simultaneously and racing them — which
violates sector 2's consume-once contract against a pooled enumerator, and
gives wrong answers rather than errors.

The correct implementation pumps both streams into a `Channel` and reads the
channel. That is the next sector, and it is the general answer whenever an
async-stream problem needs more than one thing in flight.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 - batching a stream

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB05_AsyncStreams/Ex7.cs`. Per-item awaits are the cost of
streaming; batching amortises them.

- `Batching.Chunk<T>(this IAsyncEnumerable<T> source, int size, [EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken token = default)`
  returns `IAsyncEnumerable<T[]>` of fixed-size batches, with a final partial
  batch when the source does not divide evenly.
- An empty source produces **no** batches at all — not one empty array.
- `size <= 0` throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` **eagerly**, at the call
  site, not on first enumeration.
- `Batching.WriteAllAsync(IAsyncEnumerable<int> source, int size, Func<int[], Task> write)`
  chunks and writes each batch, returning the number of write calls.
- `Batching.Writes` counts them.

Example: a source of `1..7` with `size` `3` produces `[1,2,3]`, `[4,5,6]`,
`[7]` — three batches, three writes.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb05_async_streams ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Accumulate into a buffer, yield when it is full, and flush whatever is left
after the loop. The two things to get right are the empty-source case and the
partial tail — and they are the same check in two places.

The eager argument validation needs the sector-1 split, because an async
iterator defers everything to first enumeration.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public static IAsyncEnumerable<T[]> Chunk<T>(
    this IAsyncEnumerable<T> source, int size, CancellationToken token = default)
{
    ArgumentOutOfRangeException.ThrowIfNegativeOrZero(size);   // eager
    return ChunkCore(source, size, token);
}

private static async IAsyncEnumerable<T[]> ChunkCore<T>(
    IAsyncEnumerable<T> source, int size,
    [EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken token)
{
    var buffer = new List<T>(size);
    await foreach (T item in source.WithCancellation(token).ConfigureAwait(false))
    {
        buffer.Add(item);
        if (buffer.Count == size) { yield return buffer.ToArray(); buffer.Clear(); }
    }

    if (buffer.Count > 0) yield return buffer.ToArray();
}
```

Note the attribute moves to the private core — the public wrapper is not an
iterator.

## Hint 3

Two things worth deciding rather than copying.

**`ToArray()` per batch allocates.** For a high-throughput pipeline you would
rent from `ArrayPool<T>.Shared` and yield a `ReadOnlyMemory<T>` with a
documented "valid until the next `MoveNextAsync`" contract — which is exactly
what `PipeReader` does. It is also a contract every consumer can violate, so
only do it when a profile demands it.

**Time-based flushing.** Real batchers flush on size *or* a maximum delay,
because a batch of 100 that waits an hour for its hundredth item is worse than
useless. Adding that means racing the next item against a timer, which needs
two things in flight — and therefore a `Channel`, not a plain iterator. That is
a good demonstration of where this abstraction's ceiling is.

Left to you: whether to reuse one buffer array across batches. Faster, and it
means a consumer who stores a batch gets it mutated under them. The rule of
thumb: reuse only behind an interface that says so.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Enumerate the edge cases first; there are exactly four and each has a wrong
answer that looks right:

- empty source → zero batches (not one empty batch)
- source smaller than `size` → one partial batch
- source exactly divisible → no trailing empty batch
- `size` invalid → throws, and throws *now*

If your implementation yields an empty final array for an empty source, you
flushed unconditionally.

## Hint 2

The reason batching matters is easier to feel with numbers. Streaming a million
rows one at a time costs a million `MoveNextAsync` calls, a million state
machine resumptions, and — if the consumer writes each one — a million round
trips to whatever it writes to.

At `size` 1000 that becomes a thousand of each, and the per-item cost is now
amortised over a batch that fits comfortably in cache. Every high-throughput
streaming API in .NET is batched somewhere: `PipeReader` yields buffers, EF
Core buffers rows per fetch, `Channel` consumers commonly drain in a loop.

The stream is still item-at-a-time to *its* consumer; the batching is an
internal optimisation you expose only when the consumer can use it.

## Hint 3

A subtle interaction worth knowing: batching changes cancellation granularity.
With `size` 1000, a cancelled token is noticed at most one item after it fires
inside your loop — but the *consumer* only sees the effect when the current
batch would have been delivered, and a partially filled batch at cancellation
time is normally discarded.

That is usually right, and occasionally very wrong — a batch of writes that is
dropped on cancellation may be data you needed. If partial batches matter,
flush them in a `finally` before the cancellation propagates, and be explicit
about it in the doc comment. Silently dropping buffered work on cancellation is
one of the quieter ways systems lose data.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 - adapting other things into streams

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB05_AsyncStreams/Ex8.cs`.

- `Adapt.InCompletionOrderAsync(IReadOnlyList<Task<int>> work, [EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken token = default)`
  yields results as their tasks complete — **not** in list order — using
  `Task.WhenAny` over a shrinking set.
- `Adapt.FromChannelAsync(ChannelReader<int> reader, [EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken token = default)`
  adapts a channel reader into a stream. (One line, and knowing which line is
  the point.)
- `Adapt.FromSyncAsync(IEnumerable<int> source)` lifts a synchronous sequence
  into an `IAsyncEnumerable<int>` without introducing any await.
- `Adapt.ToListAsync(IAsyncEnumerable<int> source, CancellationToken token = default)`
  materialises a stream.

Example: tasks completing in the order 3rd, 1st, 2nd yield
`third, first, second`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb05_async_streams ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Completion order needs a mutable set: await `WhenAny`, yield the winner, remove
it, repeat until empty. The subtlety is that `WhenAny` allocates and scans on
every call, so this is O(n²) for large sets — fine for a handful, wrong for
thousands.

The channel adapter is one method call. Look at `ChannelReader<T>`.

## Hint 2

```csharp
var pending = new List<Task<int>>(work);
while (pending.Count > 0)
{
    Task<int> done = await Task.WhenAny(pending).ConfigureAwait(false);
    pending.Remove(done);
    yield return await done.ConfigureAwait(false);   // rethrows its failure here
}
```

`FromChannelAsync` is `reader.ReadAllAsync(token)` — the channel already is an
async stream, which is a hint about where sector 6 is going.

`FromSyncAsync` is a `foreach` with `yield return` and no await at all;
`ToListAsync` is an `await foreach` accumulating.

## Hint 3

Two things the completion-order version quietly gets right and hand-rolled
versions often do not.

`await done` rather than `done.Result`: it rethrows the original exception
rather than an `AggregateException`, and it is not a blocking call even though
the task is already complete.

`pending.Remove(done)` uses reference equality on the task object, which is
correct — `WhenAny` returns the very instance that completed. If you had
projected the tasks (`.Select(t => t.ContinueWith(...))`) you would be removing
something that is not in the list.

And the complexity note is not academic: `WhenAny` over `n` tasks registers a
continuation on every one of them, each time round the loop. For large fan-outs
the right structure is a `Channel` that each task writes into on completion —
O(n) total, and again the answer is the next sector.

Left to you: whether completion order is what you want at all. It is right for
"show results as they arrive" and wrong for anything where the caller needs to
correlate results with inputs, because you have thrown away the index. Yielding
`(index, value)` pairs costs nothing and keeps the option open.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what each adapter is *for*, because that determines the shape:

- completion order: a UI that shows results as they land
- channel reader: a producer/consumer pipeline you want to consume with
  `await foreach`
- synchronous source: an in-memory collection satisfying a streaming interface
- `ToListAsync`: the boundary where streaming ends and buffering begins

Three of the four are trivial. The first is the one with a design in it.

## Hint 2

`FromSyncAsync` looks pointless and is not. It is the standard way to satisfy
an `IAsyncEnumerable<T>`-shaped interface from a source that has everything in
memory — a test double, a cache hit, an in-memory repository.

The compiler will warn that the method lacks an `await`. Two acceptable
responses: add `#pragma warning disable CS1998` with a comment, or make it a
non-async method returning a small hand-written enumerable. The BCL takes the
second route for `ToAsyncEnumerable`-style helpers; for a test double the
pragma is fine.

## Hint 3

`ToListAsync` deserves one warning. It is the method that undoes everything
this sector is about: memory goes from flat to proportional to the result set,
and the caller waits for the last item before seeing the first.

That is often exactly right — small results, a caller that needs random access,
a boundary that has to serialise. But its presence in the middle of a pipeline
is usually a mistake, and `await foreach` immediately after a `ToListAsync` is
always one.

Watch for it in review the same way you watch for `.ToList()` in a synchronous
LINQ chain: legitimate at the end, suspicious in the middle, and a red flag
when it appears twice.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge - a resilient paged stream

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB05_AsyncStreams/Challenge.cs`. Streaming and retry
compose badly; make them compose correctly.

```csharp
public static IAsyncEnumerable<Item> ReadAllAsync(
    Func<string?, CancellationToken, Task<Page>> fetchPage,
    int maxRetriesPerPage,
    IAsyncDisposable client,
    CancellationToken token = default);

public readonly record struct Page(Item[] Items, string? NextCursor);
public readonly record struct Item(int Id, string Value);
```

Rules:

- Yields every item of every page, in order, following `NextCursor` until it is
  `null`.
- A page fetch that throws is retried up to `maxRetriesPerPage` times **from
  the same cursor**; the retry must not re-yield items already delivered from
  an earlier page.
- Exhausting the retries lets the exception out of the enumeration.
- Cancellation is honoured at enumeration time (`[EnumeratorCancellation]`) and
  forwarded into `fetchPage`.
- `client` is disposed exactly once, whether the consumer drains the stream,
  breaks early, or the stream throws.
- Argument validation is eager.
- `Challenge.Fetches` and `Challenge.Retries` count what happened.

Example: a three-page source whose second page fails once then succeeds yields
every item once, with `Fetches` 4 and `Retries` 1.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb05_async_streams challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The state that makes retry safe is the cursor. As long as you retry the fetch
*before* yielding anything from that page, no item can be delivered twice — the
page either arrives whole or not at all.

That is the whole design. The awkward version is the one that yields items as
it parses them and then fails halfway; avoid it by fetching completely first.

## Hint 2

```csharp
private static async IAsyncEnumerable<Item> Core(
    Func<string?, CancellationToken, Task<Page>> fetchPage,
    int maxRetries,
    IAsyncDisposable client,
    [EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken token)
{
    await using (client.ConfigureAwait(false))
    {
        string? cursor = null;
        do
        {
            Page page = await FetchWithRetryAsync(fetchPage, cursor, maxRetries, token)
                .ConfigureAwait(false);

            foreach (Item item in page.Items) yield return item;
            cursor = page.NextCursor;
        }
        while (cursor is not null);
    }
}
```

`FetchWithRetryAsync` is an ordinary async method with a `for` loop and a
`catch` — no `yield` in it, so it can `try`/`catch` freely.

## Hint 3

Three constraints that shape the code more than they look like they should.

**You cannot `yield return` inside a `try` with a `catch`.** C# forbids it. So
the retry logic must live in a separate non-iterator method — which is a
blessing, because it separates "how do I get a page" from "how do I stream
pages" cleanly.

**`await using` around the whole loop handles all three exit paths.** Drain,
break and throw all unwind through it. A manual `DisposeAsync` after the loop
handles only the first.

**Eager validation needs the wrapper split**, because everything inside an
iterator is deferred to first enumeration — and the `[EnumeratorCancellation]`
attribute must then be on the *core*, not the wrapper.

Left to you: whether to retry cancellation. You must not — `OperationCanceledException`
should escape the retry loop untouched, or a cancelled enumeration will keep
fetching. That is sector 3's clause ordering, appearing for the last time.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Write the failure cases first, as a list, and decide the correct behaviour for
each before touching the code:

1. page 1 fails once, then succeeds → retry, no duplicates
2. page 2 fails `maxRetries + 1` times → exception escapes, client disposed
3. consumer breaks after item 1 → no further fetches, client disposed
4. token cancelled mid-page → no retry, exception escapes, client disposed
5. `maxRetries` negative → throws at the call site

Five cases, and four of them are about disposal or non-duplication. That ratio
is why this is the challenge.

## Hint 2

The "no duplicates" requirement is the one with a real design consequence.
Consider the tempting streaming-parse version:

```csharp
await foreach (Item item in ParseIncrementallyAsync(response, token))
    yield return item;                   // 40 items in, the connection drops
```

Now a retry from the same cursor re-delivers those 40. To make that safe you
would need to track how many items of the current page have been delivered and
skip them on retry — which works only if the source is deterministic, and is a
genuine technique for large pages.

Fetching the page whole first is simpler and costs memory proportional to one
page. Choose deliberately; both appear in real clients.

## Hint 3

One production consideration this exercise cannot gate but you should carry:
**retrying a stream is not the same as retrying a request.**

A consumer who has already processed 10,000 items and then hits an
unrecoverable page failure has done real work that your exception discards. The
answers are checkpointing (yield the cursor alongside items so the consumer can
resume), or making the stream resumable (`ReadAllAsync(fromCursor: ...)`), or
accepting that the consumer must be idempotent and restart.

All three are design decisions that belong in the signature, not in the retry
loop. A streaming API that can fail halfway and offers no way to resume is
usable only for small results — at which point you should have returned a list.

## Review 1 - reading the trace

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB05_AsyncStreams/Review1.cs`. Three streams, each with a
bug visible only from a consumer's observations. Diagnose, then write the
repaired version.

- `Audit.Diagnose(string observation)` maps evidence to cause, exactly:
  - `"the whole source was fetched before the first item"` → `"eager buffering"`
  - `"cancelling changed nothing"` → `"missing EnumeratorCancellation"`
  - `"the file stayed open after break"` → `"no finally in the iterator"`
  - `"the second enumeration returned nothing"` → `"one-shot source"`
  - anything else → `"unknown"`
- `Audit.RepairedLazy(Func<int, Task<int[]>> fetchPage, int pages)` streams
  page by page instead of loading everything first.
- `Audit.RepairedCancellable(Func<int, Task<int>> load, int count, [EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken token = default)`
  honours an enumeration-time token.
- `Audit.RepairedDisposal(List<string> log, int count)` releases its resource
  on an early break.
- `Audit.Lesson()` returns exactly:
  `"a stream is a one-shot conversation, driven entirely by the consumer"`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb05_async_streams review1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Each observation is something a consumer can measure without reading the
producer's code — memory, timing, a token that does nothing, a handle that
stays open, a second enumeration that comes back empty.

Map each to its cause first. All three repairs are patterns from earlier in the
sector, so once the diagnosis is right the code is recall.

## Hint 2

The eager-buffering bug is the one that hides best, because it compiles to a
perfectly valid async stream:

```csharp
public static async IAsyncEnumerable<int> Bad(Func<int, Task<int[]>> fetch, int pages)
{
    var all = new List<int>();
    for (int p = 0; p < pages; p++) all.AddRange(await fetch(p));   // fetches everything
    foreach (int x in all) yield return x;                           // then dribbles it out
}
```

It has the memory profile of `Task<List<int>>` and the API of a stream — the
worst of both. The repair is to yield inside the page loop.

## Hint 3

The one-shot observation is worth more thought than the others because there is
no repair listed for it, deliberately.

Most async streams cannot be enumerated twice: the second `GetAsyncEnumerator`
either re-runs everything (re-fetching, re-charging, possibly returning
different data) or, for a source backed by a channel or a network connection,
returns nothing at all because the data is gone.

The compiler-generated iterator is re-enumerable in the sense that it creates a
fresh state machine — but "runs the whole method again" is rarely what a caller
who wrote `if (await source.AnyAsync()) await foreach (...)` intended. That
pattern enumerates twice and, over a paged HTTP source, doubles your API bill.

The rule: materialise once with `ToListAsync` if you need the data twice, and
treat any `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` you did not create as single-use.

Left to you: whether to *make* a stream re-enumerable. It is possible — a
factory-backed enumerable that re-runs cleanly — and it is almost always better
expressed as a method returning a fresh stream per call, which the type system
then makes obvious.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Turn each observation into the test that would have caught it:

1. assert the source's fetch count is 1 after taking one item
2. cancel the token after two items and assert the producer stopped
3. break early and assert the resource's dispose ran
4. enumerate twice and assert the second pass sees the same data — or document
   that it must not be done

Every one of those is three lines. Streaming code is unusually well served by
tests like these, because the bugs are all about *counts and order*, which are
easy to assert and impossible to see by reading.

## Hint 2

A second lens: each bug breaks one of the four promises an async stream makes.

- laziness — "I do work only when you ask"
- cancellability — "I stop when you say so"
- cleanup — "I release what I hold when you stop"
- one-shot honesty — "I am a conversation, not a collection"

An implementation that breaks any one of them is worse than the buffered
alternative it replaced, because callers write code assuming all four. That is
the argument for reviewing streaming code carefully rather than trusting the
type.

## Hint 3

The `Lesson()` string is the sentence to carry out of the sector: *a stream is
a one-shot conversation, driven entirely by the consumer*.

Both halves do work. **One-shot** explains why you cannot enumerate twice, why
caching one is a bug, and why retry needs explicit cursors. **Driven by the
consumer** explains laziness, backpressure, disposal on `break`, the resources
held during processing, and why nothing runs until somebody asks.

Everything else in this sector — the attribute, the `ValueTask<bool>`, the
disposal ordering, the operators — is machinery in service of those two
properties. And when a problem does not fit them, the answer is not a cleverer
stream: it is a `Channel`, which is where the next sector starts.

lessons.title: V3·CB5 — IAsyncEnumerable and streaming results
lessons.summary: A Task of a collection is a promise to buffer everything. An IAsyncEnumerable is a promise to hand you items as they arrive. This sector covers the async iterator state machine, EnumeratorCancellation, backpressure, disposal through early break, and writing your own lazy operators.

# V3·CB5 — IAsyncEnumerable and streaming results

`Task<IEnumerable<T>>` and `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` look like variations on a
theme. They are opposites. The first says: go away, fetch everything, allocate
a collection large enough to hold it, and call me when it is all here. The
second says: give me one item, and I will ask again when I am ready.

For a query returning twelve rows the difference is nothing. For a query
returning two million, the first one is an `OutOfMemoryException` and a
sixty-second wait before the caller sees a single row; the second one starts
producing output immediately and never holds more than a page. That is the
whole motivation, and it is why every modern data API — EF Core's
`AsAsyncEnumerable`, `Channel.ReadAllAsync`, gRPC streaming, ASP.NET Core's
streaming JSON results — is shaped this way.

**The mechanism is two state machines fused.** C# 2 gave iterators a state
machine driven by the consumer calling `MoveNext`. C# 5 gave async methods a
state machine driven by a completed awaiter's continuation. An async iterator
is driven by both: `MoveNextAsync` returns a `ValueTask<bool>` that completes
when the next item is ready, and the compiler generates one class implementing
`IAsyncEnumerable<T>`, `IAsyncEnumerator<T>` and `IValueTaskSource<bool>` at
once — using exactly the pooled-promise machinery from sector 2, which is why
`MoveNextAsync` returns a `ValueTask<bool>` rather than a `Task<bool>`. A
buffered stream would otherwise allocate once per element, for ever, inside a
language feature.

```csharp
public static async IAsyncEnumerable<Row> ReadAsync(string path)
{
    using var reader = new StreamReader(path);
    while (await reader.ReadLineAsync() is { } line)   // suspends per line
        yield return Parse(line);                      // hands one to the consumer
}

await foreach (Row row in ReadAsync(path))
    Handle(row);
```

**Laziness is the feature, and it has consequences.** The producer body runs
only while the consumer is pulling. Between `yield return` and the consumer's
next `MoveNextAsync`, your method is suspended mid-loop with its file handle
open and its locals alive. That gives you backpressure for free — a slow
consumer automatically slows the producer, with no queue and no configuration —
and it gives you a resource held for the duration of the consumer's processing,
which is a different bill than "read it all, close the file, then process".

**`break` is a real event.** When the consumer stops early, `await foreach`
calls `DisposeAsync` on the enumerator, which resumes your iterator at the
suspension point and runs its `finally` blocks. That is what closes the file.
It is also why `await using` and `try`/`finally` inside an async iterator work
at all, and why an enumerator that is abandoned without disposal leaks — the
`finally` never runs.

**Cancellation needs one attribute, for a reason worth understanding.**
Because `GetAsyncEnumerator` is called later than the method that produced the
`IAsyncEnumerable`, a token captured as an ordinary parameter is the one from
*creation* time, not enumeration time. `WithCancellation(token)` passes a token
to `GetAsyncEnumerator`, and `[EnumeratorCancellation]` on a parameter tells
the compiler to wire that token into it — combining it with any token the
creator supplied. Leave the attribute off and your token is silently ignored,
which is the most common async-stream bug there is.

**And the honest limits.** Per-item await overhead is real: a stream of a
million tiny items costs a million `MoveNextAsync` calls, and a batched
`IAsyncEnumerable<T[]>` frequently beats an item-at-a-time one by a wide
margin. Async streams also do not fan out — one consumer, one producer, in
lockstep — so anything needing concurrency belongs in a `Channel`, which is the
next sector. And `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` cannot be enumerated twice safely unless
the source explicitly supports it, which most do not.

**Two properties define everything else.** A stream is *one-shot* and it is
*consumer-driven*. One-shot explains why you cannot safely enumerate twice, why
caching an `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` in a dictionary is a bug, and why retrying a
half-consumed stream needs explicit cursors rather than a `catch` and a loop.
Consumer-driven explains laziness, backpressure, disposal on `break`, the
resources held for the consumer's processing time, and the fact that nothing
runs until somebody asks. Every piece of machinery in this sector — the
attribute, the `ValueTask<bool>`, the disposal choreography, the operators — is
in service of those two properties, and when a problem does not fit them the
answer is not a cleverer stream. It is a `Channel`.

**Where the abstraction stops.** Three questions tell you immediately whether
you have reached its edge. *Do I want the producer running ahead of the
consumer?* — that needs a buffer, so a `Channel`. *Do I want several items in
flight at once?* — a stream is strictly sequential, so a `Channel` and workers,
or `Parallel.ForEachAsync` over the stream. *Do I want to merge two sources by
whichever produces first?* — that requires holding a `ValueTask<bool>` from
each enumerator simultaneously, which violates the consume-once contract from
sector 2 and gives wrong answers rather than errors. All three roads lead to
the same place, which is why the next sector is where it is.

**Two smaller traps worth naming now**, because they cost real money in
production. Holding a lock, a transaction or anything with a server-side
timeout across a `yield return` means holding it for the consumer's processing
time, which is unbounded — a consumer that writes each item to a slow socket
keeps your database cursor open for the duration. And an `IAsyncEnumerable<T>`
that is created but never enumerated does *nothing at all*: no fetch, no
connection, no side effect. That is either a useful property or a silent no-op,
depending entirely on whether you meant it.

The gates here drive every source with `TaskCompletionSource`, count producer
calls to prove laziness, and assert disposal ordering. Nothing sleeps.
