# Reading - csharp/v3cb05_async_streams

## Notes

**`await foreach` desugars to a loop plus `await using`.** Roughly:

```csharp
IAsyncEnumerator<T> e = source.GetAsyncEnumerator(token);
try { while (await e.MoveNextAsync()) { T item = e.Current; ... } }
finally { await e.DisposeAsync(); }
```

Every behaviour of async streams is visible in that shape: the token goes to
`GetAsyncEnumerator`, `Current` is a plain property read (never awaited), and
disposal happens in a `finally` so `break`, `return` and exceptions all reach
it.

**`ValueTask<bool>` from `MoveNextAsync` is consumed once, by the desugaring,
and never stored.** That is what makes sector 2's strict contract safe here. A
helper that captures the `ValueTask` to race two enumerators is outside the
contract, and against a compiler-generated enumerator — which *is* a pooled
`IValueTaskSource<bool>` — you get wrong answers rather than exceptions.

**`[EnumeratorCancellation]` combines rather than replaces.** The generated
code links the token passed to `GetAsyncEnumerator` with whatever token the
factory method was given, so both work. If you write the enumerator by hand you
have to do that linking yourself — `CreateLinkedTokenSource` and dispose it in
your `DisposeAsync`.

**`ConfigureAwait` on a stream.** `await foreach (var x in source.ConfigureAwait(false))`
applies to the awaits the desugaring performs, including `DisposeAsync`. It
composes with `WithCancellation`:
`source.WithCancellation(token).ConfigureAwait(false)`.

**There is no LINQ for async streams in the base library.** `System.Linq.Async`
(the Rx team's package) provides `SelectAwait`, `WhereAwait`, `ToListAsync` and
the rest. .NET 10 adds a first-party set. Until then, hand-written operators
are common — and writing a couple, as ex6 does, teaches more about laziness
than reading about it.

**`ToBlockingEnumerable()`** exists for the boundary where you must hand an
async stream to synchronous code. It blocks a thread per item. Use it at the
edge of a console app, never in a server.

## ex1

The first async iterator is deliberately paged: it makes the two levels of
laziness visible. The outer `while` fetches a page (one await, one network
round trip); the inner `foreach` yields items with no awaiting at all. That is
the shape almost every real streaming source has, and it is why
`MoveNextAsync` returning a `ValueTask` matters — most calls are synchronous.

Note that the method's body does not begin executing until the first
`MoveNextAsync`. Calling `ReadAsync(path)` does nothing; the state machine is
constructed and immediately suspended at state -1.

## ex2

`[EnumeratorCancellation]` is the single most forgotten attribute in modern
C#. Without it, this compiles and runs and ignores your token:

```csharp
await foreach (var x in Stream(source).WithCancellation(token)) { }
```

`WithCancellation` hands the token to `GetAsyncEnumerator`; the generated
enumerator has nowhere to put it unless a parameter is marked. Analyzer
**CA2016**-adjacent rule **CS8425** warns when an async-iterator method has a
`CancellationToken` parameter without the attribute — turn warnings into errors
and the mistake becomes impossible.

## ex3

Counting producer calls is the cleanest possible demonstration of laziness. A
consumer that takes three items from a stream over a thousand causes exactly
three (plus one) `MoveNextAsync` calls and, in a paged source, exactly one page
fetch. Nothing else is computed, nothing else is fetched, and nothing else is
paid for.

This is also the property that makes async streams a poor fit for anything
needing look-ahead. If you want the producer running ahead of the consumer —
prefetching, smoothing latency — you need a buffer, and a buffer with
backpressure is a `Channel`.

## ex4

Disposal ordering catches people because there are two disposals in play: the
resource inside the iterator, and the enumerator itself. The sequence on an
early `break` is: consumer breaks → `finally` in the desugaring calls
`DisposeAsync` → iterator resumes at the `yield return` → its `finally` blocks
run in reverse order of entry → `DisposeAsync`'s task completes → the loop
exits.

If any of your `finally` code awaits, all of that is asynchronous, which is
exactly why `IAsyncDisposable` exists and why `await using` is not just
`using` with extra syntax.

## ex5 - ex8

Writing the enumerator by hand once is worth the twenty minutes because it
makes every streaming API you read afterwards legible. Four members, and each
one answers a question you would otherwise discover empirically: does
`MoveNextAsync` have a synchronous fast path, is the enumeration token linked
with the creation token or dropped, does `DisposeAsync` release anything, and
is the enumerable re-enumerable or one-shot.

The operators in ex6 are where laziness becomes a property you can accidentally
destroy. Each one is an `await foreach` with a `yield return` inside, which
preserves demand-driven evaluation automatically — but the `Take(0)` case
separates a correct implementation from a plausible one, because *entering* an
`await foreach` is itself a pull. Guard before the loop.

Batching in ex7 is the honest answer to per-item overhead, and it is what every
high-throughput streaming API in .NET does somewhere: `PipeReader` yields
buffers, not bytes; EF Core buffers rows per fetch. The two decisions worth
making deliberately are whether to reuse the buffer array (faster, and mutates
under any consumer who stores a batch) and whether to flush on a timer as well
as on size — the latter needs two things in flight and therefore a `Channel`,
which is a neat demonstration of this abstraction's ceiling.

The adapters in ex8 close the loop. `reader.ReadAllAsync(token)` being a
one-line adapter is a hint about where the next sector goes, and the
completion-order stream is the exercise's quiet warning: repeated `WhenAny`
over a shrinking list is O(n²), fine for a handful and wrong for thousands, and
the O(n) version is — again — a channel.

## Further reading

- [Iterating with Async Enumerables in C# 8](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/archive/msdn-magazine/2019/november/csharp-iterating-with-async-enumerables-in-csharp-8) — the original tour, still the clearest.
- [`IAsyncEnumerable<T>`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.collections.generic.iasyncenumerable-1) — the interface, and `WithCancellation`.
- [`EnumeratorCancellationAttribute`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.runtime.compilerservices.enumeratorcancellationattribute) — why it exists, in the remarks.
- [Async streams in ASP.NET Core](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/aspnet/core/web-api/) — returning one from a controller action and what the serialiser does with it.
- [System.Linq.Async](https://github.com/dotnet/reactive) — the Rx team's operator set, and the design notes behind `SelectAwait`.
lessons.fullReadme:
# V3·CB5 — IAsyncEnumerable and streaming results

Streaming is the difference between "call me when you have all of it" and
"give me the next one when it is ready". The type says which one you mean.

## Concept 1 — the shape

```csharp
public static async IAsyncEnumerable<int> CountAsync(int n)
{
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++)
    {
        await Task.Yield();      // any await at all makes it an async iterator
        yield return i;
    }
}

await foreach (int x in CountAsync(3)) Console.WriteLine(x);
```

`async` + `yield return` + `IAsyncEnumerable<T>`. The method body does not
start until the first `MoveNextAsync`.

## Concept 2 — what await foreach really does

```csharp
IAsyncEnumerator<T> e = source.GetAsyncEnumerator(token);
try
{
    while (await e.MoveNextAsync())
    {
        T item = e.Current;     // a property, not an await
        // body
    }
}
finally { await e.DisposeAsync(); }
```

Everything about async streams follows from this: the token goes to
`GetAsyncEnumerator`; `break` and exceptions both reach the `finally`; and
`DisposeAsync` is what runs your iterator's `finally` blocks.

## Concept 3 — cancellation, and the attribute

```csharp
public static async IAsyncEnumerable<Row> ReadAsync(
    string path,
    [EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken token = default)
{
    await foreach (Page page in FetchPagesAsync(path, token))
    {
        token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested();
        foreach (Row row in page.Rows) yield return row;
    }
}

await foreach (Row row in ReadAsync(path).WithCancellation(token)) { }
```

Without the attribute the token from `WithCancellation` is silently discarded.
The compiler warns (CS8425) — do not ignore it.

## Concept 4 — laziness and backpressure

```csharp
await foreach (int x in ExpensiveAsync())
{
    if (x > 10) break;         // the producer stops here, permanently
    await SlowHandleAsync(x);  // and waits for us, with no queue anywhere
}
```

The producer runs only between `MoveNextAsync` calls. A slow consumer throttles
a fast producer automatically. There is no buffer, which is a feature — and a
limitation when you *want* the producer running ahead.

## Concept 5 — disposal

```csharp
public static async IAsyncEnumerable<string> LinesAsync(Stream stream)
{
    await using var reader = new StreamReader(stream);   // released on break too
    try
    {
        while (await reader.ReadLineAsync() is { } line) yield return line;
    }
    finally { Log("stream finished or abandoned"); }
}
```

An early `break` resumes the iterator inside `DisposeAsync` so both the
`finally` and the `await using` run. Abandon an enumerator without disposing
and neither does.

## Concept 6 — hand-written operators

```csharp
public static async IAsyncEnumerable<TOut> SelectAwait<TIn, TOut>(
    this IAsyncEnumerable<TIn> source,
    Func<TIn, ValueTask<TOut>> selector,
    [EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken token = default)
{
    await foreach (TIn item in source.WithCancellation(token).ConfigureAwait(false))
        yield return await selector(item).ConfigureAwait(false);
}
```

Lazy, cancellable, composable, and eleven lines. This is what
`System.Linq.Async` gives you a hundred of.

## Worked example — the buffering impostor

```csharp
// Looks like a stream. Behaves like Task<List<int>>.
public static async IAsyncEnumerable<int> Bad(Func<int, Task<int[]>> fetch, int pages)
{
    var all = new List<int>();
    for (int p = 0; p < pages; p++) all.AddRange(await fetch(p));
    foreach (int x in all) yield return x;
}

// Actually streams.
public static async IAsyncEnumerable<int> Good(Func<int, Task<int[]>> fetch, int pages)
{
    for (int p = 0; p < pages; p++)
        foreach (int x in await fetch(p)) yield return x;
}
```

The first has the memory profile of the buffered version and the API of a
stream — the worst of both, and it compiles perfectly. The consumer's evidence
is unmistakable: taking one item fetched every page. Any time a caller reports
"the first item took as long as all of them", this is what happened.

## Worked example — composition, and how many items get produced

```csharp
await foreach (int x in Numbers().Where(IsEven).Take(2)) { }
```

Over `0,1,2,3,4,...`, how many items does `Numbers()` produce? Three — `0`,
`1`, `2`. `Take` stops asking once it has two, and `Where` pulls only when
asked, discarding the odd one on the way. Predicting five means you are
thinking of the eager version; predicting two means you forgot the discard.

Being able to answer that in your head is what "lazy composition" means
concretely, and it is the property that makes a five-operator chain over a
paged HTTP source cost one HTTP request.

## Common mistakes

1. **Forgetting `[EnumeratorCancellation]`.** The token is silently ignored.
2. **Buffering inside the iterator.** `var all = await LoadEverythingAsync();
   foreach (...) yield return ...;` is a `Task<List<T>>` wearing a costume.
3. **Enumerating twice.** Most sources restart, re-fetch, or throw. Materialise
   once if you need it twice.
4. **Assuming disposal happened.** An abandoned enumerator's `finally` never
   runs; always `await foreach` or `await using`.
5. **Holding a lock across `yield return`.** You are suspended for as long as
   the consumer takes — which is unbounded.
6. **`ToBlockingEnumerable()` on a server.** One blocked thread per item.
7. **Per-item streams for tiny items.** Batch; `IAsyncEnumerable<T[]>` is
   often ten times faster.
8. **Expecting concurrency.** One producer, one consumer, in lockstep. Use a
   `Channel` for fan-out.

## Concept 7 — what you cannot write with yield

Some operators are impossible as async iterators, and knowing which ones saves
you an afternoon.

- **`Merge`** — interleave two streams by whichever produces first. Needs a
  `ValueTask<bool>` held from each enumerator at once, which breaks sector 2's
  consume-once contract against pooled enumerators.
- **Prefetch** — run the producer one item ahead. Needs a buffer; a stream has
  none by design.
- **Time-based batching** — flush on size *or* a deadline. Needs the next item
  raced against a timer, so again two things in flight.
- **Fan-out** — several consumers on one stream. There is one cursor.

All four are the same shape: more than one thing pending at a time. All four
are a `Channel`, and recognising the shape is faster than rediscovering the
limitation each time.

## Concept 8 — validation and the wrapper split, again

```csharp
public static IAsyncEnumerable<T[]> Chunk<T>(this IAsyncEnumerable<T> source, int size)
{
    ArgumentOutOfRangeException.ThrowIfNegativeOrZero(size);   // now
    return ChunkCore(source, size);                             // deferred
}
```

An async iterator defers its entire body to the first `MoveNextAsync`, so
argument checks inside one fire whenever somebody happens to enumerate —
possibly in another component, possibly never. The same non-async wrapper from
sector 1 applies, with one twist: `[EnumeratorCancellation]` goes on the
*core*, since the wrapper is not an iterator.

## Interview angle

> "When would you return `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` instead of `Task<List<T>>`?"

When the result set is large or unbounded, when the caller can start work
before the last item arrives, or when memory should stay flat regardless of
size — a database cursor, a log tail, a paged API, a gRPC stream. It changes
the contract from "buffer everything, then deliver" to "deliver as available",
and it gives backpressure for free because the producer only runs while the
consumer pulls. The costs: one `MoveNextAsync` per item, resources held for the
duration of consumption, no safe second enumeration, and no concurrency — one
consumer at a time. If I need the producer to run ahead of the consumer, that
is a `Channel`, not a stream.

Follow-ups: what `[EnumeratorCancellation]` is for; what happens on an early
`break`; why `MoveNextAsync` returns `ValueTask<bool>`; and how you would batch
a stream.

## Check yourself

1. What does `await foreach` desugar to?
2. When does an async iterator's body start running?
3. Why does `MoveNextAsync` return `ValueTask<bool>` rather than `Task<bool>`?
4. What does `[EnumeratorCancellation]` do, and what happens without it?
5. Trace what happens when a consumer `break`s halfway through.
6. Where does backpressure come from in an async stream?
7. Why is holding a lock across `yield return` dangerous?
8. How do you apply both `WithCancellation` and `ConfigureAwait`?
9. What is wrong with `foreach (var x in await LoadAllAsync()) yield return x;`?
10. How would you turn `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` into batches of 100?
11. Why can most async streams not be enumerated twice?
12. When is a `Channel` the better answer than an async stream?
13. What does `ToBlockingEnumerable()` cost, and where is it acceptable?
lessons.fullReading:
# Reading - csharp/v3cb05_async_streams

## Where it came from

C# had two state-machine features and no way to combine them. `yield return`
gave you lazy pull-based sequences but every `MoveNext` was synchronous;
`async` gave you non-blocking waits but a method could return only one value.
Anything that was both — a database cursor, a network stream of messages, a
paged API — had to be written by hand as an `IEnumerator`-like object with
`Task`-returning methods, and everybody's hand-written version was subtly
different.

C# 8 fused them. The compiler generates a single class implementing
`IAsyncEnumerable<T>`, `IAsyncEnumerator<T>` and — importantly —
`IValueTaskSource<bool>`, so the per-item promise is reused rather than
allocated. `MoveNextAsync` returns `ValueTask<bool>` precisely because the
common case is a buffered source that already has the next item: no
allocation, no suspension, just a branch. Sector 2's contract is what makes
that safe, and the reason it is safe here is that exactly one consumer — the
`await foreach` desugaring — ever touches that value, exactly once.

The interface deliberately does not include a `Reset`, a `Count`, or any way to
enumerate twice. Those omissions are the design: a stream is a one-shot
conversation with a producer, and pretending otherwise is what
`Task<List<T>>` is for.

## The cancellation design, and why it looks odd

`[EnumeratorCancellation]` is the piece everyone trips over, and the reason is
worth understanding rather than memorising.

An async-iterator method returns immediately, having run none of its body. The
`IAsyncEnumerable<T>` it produced is a *factory*: `GetAsyncEnumerator(token)`
is what actually starts anything, possibly much later, possibly in a different
component. So there are two moments at which a caller might supply a token —
when creating the sequence, and when enumerating it — and they can be different
callers entirely.

`WithCancellation(token)` supplies the enumeration-time one.
`[EnumeratorCancellation]` marks which parameter should receive it, and the
generated code *combines* the two tokens rather than replacing one with the
other, so a stream created with one token and enumerated with another honours
both. Without the attribute the enumeration-time token has nowhere to go and is
dropped silently — hence compiler warning CS8425, which is one of the few
warnings worth promoting to an error on sight.

Writing an enumerator by hand means doing the combination yourself:
`CancellationTokenSource.CreateLinkedTokenSource(creationToken, enumerationToken)`
in `GetAsyncEnumerator`, and disposing it in `DisposeAsync`. That is one of
several reasons to prefer `yield return`.

## Performance notes

Three costs dominate, and they push in different directions.

**Per-item overhead.** Each element costs a `MoveNextAsync` call, a
`ValueTask<bool>` check, a `Current` read, and a state-machine resumption. For
a synchronous buffered source that is a handful of nanoseconds; for a
suspending source it is a full async suspension. Streaming a million
one-integer items is therefore genuinely slower than returning an array — and
streaming a million rows is genuinely faster, because the array version also
allocates a million rows at once.

**The crossover is batching.** `IAsyncEnumerable<T[]>` or
`IAsyncEnumerable<ReadOnlyMemory<T>>` amortises the per-item cost across a
whole chunk while keeping memory flat. Most high-throughput streaming APIs are
shaped this way — `PipeReader` reads buffers, not bytes; `ChannelReader<T>` is
per-item but the items are usually messages, not integers. If you are
streaming primitives, batch.

**Held resources.** A suspended iterator keeps its connection, file handle,
transaction and locals alive for as long as the consumer takes. Streaming two
million rows to a slow consumer means holding a database cursor open for
minutes, which some databases will tolerate and some will not. The buffered
alternative holds memory instead of a connection; which of those you can afford
is a property of your system, not of the API.

## What a suspended iterator is holding

Between one `yield return` and the consumer's next `MoveNextAsync`, your method
is a live object on the heap holding every local that crosses that suspension.
For a paged database reader that means: an open connection, a server-side
cursor, possibly a transaction, the current page's buffer, and whatever else
was in scope. All of it is rooted for as long as the consumer takes.

That is a different bill from the buffered version, and it is the bill people
forget to read. Buffering trades memory for a short connection hold; streaming
trades a long connection hold for flat memory. Which you can afford is a
property of your infrastructure — a database with a thirty-second cursor
timeout and a consumer that writes each row to a slow downstream will fail at
minute two, and the stack trace will point at the database driver rather than
at the design decision.

Three practical consequences. **Never hold a lock across `yield return`** — the
hold time is the consumer's processing time, which is unbounded, and a consumer
whose body touches the same lock deadlocks immediately. **Scope large locals
tightly** so they die before the suspension rather than being hoisted into the
state machine. And **treat a long-lived cursor as a resource with a budget**:
if the consumer might be slow, buffer a page, release the connection, and hand
out the page — which is exactly why batching keeps appearing as the answer.

## When not to stream

**When the result is small and bounded.** Ten rows do not need a state machine.
`Task<List<T>>` is simpler, safe to enumerate repeatedly, easy to cache, and
trivially serialisable.

**When the caller needs the whole thing anyway.** If every consumer's first
line is `ToListAsync()`, the stream is ceremony. Return the list.

**When you need concurrency.** Async streams are strictly sequential: one item
at a time, producer and consumer in lockstep. Processing items in parallel
means pumping the stream into a `Channel` and running workers off it, or using
`Parallel.ForEachAsync` over the stream — both of which are the next two
sectors, and both of which mean you have left the streaming abstraction behind.

**When the source cannot be re-read and the consumer might need to retry.** A
stream consumed halfway and then abandoned has done work you cannot undo, and
restarting means re-fetching from the beginning — or worse, from an
indeterminate position. Streaming and retry compose badly; you need explicit
checkpointing, which is what the challenge in this sector is about.

**When you are tempted to cache it.** An `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` in a
`ConcurrentDictionary` is a bug waiting to happen: the first consumer drains
it and every later one gets nothing, or the source restarts and everyone pays
full price. Cache the materialised result, not the sequence.

## A note on the ecosystem

The base class library still ships no LINQ operators for `IAsyncEnumerable<T>`
— `System.Linq.Async` from the Rx team fills the gap, and .NET 10 adds a
first-party set. Until you are on that, expect to see three things in
codebases: the Rx package, a small hand-rolled `AsyncEnumerableExtensions`
file, and `await foreach` loops written out longhand because somebody decided
two dependencies were worse than four extra lines.

All three are defensible. What is not defensible is a hand-rolled operator that
loses cancellation or laziness — which is exactly what ex6 makes you get right,
and exactly what makes reviewing somebody else's version worth doing carefully.
