## Exercise 1 - the simplest pipeline

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB06_Channels/Ex1.cs`.

- `Simple.ProduceAsync(ChannelWriter<int> writer, int count)` writes `0`
  through `count - 1` and completes the channel — in a `finally`, so a failure
  still terminates the consumer.
- `Simple.ConsumeAsync(ChannelReader<int> reader)` sums everything with
  `ReadAllAsync` and returns the total. It must end because the writer
  completed, not because of a sentinel value or a count.
- `Simple.RunAsync(int count)` creates an unbounded channel, starts the
  producer, consumes, awaits both, and returns the sum.
- `Simple.EndedByCompletion(ChannelReader<int> reader)` returns `true` when the
  reader's `Completion` task has finished.

Example: `RunAsync(4)` returns `6`, and the consumer's loop exits on its own.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb06_channels_pipelines ex1
```
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask what makes the consumer stop, and reject every answer except one.

Not a count — the consumer does not know how many there will be. Not a sentinel
— that breaks the moment the sentinel is legal data. Not a flag — checking it
races with the last item. Not cancellation — that is an abnormal end, not a
normal one.

`Complete()` is the only mechanism that is both correct and race-free, and
recognising why the alternatives fail is worth more than the code.

## Hint 2

A useful way to see the channel's two halves: think of `ChannelWriter<T>` and
`ChannelReader<T>` as capabilities you hand out. A method that receives a
writer *cannot* read, cannot peek at the queue depth, and cannot be tempted to
"just check" whether the consumer is keeping up.

That is the same discipline as passing a `CancellationToken` rather than a
`CancellationTokenSource`: give each side the narrowest view that does its job,
and a whole category of misuse becomes unrepresentable.

## Hint 3

Once it passes, try the experiment that makes `Completion` concrete: after the
consumer's loop ends, inspect `reader.Completion`.

It is a `Task` that completes when the channel is finished *and drained*. It
faults if the writer completed with an exception. That makes it the natural
thing for a supervisor to await — one task per pipeline that tells you whether
the pipeline ended normally or died, without the supervisor needing to know
anything about the stages.

That pattern scales: a pipeline of four stages exposes four `Completion` tasks,
and `Task.WhenAll` over them is your "the pipeline is finished" signal, while
`Task.WhenAny` over them is your "something died" signal.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 - measuring backpressure

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB06_Channels/Ex2.cs`.

- `Pressure.RunAsync(int items, int capacity)` creates a **bounded** channel of
  `capacity`, runs a producer that writes `0..items-1` recording
  `Pressure.MaxAhead` — the largest gap between "items written" and "items
  read" — and a consumer that reads them one at a time.
- The gate asserts `MaxAhead` never exceeds `capacity`, exactly, for capacities
  1, 2 and 5.
- `Pressure.Written` and `Pressure.Read` are the two counters.
- `Pressure.WouldGrowUnbounded(BoundedChannelFullMode mode)` returns `true`
  only for a mode that never makes the writer wait — that is, anything except
  `Wait`.

Example: with `capacity` 2 and 10 items, the producer is never more than two
items ahead of the consumer, and both counters end at 10.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb06_channels_pipelines ex2
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

You do not implement backpressure — you observe it. `WriteAsync` on a full
channel simply does not complete until the consumer takes something, so the
producer's own loop is throttled with no code on your part.

The measurement is the exercise: increment a counter before each write,
increment another after each read, and track the maximum difference.

## Hint 2

```csharp
Channel<int> channel = Channel.CreateBounded<int>(new BoundedChannelOptions(capacity)
{
    FullMode = BoundedChannelFullMode.Wait,
});

// producer
await writer.WriteAsync(i).ConfigureAwait(false);
Written++;
MaxAhead = Math.Max(MaxAhead, Written - Read);
```

Take the measurement *after* the write completes: before it, the write may be
waiting, which is exactly the state you are trying to prove exists.

## Hint 3

The number to reason about is what "capacity" actually means: how far the
producer may run ahead. That makes it a latency knob as much as a memory one.

- Capacity 1 — nearly lockstep. Minimum memory, no smoothing, any consumer
  jitter stalls the producer immediately.
- Capacity 100 — absorbs bursts of up to 100, and an item entering a full queue
  waits for 100 items to be processed before anyone looks at it.
- Capacity 100,000 — you have chosen memory over feedback, and an item can
  wait minutes.

The honest way to pick it: decide the longest an item may sit unprocessed, and
divide by your per-item processing time.

Left to you: whether the counters should use `Interlocked`. With one producer
and one consumer on different tasks they genuinely race, and sector 7 will make
you fix exactly this. Here, note that the gate's assertion is about a maximum,
which is tolerant of a slightly stale read — and that "tolerant of staleness"
is a claim you should be suspicious of when you hear yourself making it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Predict the assertion before running it. With capacity 2, what is the largest
possible value of `Written - Read`?

Three, briefly — the two in the queue plus the one the consumer has taken but
not yet counted — or two, depending on exactly where you increment. Working out
which, and why, tells you whether your instrumentation is measuring the channel
or measuring your own bookkeeping.

The gate is lenient about that boundary; your understanding should not be.

## Hint 2

The comparison worth making is against the unbounded version. Run the same test
with `Channel.CreateUnbounded<int>()` and a consumer that is deliberately slow:
`MaxAhead` grows to the full item count, because the producer never waits.

Now imagine that with a million items arriving per minute and a consumer that
is 5% too slow. The queue grows by 50,000 items a minute, memory climbs
steadily, and the process dies about an hour later — long after the deploy that
caused it, with a heap full of queued work and no obvious culprit.

That is the failure mode a bound removes.

## Hint 3

`WouldGrowUnbounded` is pointing at something worth stating plainly: **the
three dropping modes are also "never wait" modes**. With `DropOldest`,
`DropNewest` or `DropWrite`, the writer is never throttled — capacity bounds
memory, but the producer runs at full speed and data is silently discarded.

So there are really three regimes, not two:

- unbounded: never waits, never drops, unbounded memory
- bounded + `Wait`: waits, never drops, bounded memory
- bounded + drop: never waits, drops, bounded memory

You may pick any two of "never wait", "never drop", "bounded memory". Being
able to state that trilemma is what makes the `FullMode` choice a decision
rather than a default.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 - the writer protocol

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB06_Channels/Ex3.cs`. `WriteAsync` per item is fine;
`WaitToWriteAsync` plus `TryWrite` is what a hot producer does.

- `Protocol.PumpAsync(ChannelWriter<int> writer, IEnumerator<int> source, CancellationToken token)`
  writes everything from `source` using the wait-then-burst loop, completes the
  writer when the source is exhausted, and returns the number of items written.
- A `TryWrite` returning `false` must send you back to `WaitToWriteAsync` — not
  spin, not sleep, not throw.
- `WaitToWriteAsync` returning `false` means the channel is closed: stop, and
  return what you managed.
- `Protocol.Waits` counts how many times the loop had to wait.
- `Protocol.Classify(bool tryWriteResult, bool waitResult)` returns `"burst"`,
  `"full"`, or `"closed"` for the three meaningful combinations.

Example: over a bounded channel of capacity 2 with a consumer reading on
demand, pumping 10 items writes all 10 and waits several times.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb06_channels_pipelines ex3
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Two nested loops, and each `while` means something different. The outer one
waits for capacity; the inner one uses as much of that capacity as it can
before waiting again.

Write the outer loop's condition first and be precise about what its `false`
means — it is the terminal condition, not a retry.

## Hint 2

```csharp
while (await writer.WaitToWriteAsync(token).ConfigureAwait(false))
{
    while (source.MoveNext())
    {
        if (!writer.TryWrite(source.Current))
        {
            pending = source.Current;    // hold the item we could not write
            goto waitAgain;              // or restructure to avoid the goto
        }

        written++;
    }

    writer.Complete();
    return written;
}
```

The awkward part is the item you pulled from the source but could not write —
you must not lose it. Hold it in a local and write it first on the next pass, or
restructure so you only `MoveNext` after a successful write.

## Hint 3

Why the double loop exists at all: `WriteAsync` allocates a `ValueTask` and
goes through the wait machinery for every single item, even when there is
plenty of room. `TryWrite` is a synchronous attempt with no allocation, so a
burst of 100 writes into a channel with space costs one `WaitToWriteAsync` and
100 cheap calls.

On a channel doing thousands of items per second that is measurable. On one
doing dozens, `await writer.WriteAsync(item, token)` in a plain `foreach` is
clearer and you should write that instead.

The three-way `Classify` is the mental model: `TryWrite` true is "keep going",
`TryWrite` false is "full, go wait", `WaitToWriteAsync` false is "closed,
stop". Those are the only three outcomes, and conflating the last two is the
bug this exercise exists to prevent.

Left to you: whether to complete the writer inside this method at all. A pump
that completes assumes it is the only producer — true here, false in ex5. Real
helpers usually take a `bool completeWhenDone` or leave completion to the
caller.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Enumerate the states before coding. At any moment the pump is in one of four
situations:

1. space available, items remaining → write
2. no space, items remaining → wait
3. items exhausted → complete and stop
4. channel closed → stop, without completing

Four states, and the code is a transcription. The bug people ship is merging
(2) and (4), because both come back from the same pair of methods returning
`false`.

## Hint 2

The lost-item problem is worth solving carefully because it is the same shape
as every buffered-reader bug. Once you call `source.MoveNext()`, that item is
out of the source and exists only in your hand. If `TryWrite` then fails and
you loop back to `WaitToWriteAsync`, the naive next iteration calls
`MoveNext()` again and the item is gone.

Two clean fixes: hold the pending item in a local and try it first on the next
pass, or invert the loop so `MoveNext` happens only after a write succeeds. The
second is tidier and slightly harder to write; either is fine as long as you
can point at why no item can be dropped.

## Hint 3

There is a third writer method worth knowing about: `writer.TryComplete()`,
which returns `false` instead of throwing when the channel is already complete.

Use `Complete()` when completing twice would be a bug you want to hear about,
and `TryComplete()` in `finally` blocks and shutdown paths where a second call
is plausible and harmless. The pair mirrors `SetResult`/`TrySetResult` from
sector 1, for the same reason: completion is a race in any system with more
than one exit path, and the `Try` form is how you say "I am one of several
plausible finishers".

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 - dropping on purpose

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB06_Channels/Ex4.cs`. Two sinks with opposite policies.

- `Sinks.LatestWins(int capacity)` returns a bounded channel with
  `BoundedChannelFullMode.DropOldest` — a telemetry sink where the newest value
  supersedes the old.
- `Sinks.RejectWhenFull(int capacity)` returns one with `DropWrite`, so an
  incoming item is discarded when the queue is full.
- `Sinks.WriteAllAsync(ChannelWriter<int> writer, int count)` writes
  `0..count-1` and returns how many `TryWrite` calls reported success.
- `Sinks.DrainAsync(ChannelReader<int> reader)` returns everything currently
  queued, as a list, without waiting for more.
- `Sinks.Dropped(int written, int read)` returns the difference — the only way
  to know, since the channel will not tell you.

Example: `LatestWins(2)` written with `0..9` and then drained gives `[8, 9]`,
and `Dropped(10, 2)` is `8`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb06_channels_pipelines ex4
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Both sinks are one `BoundedChannelOptions` each; the exercise is in
understanding what they do to your ability to observe.

Under a dropping mode, `TryWrite` returns `true` even when it just evicted
something, and `WriteAsync` completes immediately. Nothing in the API tells you
data was lost.

## Hint 2

```csharp
Channel.CreateBounded<int>(new BoundedChannelOptions(capacity)
{
    FullMode = BoundedChannelFullMode.DropOldest,
});
```

For `DrainAsync`, use the synchronous drain shape rather than `ReadAllAsync`,
which would wait for more items:

```csharp
var items = new List<int>();
while (reader.TryRead(out int item)) items.Add(item);
```

`TryRead` returning `false` on a non-completed channel means "empty right now",
which is exactly what draining wants.

## Hint 3

The counting requirement is the real lesson. With `DropOldest` you can write
one million items into a channel of capacity 100 and your writer's success
count says one million. The reader sees at most 100 plus whatever it consumed
along the way.

So every dropping channel needs a dropped counter next to it, computed as
"written minus read" or tracked explicitly by a wrapper. A telemetry pipeline
without one is a pipeline that will confidently report healthy while
discarding 90% of its data — and that failure is invisible in exactly the
metrics you would use to detect it.

Left to you: which mode a real telemetry sink should use. `DropOldest` if the
newest value is the truth (a gauge, a temperature, a position).
`DropWrite` if the *earliest* observations matter most, which is rarer than
people assume. And `Wait` if the data is actually important, at which point you
have decided that telemetry may slow down your application — a decision worth
making explicitly rather than by leaving a default.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Frame it as a question about meaning, not mechanics: when the system is
overloaded, which items are worth keeping?

- The newest, because old values are stale → `DropOldest`
- The oldest, because they are earliest in a sequence you must preserve →
  `DropNewest`
- Whatever is already accepted; refuse new work → `DropWrite`
- All of them, and slow the producer down → `Wait`

Four answers, four modes. Pick from the meaning, not from the performance.

## Hint 2

An experiment that makes the semantics concrete: create a capacity-3
`DropOldest` channel, write `1..10` with no reader, then drain.

You get `[8, 9, 10]`. Now do the same with `DropNewest`: you get `[1, 2, 3]`.
And with `DropWrite`: also `[1, 2, 3]` — the difference between the last two
only shows when items are being read concurrently, since `DropNewest` evicts
the newest *queued* item to make room while `DropWrite` discards the incoming
one without touching the queue.

Ten seconds of experimentation removes a paragraph of documentation.

## Hint 3

One design pattern worth carrying: for telemetry, wrap the writer rather than
using it raw.

```csharp
public bool TryPublish(Metric m)
{
    if (writer.TryWrite(m)) return true;
    Interlocked.Increment(ref dropped);      // never reached under DropOldest
    return false;
}
```

Under `Wait` or a non-dropping bound that counter is meaningful. Under a
dropping mode it never fires, so the wrapper must instead compare its own write
count against the reader's consumption — which means the reader has to report,
and now you have designed a small system rather than called a method.

That is the honest cost of silent dropping, and it is why `Wait` remains the
right default for anything you would be upset to lose.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 - many producers, one completion

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB06_Channels/Ex5.cs`.

- `Fan.ProduceAsync(ChannelWriter<int> writer, int start, int count, CancellationToken token)`
  writes `count` items beginning at `start`. It must **not** complete the
  channel — it is one of several.
- `Fan.RunAsync(int producers, int perProducer)` starts that many producers,
  completes the channel exactly once after all of them finish, consumes
  everything, and returns the total count read.
- A producer that throws must still result in the channel being completed, and
  the failure must reach the consumer.
- `Fan.Completions` counts how many times `Complete` was called successfully —
  the gate asserts it is `1`.
- `Fan.SecondCompleteThrows(ChannelWriter<int> writer)` returns `true` when a
  second `Complete()` throws, and demonstrates `TryComplete()` as the
  alternative.

Example: 3 producers × 4 items each yields 12 items read and exactly one
completion.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb06_channels_pipelines ex5
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The bug this exercise exists to prevent: each producer completing the channel
when it finishes. The first one to finish truncates the pipeline; the second
one throws.

So completion belongs to whoever *knows* they are all done — which is the code
that started them, not any of them.

## Hint 2

```csharp
Task[] producers = [.. Enumerable.Range(0, count)
    .Select(i => ProduceAsync(writer, i * perProducer, perProducer, token))];

_ = Task.Run(async () =>
{
    try { await Task.WhenAll(producers).ConfigureAwait(false); writer.Complete(); }
    catch (Exception ex) { writer.Complete(ex); }
});
```

Or, without the extra task: consume in one task and await the producers in the
main flow, completing after. Either is fine; the invariant is one `Complete`,
after all producers.

## Hint 3

Three details worth getting exactly right.

**`Complete(ex)` rather than swallowing.** A producer that dies must fault the
channel, or the consumer waits for items that will never arrive and your
shutdown hangs on a failure you never logged.

**`Task.WhenAll` waits for every producer even after one fails** — which is
what you want here: completing the channel while other producers are still
writing throws `ChannelClosedException` inside *them*, turning one failure into
several confusing ones.

**`TryComplete` versus `Complete`.** Use `Complete` where a second call is a
bug you want to hear about, and `TryComplete` in `finally` blocks and shutdown
paths where two exits are plausible. It mirrors `SetResult`/`TrySetResult` from
sector 1, for the same reason.

Left to you: whether producers should receive a `ChannelWriter<T>` at all, or a
narrower `Func<int, ValueTask>`. Handing out the writer is conventional and
means any producer *could* complete it; handing out a write delegate makes that
unrepresentable. For a codebase where this bug has bitten once, the delegate is
worth the indirection.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Ask who has the information. A producer knows when *it* is done. Only the code
that started all of them knows when *they all* are. Completion is a statement
about the whole set, so it belongs to whoever holds the set.

That is a general principle for concurrent code, and it generalises: any
"everyone has finished" signal belongs to the joiner, never to a participant.

## Hint 2

The failure mode is worth simulating once so you recognise it. Make each
producer call `writer.Complete()` when it finishes, then run three of them.

You get one of two outcomes depending on timing: a truncated result (the first
producer finished and completed the channel while others still had items), or
an `InvalidOperationException` from the second `Complete`, thrown inside a task
nobody is awaiting — which surfaces as an unobserved task exception minutes
later.

Non-deterministic truncation plus a delayed unrelated-looking exception is
about as unpleasant as debugging gets, and it is caused by one line in the
wrong place.

## Hint 3

There is a variation worth knowing for long-running pipelines: producers that
are not a fixed set.

If producers can be added while the pipeline runs — a connection handler
spawning a producer per client, say — then "all producers finished" is not a
`WhenAll` over a known array. The standard shape is a counter:
`Interlocked.Increment` when a producer starts, `Interlocked.Decrement` when it
finishes, and the one that decrements to zero completes the channel — plus a
"no more producers will be added" flag that must be set before the last one
finishes, or the count can hit zero and then rise again.

That is genuinely tricky, and it is the point at which many teams reach for a
dedicated supervisor object. Recognising that a moving producer set is a
different problem from a fixed one is most of the battle.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 - a worker pool

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB06_Channels/Ex6.cs`. One channel, several consumers, and
an aggregation that does not depend on completion order.

- `Pool.RunAsync(int[] input, int workers, Func<int, Task<int>> transform)`
  writes every input into a bounded channel, runs `workers` consumers that each
  read from it, applies `transform`, and writes results into a second channel.
- Each input must be handled by **exactly one** worker.
- Results are collected and returned **sorted**, so the assertion does not
  depend on the non-deterministic completion order.
- `Pool.PerWorker` records how many items each worker handled; the gate asserts
  the counts sum to `input.Length`.
- `Pool.MaxConcurrent` records the highest number of transforms in flight at
  once; the gate asserts it never exceeds `workers`.

Example: 10 inputs across 3 workers yields 10 sorted results, with the
per-worker counts summing to 10 and no more than 3 transforms in flight.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb06_channels_pipelines ex6
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

The channel does the distribution for you. Each item is dequeued by exactly one
reader — that is a property of the queue, not something you coordinate. So the
"exactly once" requirement needs no code at all.

The parts you do write: N consumer loops over the same reader, a results
channel, and a completion for each.

## Hint 2

```csharp
Task[] workers = [.. Enumerable.Range(0, count).Select(id => Task.Run(async () =>
{
    await foreach (int item in input.Reader.ReadAllAsync().ConfigureAwait(false))
    {
        int result = await transform(item).ConfigureAwait(false);
        await output.Writer.WriteAsync(result).ConfigureAwait(false);
    }
}))];

_ = Task.Run(async () =>
{
    await Task.WhenAll(workers).ConfigureAwait(false);
    output.Writer.Complete();          // one completion, after all workers
});
```

Same rule as ex5: the output channel is completed once, by whoever knows all
the workers are done.

## Hint 3

Two measurement details that are easy to get wrong.

`MaxConcurrent` must be incremented *before* the transform and decremented
after, with the maximum sampled while the counter is high. Use `Interlocked`
for both, because several workers touch it concurrently — this is the first
exercise in the course where a plain `++` is genuinely, observably wrong, and
sector 7 is about exactly that.

Sorting the results is not laziness; it is how you write a deterministic
assertion about a non-deterministic process. The general technique — normalise
the output so the test asserts on the set rather than the order — is what makes
concurrent code testable at all.

Left to you: whether `Task.Run` around each worker is needed. It is not: the
worker body is already async, so calling it directly starts it just as well and
saves a pool hop, exactly as in sector 1. `Task.Run` here is habit rather than
requirement.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Start by asking what could make an item processed twice, or not at all. With a
channel, neither is possible: a dequeued item is gone, and a channel that is
completed and drained has delivered everything.

Compare that with the hand-rolled alternative — a shared list plus an index and
a lock — where "exactly once" is something you must implement and can get
wrong. The channel is not just more convenient; it removes a correctness
obligation.

## Hint 2

Think about what sets the degree of parallelism here. It is the number of
worker loops, not the channel's capacity and not the thread pool.

That is worth being explicit about, because it is the knob you actually tune.
Capacity controls how far the producer may run ahead; worker count controls how
many items are being processed at once. Confusing the two leads to
"I increased the buffer and it did not get faster", which is the most common
misdiagnosis in pipeline tuning.

## Hint 3

One structural warning for real pipelines: **a worker that throws kills only
itself**, silently, unless you handle it.

```csharp
await foreach (int item in reader.ReadAllAsync())
{
    try { await HandleAsync(item); }
    catch (Exception ex) { log.LogError(ex, "item {Item} failed", item); }
}
```

Without that `try`, one bad item terminates its worker's loop. With three
workers you now have two, then one, and eventually a pipeline that appears to
be running but processes nothing — and the exceptions were on tasks nobody
awaited.

Decide deliberately: isolate per item (the loop above), or let the worker die
and have a supervisor notice via `Task.WhenAny` over the worker tasks. The
challenge in this sector requires the first.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 - propagating failure through the channel

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB06_Channels/Ex7.cs`.

- `Failures.ProduceThenFailAsync(ChannelWriter<int> writer, int goodItems, Exception error)`
  writes `goodItems` items, then completes the channel **with** `error`.
- `Failures.ConsumeAsync(ChannelReader<int> reader)` returns `"ok: <count>"`
  when the channel completed normally, `"failed: <Type> after <count>"` when it
  completed with an exception, and lets `OperationCanceledException` out
  untouched.
- The consumer must still see the good items before the failure: a faulted
  completion drains the queue first.
- `Failures.ObserveCompletion(ChannelReader<int> reader)` returns `"ok"`,
  `"faulted:<Type>"` or `"pending"` by inspecting `reader.Completion` **without**
  awaiting it.
- `Failures.HangsWithoutCompletion()` returns `true` — a producer that dies
  without completing leaves its consumer waiting for ever.

Example: 3 good items then an `IOException` gives
`"failed: IOException after 3"`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb06_channels_pipelines ex7
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

`Complete(exception)` is the whole feature. It says "no more items, and by the
way, here is why" — and readers observe the exception only after they have
drained everything already queued.

So the consumer's shape is an ordinary `ReadAllAsync` loop inside a `try`, with
the count incremented in the loop so it is still correct when the throw
arrives.

## Hint 2

```csharp
public static async Task<string> ConsumeAsync(ChannelReader<int> reader)
{
    int count = 0;
    try
    {
        await foreach (int _ in reader.ReadAllAsync().ConfigureAwait(false)) count++;
        return $"ok: {count}";
    }
    catch (OperationCanceledException) { throw; }
    catch (Exception ex) { return $"failed: {ex.GetType().Name} after {count}"; }
}
```

The cancellation clause first, for the fourth sector running. `ReadAllAsync`
rethrows whatever the writer passed to `Complete`, unwrapped — not an
`AggregateException`.

## Hint 3

`Reader.Completion` is the other half of this, and it is what a supervisor
watches. It is a `Task` that completes when the channel is finished *and*
drained, and it faults with the writer's exception.

That gives you a clean division of responsibilities in a real pipeline: the
consumer loop handles items, and `Completion` tells the code that owns the
pipeline whether it ended normally or died. A supervisor can `Task.WhenAll`
over every stage's `Completion` for "the pipeline finished", or
`Task.WhenAny` for "something broke".

Note that inspecting `Completion` without awaiting is the sector-4 status
pattern again: check `IsCompletedSuccessfully`, `IsFaulted`, and read
`Exception?.InnerException` only after establishing it is faulted.

Left to you: whether a consumer should catch at all. In a pipeline where the
supervisor watches `Completion`, a consumer that swallows the failure has
hidden it from the supervisor. Returning a description is right for this
exercise; in production, letting it propagate and reporting once, centrally, is
usually better than reporting in every stage.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Compare the three ways a producer can stop and what each does to the consumer:

1. **`Complete()`** — consumer drains, loop ends, everything is fine.
2. **`Complete(ex)`** — consumer drains, then sees `ex`. It knows what
   happened.
3. **Nothing** — consumer waits for ever. Shutdown hangs. The original
   exception is on an unobserved task.

Only two of those are acceptable, and the third is what you get by default from
a producer that throws outside a `finally`.

## Hint 2

A subtlety worth checking in your own implementation: does the consumer see the
good items *before* the exception, or does the exception arrive immediately?

It drains first. `Complete(ex)` marks the channel as finished-with-error, but
the queued items are still there and `ReadAllAsync` yields every one of them
before throwing. That is deliberate and it matters: a producer that fails after
writing 10,000 items has not invalidated those items, and a consumer that
discards them because of a failure at the end is losing work unnecessarily.

If you *want* fail-fast semantics instead, that is a separate mechanism —
cancel the consumer's token rather than faulting the channel.

## Hint 3

The one-line rule from this exercise, worth carrying into every pipeline you
build: **a producer's `finally` must complete the channel, and its `catch` must
complete it with the exception.**

```csharp
try { ... }
catch (Exception ex) { writer.TryComplete(ex); throw; }
finally { writer.TryComplete(); }
```

`TryComplete` in both places, because the `catch` may have already completed
it. Four lines, and they convert every hang in this sector into a logged error
with a stack trace. Hand-rolled queues almost never have them, which is why
hand-rolled pipelines fail as "the service stopped responding" instead of "the
database refused the connection".

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 - two stages, two capacities

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB06_Channels/Ex8.cs`. A pipeline is stages, each with its
own bound.

```csharp
public static Task<List<string>> RunAsync(
    IEnumerable<string> input,
    int parseCapacity,
    int formatCapacity,
    CancellationToken token);
```

- Stage 1 reads `input`, parses each entry to an `int` with `int.TryParse`, and
  writes successes into a bounded channel of `parseCapacity`. Unparseable
  entries are counted, not written.
- Stage 2 reads that channel, formats each value as `$"#{value}"`, and writes
  into a second bounded channel of `formatCapacity`.
- The caller collects stage 2's output into a list, in order.
- Each stage completes its own output channel exactly once, in a `finally`, and
  a failure in either stage faults the downstream channel.
- Cancellation reaches both stages: one token, forwarded everywhere.
- `Stages.Skipped` counts unparseable entries; `Stages.Stage1`/`Stages.Stage2`
  count items each stage emitted.

Example: `["1", "x", "2"]` produces `["#1", "#2"]` with `Skipped` 1.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb06_channels_pipelines ex8
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Write one helper and use it twice. Both stages have the same shape: read from
something, transform, write to a channel, complete the writer in a `finally`.

The only differences are the transform and whether the input is an
`IEnumerable<T>` or a `ChannelReader<T>`.

## Hint 2

```csharp
static async Task PumpAsync<TIn, TOut>(
    IAsyncEnumerable<TIn> source,
    ChannelWriter<TOut> output,
    Func<TIn, (bool Keep, TOut Value)> transform,
    CancellationToken token)
{
    try
    {
        await foreach (TIn item in source.WithCancellation(token).ConfigureAwait(false))
        {
            (bool keep, TOut value) = transform(item);
            if (keep) await output.WriteAsync(value, token).ConfigureAwait(false);
        }
    }
    catch (Exception ex) { output.TryComplete(ex); throw; }
    finally { output.TryComplete(); }
}
```

`reader.ReadAllAsync(token)` gives you the `IAsyncEnumerable<T>` for stage 2,
which is sector 5's adapter earning its keep.

## Hint 3

The two capacities are the point, so choose them meaningfully rather than
copying one number.

`parseCapacity` is how far the parser may run ahead of the formatter;
`formatCapacity` is how far the formatter may run ahead of the collector. Each
one is a separate latency-versus-smoothing decision, and having them separate
is precisely what makes a staged pipeline tunable: if the formatter is the
bottleneck, its *input* queue will sit full, which tells you which stage to
scale.

That observability is worth designing for. A single fused loop has one implicit
buffer of size zero and tells you nothing about where the time went.

Left to you: whether to run the stages with `Task.Run` or just call them. Call
them — they are already async, and the pool hop buys nothing (sector 1). And
whether the collector should be a third stage or the caller's loop; making it
the caller's loop means the caller's speed is the final backpressure boundary,
which is usually what you want.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Draw the pipeline before writing it, with the queues explicit:

```
input --> [parse] --(cap: parseCapacity)--> [format] --(cap: formatCapacity)--> caller
```

Three participants, two queues, two completions. Every bug in staged pipelines
is a missing completion or a queue you forgot to bound, and the diagram makes
both visible.

## Hint 2

Think about what happens when stage 2 is slow. Its input channel fills, so
stage 1's `WriteAsync` starts waiting, so stage 1 stops reading `input`. The
backpressure propagates all the way to the source without a single line of code
coordinating it.

Now consider the same pipeline with unbounded channels. Stage 1 races through
the entire input, allocating as it goes, and the memory profile of your service
is now "the size of the largest input we ever see". The bound is what turns a
pipeline from a memory risk into a self-regulating system.

## Hint 3

One rule for staged pipelines that is not obvious until it bites: **each stage
completes only its own output channel, never its input.**

A stage that completes its input is telling its *upstream* to stop, which is a
signal travelling the wrong way, and it will throw
`ChannelClosedException` inside a producer that is still writing. If a
downstream stage genuinely needs to say "stop, I have had enough" — a `Take`-like
early exit — the mechanism is cancellation, not completion.

Completion flows downstream; cancellation flows upstream. Keeping those two
directions straight makes shutdown logic much easier to reason about, and it is
the same distinction as sector 5's "the consumer's `break` disposes the
producer" — a stream expresses upstream stop through disposal, a pipeline
through a token.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge - an ingest pipeline that survives bad items

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB06_Channels/Challenge.cs`. Everything the sector covers,
in one component.

```csharp
public static Task<IngestReport> RunAsync(
    IEnumerable<string> input,
    int capacity,
    int workers,
    Func<string, CancellationToken, Task<int>> handle,
    CancellationToken token);

public readonly record struct IngestReport(int Processed, int Failed, int Total);
```

Rules:

- A bounded input channel of `capacity`, and `workers` consumers reading it.
- **One bad item must not kill the pipeline**: a `handle` that throws increments
  `Failed` and the worker carries on. A worker must never die from item
  failure.
- Results go into a second channel; the caller sums them.
- No item is lost and none is processed twice.
- Exactly one completion per channel, and a producer failure faults the input
  channel so the workers stop rather than hang.
- Cancellation reaches the producer, the workers, and `handle`; a cancelled run
  throws `OperationCanceledException` rather than returning a report.
- `Processed + Failed == Total` when the run completes normally.

Example: 10 inputs, 3 workers, every third one throwing, gives
`Processed 7, Failed 3, Total 10`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb06_channels_pipelines challenge
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Failure isolation is one `try` in one place: inside the worker's loop, around
the `handle` call only. Put it around the whole loop and one bad item ends that
worker; leave it out and the worker dies with an unobserved exception.

That single placement decision is most of the challenge.

## Hint 2

```csharp
await foreach (string item in input.Reader.ReadAllAsync(token).ConfigureAwait(false))
{
    try
    {
        int value = await handle(item, token).ConfigureAwait(false);
        await results.Writer.WriteAsync(value, token).ConfigureAwait(false);
        Interlocked.Increment(ref processed);
    }
    catch (OperationCanceledException) { throw; }      // cancellation kills the worker
    catch (Exception) { Interlocked.Increment(ref failed); }
}
```

Note the two clauses and their order: cancellation must *not* be isolated —
a cancelled run should stop, not count 10,000 "failures" as it burns through
the queue.

## Hint 3

The counters need `Interlocked` because several workers touch them
concurrently. A plain `failed++` here is not a theoretical race: it is a lost
update you can observe, and it is exactly the subject of the next sector.

Three more details the gate checks.

**Exactly one completion each.** The input channel is completed by the producer
(in a `finally`); the results channel by whoever awaits all the workers. Two
different owners, one call each.

**No item lost.** `Processed + Failed == Total` is the invariant, and it holds
only if every dequeued item goes down exactly one of the two paths. An early
`continue` or a `break` on failure breaks it.

**Cancellation propagates.** The token goes into `WriteAsync`, `ReadAllAsync`
and `handle`. Missing any one of them leaves a stage that keeps working after
the caller has gone — sector 3's chain discipline, in a pipeline.

Left to you: whether failed items should be dead-lettered rather than counted.
Counting is the minimum; a real ingest pipeline writes the item and its
exception somewhere durable, because "3 failed" without the payloads is an
alert nobody can act on.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Write the invariants down first — they are what the gate asserts and what makes
the design decisions for you:

1. `Processed + Failed == Total`
2. every item is dequeued exactly once
3. every channel is completed exactly once
4. no worker terminates because of an item failure
5. a cancelled run produces an exception, not a report

Then, for each line of code you write, ask which invariant it protects. Lines
that protect none are usually the bugs.

## Hint 2

Think about the failure-isolation boundary as a policy decision rather than a
`try` placement. There are three defensible policies:

- **isolate per item** — the pipeline is resilient, bad data is counted, the
  run always completes. Right for ingest.
- **fail the batch** — the first failure faults everything and the run stops.
  Right for a transactional import where partial success is meaningless.
- **circuit break** — isolate until the failure *rate* crosses a threshold,
  then stop. Right when failures indicate a downstream outage rather than bad
  data.

The gate wants the first. Knowing that the other two exist, and which one a
given system needs, is what distinguishes a pipeline from a loop.

## Hint 3

One more production concern the exercise cannot gate: **ordering**.

With `workers > 1`, results arrive in a non-deterministic order, and this
challenge sums them so it does not matter. If the downstream *does* care about
order — a change feed, an event stream per entity — you have three choices:
one worker (giving up parallelism), partitioning by key so each key's items go
to a fixed worker (parallelism without cross-key ordering), or reassembling by
sequence number downstream (buffering, and a head-of-line blocking problem).

Partitioning is usually the answer, and it is worth recognising that it is a
*hashing* problem hiding inside a concurrency problem: `hash(key) % workers`
picks the channel, and each worker gets its own channel rather than sharing
one. That is a different topology from this exercise, and the moment somebody
says "but these must stay in order per customer", it is the one you want.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 - four hung pipelines

Edit `src/Lessons/V3CB06_Channels/Review1.cs`. Four pipelines that hang, leak
or throw. Diagnose from the symptom, then write the corrected shape.

- `Triage.Diagnose(string symptom)` maps symptom to cause, exactly:
  - `"the consumer never finishes"` → `"nobody completed the channel"`
  - `"ChannelClosedException on the second producer"` → `"completed by each producer"`
  - `"memory grows under a slow consumer"` → `"unbounded channel"`
  - `"reading after the end throws"` → `"ReadAsync on a completed channel"`
  - anything else → `"unknown"`
- `Triage.RepairedCompletion(ChannelWriter<int> writer, int count)` — completes
  in a `finally`.
- `Triage.RepairedMultiProducer(Task[] producers, ChannelWriter<int> writer)` —
  one completion, after all producers, faulting on failure.
- `Triage.RepairedBound(int capacity)` — returns a bounded channel with `Wait`.
- `Triage.RepairedDrain(ChannelReader<int> reader)` — reads to the end without
  throwing at the end, returning the count.
- `Triage.Rule()` returns exactly:
  `"bound the channel, complete it once, and let failure travel with it"`.

```
uv run dojo test csharp v3cb06_channels_pipelines review1
```
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1

Each symptom is something an operator reports before anyone opens the code, and
each maps to exactly one mistake from this sector. Do the mapping first; the
four repairs are all shapes you have already written.

The fourth is the only one that is a pure API mistake rather than a design one.

## Hint 2

`RepairedDrain` is about choosing the right read method:

```csharp
int count = 0;
await foreach (int _ in reader.ReadAllAsync().ConfigureAwait(false)) count++;
return count;
```

`ReadAllAsync` and `WaitToReadAsync` both end cleanly at the end of a completed
channel. `ReadAsync` throws `ChannelClosedException` when there is nothing left
and the channel is complete — it is for when you already know an item is there.

`TryRead` is the third option, and it is the one for "drain whatever is here
right now without waiting".

## Hint 3

The multi-producer repair is worth writing out because it is the one with a
race in it:

```csharp
try { await Task.WhenAll(producers).ConfigureAwait(false); writer.TryComplete(); }
catch (Exception ex) { writer.TryComplete(ex); }
```

`WhenAll` rather than a loop of awaits, so that one producer failing does not
leave the others writing into a channel you are about to close.
`TryComplete` rather than `Complete`, so a shutdown path that also completes is
harmless. And the `catch` completing *with* the exception, so the consumer
learns why rather than merely learning that it is over.

Left to you: whether the consumer should be given `reader.Completion` to
observe as well. In a supervised pipeline, yes — the consumer handles items and
the supervisor handles outcomes, and mixing those two responsibilities is how
you end up with error handling in five places and reporting in none.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1

Turn each symptom into the test that would have caught it:

1. run the pipeline with a producer that throws, assert the consumer finishes
2. run with three producers, assert no exception and a full result
3. run with a fast producer and a slow consumer, assert queue depth stays
   bounded
4. drain a completed channel, assert no exception

Four tests, none longer than five lines, and each catches a bug that otherwise
shows up as a hang in production at 4am.

## Hint 2

A useful review heuristic for any channel code, in the order the problems
appear:

- Is the channel bounded? If not, why not?
- Is there exactly one `Complete`, and is it in a `finally`?
- Does a producer failure reach the consumer?
- Does the token reach both ends?
- Under a dropping `FullMode`, is anything counting the drops?

Five questions, and they find essentially every channel bug. Write them on the
pull-request template if your team builds pipelines.

## Hint 3

The `Rule()` string is the sector in one line: **bound the channel, complete it
once, and let failure travel with it.**

Bounding is what keeps memory finite and makes overload visible as latency
rather than as a heap dump. Completing exactly once is what lets consumers
terminate without sentinels or counts. And letting failure travel — through
`Complete(exception)` — is what turns a hang into a diagnosis.

Every mistake in this sector is a violation of one of the three, and every
pipeline that has ever woken you up violated at least one. The next sector
moves inside the queue, to the shared state that channels have been protecting
you from all along.

lessons.title: V3·CB6 — Channels and producer/consumer pipelines
lessons.summary: A Channel is an async queue with a bound, and the bound is the point: it is where backpressure lives. This sector covers the writer and reader protocols, BoundedChannelFullMode, completing exactly once, error propagation, fan-out worker pools, and the pipelines you build from them.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·CB6 — Channels and producer/consumer pipelines

The previous sector ended at a wall. An async stream is strictly sequential:
one producer, one consumer, in lockstep, with no buffer between them. The
moment you want the producer running ahead, several items in flight, two
sources merged, or a pool of workers, you need something with a queue in it.

`System.Threading.Channels` is that something. A `Channel<T>` is a queue where
both ends are asynchronous: writers await space, readers await items, and
nobody blocks a thread waiting. That last clause is the whole reason it exists
rather than `BlockingCollection<T>`, which does the same job by parking a
thread per waiting participant — fine for a handful of dedicated threads,
catastrophic on a server where those threads come from the pool that is also
serving requests.

**The bound is the feature.** An unbounded channel is a queue that grows until
the process dies; it converts "my consumer is slower than my producer" from a
visible stall into an invisible memory leak that kills you an hour later, far
from the cause. A bounded channel makes the mismatch immediate and local: the
producer's `WriteAsync` simply does not complete until there is room.

```csharp
var channel = Channel.CreateBounded<Work>(new BoundedChannelOptions(100)
{
    FullMode = BoundedChannelFullMode.Wait,   // the default, and usually right
    SingleReader = false,
    SingleWriter = false,
});
```

That is backpressure, and it is worth being precise about what it buys: the
slowest stage in your pipeline sets the pace for every stage upstream, memory
stays bounded by construction, and the failure mode of overload is latency
rather than an `OutOfMemoryException`. `FullMode` is where you decide what
"full" means — wait, drop the oldest, drop the newest, or refuse the write.
Telemetry usually wants `DropOldest`; a work queue almost always wants `Wait`.

**Two protocols, each with a shape worth memorising.** The reader's is easy:

```csharp
await foreach (Work item in channel.Reader.ReadAllAsync(token))
    await HandleAsync(item);
```

That loop ends when the writer completes the channel — not on a sentinel value,
not on a flag. The writer's is the one people get wrong:

```csharp
while (await writer.WaitToWriteAsync(token))
    while (writer.TryWrite(next()))
        if (done) { writer.Complete(); return; }
```

`WaitToWriteAsync` returns `false` when the channel is closed; `TryWrite`
returns `false` when it is momentarily full. Using `WriteAsync` in a loop is
simpler and slightly slower; using `TryWrite` alone is a spin.

**Completion is a contract, and it belongs to the writer.** `Complete()` says
"no more items will ever be written". Readers then drain what is left and their
`ReadAllAsync` loop ends. Two failure modes bracket this: never completing —
the consumer waits for ever and your pipeline hangs on shutdown — and
completing twice, or from the wrong side, which throws. With several producers
the correct shape is `Task.WhenAll(producers)` followed by exactly one
`Complete()`.

**Failure travels through the channel.** `Complete(exception)` completes the
channel *faulted*: readers observe the exception when they reach the end, so a
producer that dies does not leave its consumer waiting for items that will
never come. This is the piece hand-rolled queues almost always miss, and it
turns "the service hung" into "the service logged the real error".

**And a channel is one hop, not a system.** Real pipelines are stages: parse →
enrich → write, each with its own channel, its own bound, and its own worker
count. That structure is worth building deliberately, because it makes each
stage's capacity an explicit number you can tune rather than an emergent
property of how fast the code happens to run.

**The trilemma worth memorising.** You may have any two of: the producer never
waits, no data is ever dropped, memory stays bounded. Unbounded gives you the
first two and unbounded memory. `Wait` gives you the last two and a throttled
producer. The dropping modes give you the first and last, silently. There is no
fourth option, and every argument about queue configuration is really an
argument about which of those three you are giving up. Say which one out loud
and the discussion finishes in a minute.

**Choosing the capacity is a latency decision.** People treat it as a memory
knob and then wonder why raising it did not help. Capacity is how far the
producer may run ahead, which means an item entering a full queue of 10,000
waits for 10,000 items to be processed before anyone looks at it. Capacity 1 is
nearly lockstep with no smoothing at all; the tens-to-low-hundreds range is
where most work pipelines belong. The honest method: decide the longest an item
may sit unprocessed, divide by your per-item processing time, and use that.

**And the flags are promises, not requests.** `SingleReader = true` and
`SingleWriter = true` let the implementation pick faster internal structures, on
the understanding that you have guaranteed the topology. Violate one and you get
corruption rather than an exception — nothing checks.
`AllowSynchronousContinuations = true` lets a write run a waiting reader's
continuation inline, which is sector 1's hijacking made opt-in, with the same
advice: leave it off unless a profile says otherwise.

Every gate here is deterministic: bounds are small, completion is explicit, and
nothing depends on timing.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - csharp/v3cb06_channels_pipelines

## Notes

**`Channel<T>` is a factory plus two halves.** `Channel.CreateUnbounded<T>()`
and `Channel.CreateBounded<T>(capacity)` return a `Channel<T>` exposing
`Reader` and `Writer`. Hand each half to the code that needs it — a producer
should receive a `ChannelWriter<T>`, not the whole channel, because then it
cannot read and cannot be tempted to.

**The options flags are real optimisations with real preconditions.**
`SingleReader = true` and `SingleWriter = true` let the implementation select
faster internal structures, and they are *promises*, not requests: violate them
and you get corruption, not an exception. `AllowSynchronousContinuations = true`
lets a completing write run a waiting reader's continuation inline — sector 1's
hijacking, opt-in, and the same advice applies: leave it off unless you have
measured a reason.

**`FullMode` decides the semantics of overload.** `Wait` (default) applies
backpressure. `DropOldest` keeps the newest N — the right answer for
telemetry, position updates, anything where stale data is worthless.
`DropNewest` keeps the oldest. `DropWrite` discards the incoming item. The
three dropping modes make `WriteAsync` always complete immediately, and
`TryWrite` always return `true`, which means **you cannot tell that data was
dropped** unless you count it yourself.

**`ReadAsync` on a completed empty channel throws `ChannelClosedException`.**
`ReadAllAsync` and `WaitToReadAsync` do not — they return cleanly. Prefer them;
reach for `ReadAsync` only when you already know an item is there.

**`Reader.Completion`** is a `Task` that completes when the channel is finished
and drained. It faults if the writer completed with an exception, which is how
a supervisor learns that a producer died.

**Cancellation applies to the wait, not the queue.** A cancelled
`ReadAsync(token)` stops your read; items already in the channel stay there.
Draining on shutdown therefore means completing the writer and reading to the
end *without* the stop token, on a separate budget — sector 3's rule about
cleanup not using the stopping token, in a new costume.

**Channels versus TPL Dataflow.** Dataflow gives you blocks, linking,
propagation and a lot of machinery; channels give you a queue. For most
pipelines the queue plus explicit `Task`s is easier to read and to debug.
Dataflow still wins when you want its declarative graph, batching blocks and
built-in parallelism knobs.

## ex1

The first pipeline is deliberately minimal so the termination condition stands
out. The consumer's loop ends because the writer called `Complete()`, and for
no other reason. Sentinel values (`null`, `-1`, a special record) are what
people invent when they have not met `Complete`, and they fail the moment the
sentinel is a legal value.

Note the shape of the producer's `finally`: completing in a `finally` means a
producer that throws still terminates its consumer, rather than leaving it
waiting for ever. That single habit prevents most channel hangs.

## ex2

Backpressure is easiest to believe when you have measured it. With a capacity
of two and a consumer that reads on demand, the producer can be at most two
items ahead — the assertion is exact, not statistical, because `WriteAsync`
does not complete until there is space.

That is also the tuning knob: capacity is how much the producer may run ahead,
which is how much latency you are willing to trade for smoothing. Capacity 1 is
nearly lockstep; capacity 10,000 is a memory decision disguised as a
performance one.

## ex3

The `WaitToWriteAsync`/`TryWrite` loop exists because `WriteAsync` allocates a
`ValueTask` per item and, on a hot path, that adds up. The double-loop shape —
wait once, then write as many as you can — amortises the wait across a burst.

The trap is treating `TryWrite`'s `false` as an error. It means "full right
now"; the correct response is to go back to `WaitToWriteAsync`, not to spin,
not to sleep, and not to throw. `WaitToWriteAsync` returning `false` is the
real terminal condition: the channel is closed.

## ex4

The dropping modes are the ones that silently change your program's meaning.
With `DropOldest`, `TryWrite` always succeeds and always returns `true`, so a
naive counter records "wrote 1,000,000" while the reader saw 4,000. Counting
drops means counting on your side: compare what you wrote with what was read,
or track the reader's count against the writer's.

Choose `DropOldest` when the newest value supersedes the old (a price, a
position, a gauge) and `Wait` when every item matters (a job, a payment, a log
line you promised to persist).

## ex5 - ex8

The multi-producer completion in ex5 is the sector's sharpest rule: completion
is a statement about the whole set, so it belongs to the joiner, never to a
participant. Each producer completing when it finishes gives you either a
truncated pipeline (the first one closed the channel while others were still
writing) or a `ChannelClosedException` thrown inside a task nobody awaits —
non-deterministic data loss plus a delayed, unrelated-looking exception. One
line in the wrong place.

The worker pool in ex6 makes a quieter point: the channel gives you
"exactly-once delivery to one worker" as a property of the queue, not as
something you implement. Compare the hand-rolled alternative — a shared list,
an index and a lock — where exactly-once is a correctness obligation you can
get wrong. Note also which knob sets parallelism: the number of worker loops,
not the capacity. "I increased the buffer and it did not get faster" is the
most common pipeline misdiagnosis there is.

Ex7's `Complete(exception)` is what separates a diagnosis from a hang, and its
draining behaviour is deliberate: queued items are delivered *before* the
failure surfaces, because a producer dying after 10,000 successful items has
not invalidated those items. Fail-fast is a different mechanism — cancel the
consumer's token instead.

Ex8's two capacities exist to be tuned separately. When the formatter is the
bottleneck, its input queue sits full, and that is your instrumentation telling
you which stage to scale. A single fused loop has one implicit buffer of size
zero and tells you nothing.

## Further reading

- [An Introduction to System.Threading.Channels](https://devblogs.microsoft.com/dotnet/an-introduction-to-system-threading-channels/) — Stephen Toub's introduction, and still the best one.
- [`Channel`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.channels.channel) — the factory methods and both option types.
- [`BoundedChannelFullMode`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.channels.boundedchannelfullmode) — the four overload behaviours.
- [`ChannelWriter<T>.Complete`](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/api/system.threading.channels.channelwriter-1.complete) — including the faulting overload.
- [TPL Dataflow](https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/parallel-programming/dataflow-task-parallel-library) — the alternative, for when you want the graph.

# V3·CB6 — Channels and producer/consumer pipelines

A channel is an async queue with a bound. Everything interesting follows from
those two words.

## Concept 1 — creating one

```csharp
Channel<int> unbounded = Channel.CreateUnbounded<int>();     // grows for ever

Channel<int> bounded = Channel.CreateBounded<int>(new BoundedChannelOptions(100)
{
    FullMode = BoundedChannelFullMode.Wait,
    SingleReader = true,      // a promise, not a request
    SingleWriter = false,
    AllowSynchronousContinuations = false,
});
```

Hand `channel.Writer` to producers and `channel.Reader` to consumers. Neither
should hold the whole `Channel<T>`.

## Concept 2 — the reader protocol

```csharp
await foreach (int item in channel.Reader.ReadAllAsync(token))
    await HandleAsync(item);
// falls out of the loop when the writer completes and the queue drains
```

The lower-level form, when you need to batch or peek:

```csharp
while (await reader.WaitToReadAsync(token))
    while (reader.TryRead(out int item))
        Handle(item);
```

`ReadAsync` on a completed, empty channel throws `ChannelClosedException`. The
two forms above do not.

## Concept 3 — the writer protocol

```csharp
// simple
foreach (int item in source)
    await writer.WriteAsync(item, token);
writer.Complete();

// hot path: amortise the wait across a burst
while (await writer.WaitToWriteAsync(token))
{
    while (source.MoveNext() && writer.TryWrite(source.Current)) { }
    if (source.Done) { writer.Complete(); break; }
}
```

`TryWrite` returning `false` means "full right now" — go back to
`WaitToWriteAsync`. `WaitToWriteAsync` returning `false` means "closed".

## Concept 4 — completion, exactly once

```csharp
Task[] producers = [.. sources.Select(s => ProduceAsync(s, writer, token))];
try { await Task.WhenAll(producers); writer.Complete(); }
catch (Exception ex) { writer.Complete(ex); }     // readers see the failure
```

Never completing hangs the consumer. Completing twice throws. Completing from
the reader side is a design error. One writer-side `Complete`, in a `finally`
or a `catch`, always.

## Concept 5 — full-mode semantics

| mode | on full | can you tell? |
|---|---|---|
| `Wait` | writer waits | yes: latency |
| `DropOldest` | evicts the oldest | no: count it yourself |
| `DropNewest` | evicts the newest queued | no |
| `DropWrite` | discards the incoming item | no |

The dropping modes make `WriteAsync` complete instantly and `TryWrite` always
return `true`. Silent data loss is the price of never blocking.

## Concept 6 — a worker pool

```csharp
Task[] workers = [.. Enumerable.Range(0, 4).Select(async _ =>
{
    await foreach (Work w in reader.ReadAllAsync(token))
        await HandleAsync(w, token);
})];

await Task.WhenAll(workers);
```

Four consumers on one channel: the channel is thread-safe, each item goes to
exactly one worker, and the degree of parallelism is a number you chose rather
than one that emerged.

## Concept 7 — stages

```csharp
Channel<Raw> parsed = Channel.CreateBounded<Raw>(1000);
Channel<Row> enriched = Channel.CreateBounded<Row>(100);

Task stage1 = PumpAsync(input, parsed.Writer, Parse, token);
Task stage2 = PumpAsync(parsed.Reader, enriched.Writer, Enrich, token);
Task stage3 = ConsumeAsync(enriched.Reader, Write, token);
```

Each stage has its own capacity, so each backpressure boundary is an explicit
number you can tune.

## Worked example — the trilemma, in code

```csharp
// never waits, never drops, unbounded memory
Channel.CreateUnbounded<T>();

// never drops, bounded memory, producer waits
Channel.CreateBounded<T>(new BoundedChannelOptions(100)
    { FullMode = BoundedChannelFullMode.Wait });

// never waits, bounded memory, drops silently
Channel.CreateBounded<T>(new BoundedChannelOptions(100)
    { FullMode = BoundedChannelFullMode.DropOldest });
```

Any two of "never waits", "never drops", "bounded memory". There is no fourth
line. Choosing unbounded is choosing to fail later and less legibly; choosing a
dropping mode is choosing to lose data you will not be told about.

## Worked example — the producer template

```csharp
static async Task ProduceAsync(ChannelWriter<T> writer, IEnumerable<T> source,
    CancellationToken token)
{
    try
    {
        foreach (T item in source)
            await writer.WriteAsync(item, token).ConfigureAwait(false);
    }
    catch (Exception ex)
    {
        writer.TryComplete(ex);      // the consumer learns why, instead of waiting
        throw;
    }
    finally
    {
        writer.TryComplete();        // no-op if the catch already completed it
    }
}
```

Those four lines convert every hang in this sector into a logged error with a
stack trace. `TryComplete` in both places because a pipeline has more than one
plausible exit and completion is a race between them — the same reasoning as
`TrySetResult` in sector 1.

## Worked example — counting what a dropping channel discards

```csharp
Channel<Metric> sink = Channel.CreateBounded<Metric>(
    new BoundedChannelOptions(1000) { FullMode = BoundedChannelFullMode.DropOldest });

sink.Writer.TryWrite(metric);        // always true, even when it just evicted one
```

Write a million items into a capacity-1000 `DropOldest` channel and your
writer's success count says a million. The reader saw a few thousand. Nothing
in the API will ever tell you, so a dropping channel needs a dropped counter
next to it, computed as written-minus-read. A telemetry pipeline without one
reports healthy while discarding most of its data — and it does so in exactly
the metrics you would use to notice.

## Common mistakes

1. **Unbounded by default.** A memory leak with extra steps.
2. **Never completing.** The consumer waits for ever; shutdown hangs.
3. **Completing twice, or from the reader.** Throws.
4. **A sentinel value instead of `Complete()`.** Breaks when the sentinel is
   legal data.
5. **Treating `TryWrite == false` as an error.** It means "full now".
6. **`ReadAsync` on a completed channel.** `ChannelClosedException`.
7. **Setting `SingleReader`/`SingleWriter` optimistically.** They are promises;
   violating them corrupts.
8. **Not counting drops** under a dropping `FullMode`.
9. **Draining with the stop token.** Cancels the drain you were trying to do.

## Interview angle

> "How would you build a producer/consumer pipeline in .NET?"

A bounded `Channel<T>`. Producers `await writer.WriteAsync(item, token)`;
consumers `await foreach (var item in reader.ReadAllAsync(token))`. The bound
is the important part — it is where backpressure lives, so a slow consumer
slows the producer instead of growing a queue until the process dies. Exactly
one side completes the channel, on the writer side, in a `finally`, and
`Complete(exception)` propagates a producer failure to the consumer instead of
leaving it waiting. For parallelism, run N consumers on the same reader; for
stages, chain channels with their own capacities. `BlockingCollection<T>` does
the same job but blocks a thread per waiting participant, which on a server
means starving the pool that serves requests.

Follow-ups: what `BoundedChannelFullMode` options mean and when you would drop;
what `SingleReader` actually promises; and how you would shut the pipeline down
cleanly.

## Check yourself

1. Why is an unbounded channel usually the wrong default?
2. What ends a `ReadAllAsync` loop?
3. What does `TryWrite` returning `false` mean, and what should you do?
4. What does `WaitToWriteAsync` returning `false` mean?
5. Who is allowed to call `Complete()`, and how many times?
6. How do you tell a consumer that a producer failed?
7. What are the four `BoundedChannelFullMode` values and when is each right?
8. Under `DropOldest`, how do you know how much was dropped?
9. What exactly does `SingleReader = true` promise?
10. What does `AllowSynchronousContinuations` change, and what is the risk?
11. What does `Reader.Completion` tell you?
12. Sketch a two-stage pipeline with independent capacities.
13. How do you drain a channel during graceful shutdown?
14. When would you use TPL Dataflow instead?

# Reading - csharp/v3cb06_channels_pipelines

## Why a new type

.NET already had queues. `Queue<T>` is not thread-safe.
`ConcurrentQueue<T>` is thread-safe but has no way to *wait* for an item —
consumers poll, which either burns CPU or adds latency.
`BlockingCollection<T>` adds waiting, but it does so by blocking a thread, and
it was designed in 2010 when "a thread per consumer" was a normal shape.

On a modern server that shape is the problem. A blocked thread-pool thread is a
thread not serving requests, and a pipeline with sixteen blocked consumers has
quietly removed sixteen threads from the pool that its own web layer depends
on. Under load the pool grows — slowly, by design, roughly one thread per
second — and the symptom is a service that gets *worse* as it gets busier, in a
way that looks nothing like the actual cause.

`System.Threading.Channels`, shipped in .NET Core 3.0, is the queue rewritten
for `await`: waiting suspends a state machine instead of a thread, so a
pipeline with sixteen idle consumers uses zero threads. It also chose to make
bounding a first-class, deliberate decision rather than an option nobody sets.

## The bound, and why it is a design decision rather than a tuning knob

An unbounded queue does not remove the mismatch between producer and consumer;
it hides it. Items accumulate, memory grows, the GC works harder, latency
climbs because every item now waits behind a longer queue, and eventually the
process dies — at a moment unrelated to the code that caused it.

A bound converts that into something local and observable. The producer's
`WriteAsync` takes longer; the queue depth sits at its maximum; the pipeline
runs at the speed of its slowest stage, which is the speed it was always going
to run at. Nothing has been lost except the illusion.

Choosing the number is a latency-versus-smoothing trade. Capacity 1 is nearly
lockstep — minimum memory, minimum smoothing, and any jitter in the consumer
immediately stalls the producer. Large capacities absorb bursts but add queue
latency: an item entering a full 10,000-slot queue waits for 10,000 items to be
processed before it is seen. For most work pipelines a bound in the tens to low
hundreds is right, and the honest way to pick it is to ask how long you are
willing for an item to sit.

The dropping modes change the question entirely. `DropOldest` says the newest
value supersedes the old, which is exactly right for a gauge, a price tick, a
position update, a progress report — and exactly wrong for a job queue. The
critical property to remember is that dropping is *silent*: `TryWrite` returns
`true`, `WriteAsync` completes immediately, and unless you count both ends you
will never know it happened. Every telemetry channel should have a dropped
counter next to it.

## Completion, and the two ways pipelines hang

`Complete()` is the only thing that ends a consumer's loop, which makes it the
single most important call in the pipeline and the one most often forgotten.

The first hang: nobody completes. The consumer's `ReadAllAsync` waits for an
item that will never arrive, the shutdown path waits for the consumer, and the
process sits there until something kills it. This is why `Complete()` belongs
in a `finally` — a producer that throws must still terminate its consumer.

The second hang is subtler: **several producers, one completion**. Each
producer finishing does not mean the channel is finished, so the completion has
to happen after all of them. The shape is `await Task.WhenAll(producers)` and
then one `Complete()`. Getting it wrong in the other direction — each producer
calling `Complete()` — throws `ChannelClosedException` on the second call, and
worse, truncates the pipeline the first time.

`Complete(exception)` is the piece that turns a hang into a diagnosis. A
producer that dies mid-stream completes the channel faulted; the consumer's
`ReadAllAsync` throws that exception when it reaches the end of the buffered
items; the supervisor logs the real error. Hand-rolled queues almost never do
this, which is why hand-rolled pipelines fail as "the service stopped
responding" rather than "the database connection was refused".

## Performance notes

A channel write and read is on the order of tens of nanoseconds when the
channel is neither empty nor full — a lock-free path in the unbounded case, a
short lock in the bounded one. That is fast enough that the channel is
essentially never the bottleneck in a pipeline doing real work per item, and
slow enough to matter if you are pushing individual integers through it at
millions per second. If you are, batch: a channel of `T[]` amortises everything.

The flags earn their keep in specific shapes. `SingleReader = true` allows a
simpler internal queue and avoids some interlocked work; `SingleWriter = true`
does the same on the other end. Both are *promises* — the runtime does not
check, and violating one produces corruption rather than an exception, so set
them only where the topology is structurally guaranteed.

`AllowSynchronousContinuations = true` lets the thread that writes an item run
the waiting reader's continuation inline, saving a queue hop. It is the same
hijacking mechanism as sector 1's `TaskCompletionSource`, with the same hazard:
your producer's thread ends up executing consumer code, under whatever locks
the producer holds. Leave it off unless a profile says otherwise.

## When not to use a channel

**When there is no queue in the problem.** One producer, one consumer, no
buffering wanted — that is an `IAsyncEnumerable<T>`, and it is simpler,
lazier, and cheaper.

**When you need routing, joining, or a graph.** TPL Dataflow exists for that:
`TransformBlock`, `BatchBlock`, `BroadcastBlock`, linking with propagation, and
per-block parallelism options. Rebuilding half of Dataflow out of channels is a
common and regrettable project. The line I would draw: one or two linear
stages, channels; a graph with fan-in, fan-out and routing, Dataflow.

**When durability matters.** A channel is memory. If the process dies, the
queued items are gone. Anything that must survive a restart needs a real queue
— a database table, a message broker — and a channel in front of it at most as
an in-process buffer whose loss you can tolerate.

**When the consumer must see every item and the producer must never wait.**
Those two requirements are contradictory with a finite queue. One of them has
to give: either the producer waits (`Wait`), or you drop, or you buy unbounded
memory. Pretending otherwise by choosing unbounded is choosing to fail later
and less legibly.

Finally, a note on shutdown, because it combines this sector with sector 3.
Draining is: stop accepting new work, complete the writer, and read to the end
on a *separate* budget. Passing the stopping token into the drain cancels the
drain — the same mistake as passing it into a flush, and it will lose exactly
the items you were trying to save.
